question: A program you can chat with in plain English, like ChatGPT or Claude, is built on a 'large language model.' What's the short name for this kind of model?
answer: An LLM (Large Language Model)
choices: An LLM (Large Language Model)
A search engine for old maps
A web browser like Chrome
A spreadsheet app for cells
context: LLM stands for Large Language Model. These are programs trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word in a sequence. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all chatbots built on LLMs. Knowing the term is the first step — when you hear 'LLM,' you know what kind of system someone is talking about.

question: GPT in 'ChatGPT' is an acronym for three words. What are they?
answer: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
choices: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
Google's Public Translator system
General Purpose Telephone helper
Graphic Processing Toolkit display
context: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. 'Generative' = produces new text. 'Pre-trained' = learned from huge amounts of text before you ever used it. 'Transformer' = the network architecture, introduced in a 2017 Google paper called 'Attention Is All You Need.'

question: The 'T' in GPT stands for Transformer. Transformers are a kind of:
answer: Neural network architecture
choices: Neural network architecture
Robot from a movie series
Magic wand from a story
Brand of toaster appliance
context: In AI, 'Transformer' refers to a specific design (architecture) of neural network, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need.' It became the foundation for almost every modern chatbot — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama. The name is unrelated to the robot toys; the AI architecture came later.

question: Why is 'Pre-trained' in GPT's name important?
answer: It learns once, then just responds
choices: It learns once, then just responds
It rehearses for the singing show
It practices old guitar chords
It folds new origami cranes
context: Pre-training is a giant one-time computing job. The model studies huge amounts of text and adjusts its internal numbers (parameters). When you chat with the trained model, it's just running — not learning from your messages. Each new conversation starts fresh. This is why 'pre-trained' matters: training is past, response is present.

question: A chatbot writes 'I'm sorry to hear that' when you tell it sad news. Is it actually feeling sorry?
answer: No, those are just words it learned to produce
choices: No, those are just words it learned to produce
Yes, modern chatbots have real emotions of their own
Maybe, nobody can know for sure either way
Only if it has been running for a long time today
context: LLMs produce text by predicting which word is likely to come next. 'I'm sorry to hear that' is just a string of words it learned from human writing. Nothing is feeling anything underneath. Capability isn't the same as consciousness — a calculator can solve math without knowing what math is.

question: Which of these is the BEST tool to use when you want to look up the latest news from today?
answer: A search engine like Google
choices: A search engine like Google
A chatbot like ChatGPT
A photo app on your phone
A calculator program
context: Search engines crawl the live web. Chatbots are pattern-completion programs trained months ago and don't know what happened today (unless given a search tool). For 'what just happened,' use search. For 'help me draft something,' a chatbot can help.

question: An LLM chatbot is not a calculator. For careful arithmetic, what's the safer tool to use?
answer: A calculator app
choices: A calculator app
Two different chatbots
A voice assistant only
A guessing game
context: LLMs predict text, not numbers. They can get arithmetic wrong, especially with large numbers or many steps. For careful math, use an actual calculator or a math program. If you do use a chatbot, double-check the answer.

question: A chatbot confidently writes that a famous book has a chapter that doesn't actually exist. What's the common nickname for this?
answer: Hallucination
choices: Hallucination
Recovery
Translation
Recursion
context: When an LLM confidently invents false information, people call it 'hallucination.' It happens because the model is predicting plausible-sounding text, not looking facts up. Watch out for invented book chapters, fake quotes, made-up court cases, and wrong dates.

question: A basic chatbot has no live internet. So if you ask 'what's the weather tomorrow,' it usually:
answer: Cannot really answer with live data
choices: Cannot really answer with live data
Calls a local weather station live
Gives the perfectly correct forecast
Sends a drone to check the sky now
context: An LLM by itself has no web access — it's just a trained model. Unless given a specific 'tool' to search the web or check weather, it can only guess. Some chatbot products bolt search on as a feature, but the basic model alone has no live internet.

question: You chat with ChatGPT today and tell it your favorite color. Tomorrow you open a new chat. By default, will it remember?
answer: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
choices: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
Yes, it remembers everything you ever said
Yes, but only for the next seven days
Only if you pay an extra monthly fee
context: LLMs don't remember between separate conversations by default. Each new chat starts blank. Some chat products bolt on a 'memory' feature that stores notes between sessions, but the underlying model itself has no built-in memory of you.

question: Every chatbot was trained on text up to a certain date and has no information from later. What's this date called?
answer: The training cutoff
choices: The training cutoff
The expiration date
The opening line
The starter pack
context: Each model has a training cutoff — the date when training data collection stopped. The model has no information about events after that point. If you ask about something that happened last week, it either guesses or says it doesn't have that information. Many chatbots will report their cutoff if you ask.

question: AI chatbots run on something called a 'neural network.' The name comes from a loose comparison to:
answer: Cells in animal brains
choices: Cells in animal brains
Cables in a power grid
Stars in a galaxy
Roads in a city
context: Neural networks are layers of simple math units, loosely inspired by how brain cells (neurons) pass signals. They are NOT literal brains — they're math. The biology comparison is mostly historical naming; underneath, it's all numbers and equations.

question: An LLM has billions of small numbers inside that get adjusted during training. What are those numbers usually called?
answer: Parameters
choices: Parameters
Passwords
Pictures
Pages
context: Parameters are the adjustable numbers (weights and biases) inside a model. GPT-3 had 175 billion of them. Training is the process of slowly tuning these numbers so the model produces better outputs. Bigger models often have more parameters — but bigger doesn't always mean better.

question: There are two big stages for an AI model: first it learns from data, then it answers your questions. What's the first stage called?
answer: Training
choices: Training
Sleeping
Selling
Stopping
context: Training is the stage where the model adjusts its parameters by studying huge amounts of data. It's done once, in a giant computing job. The second stage — when you actually ask it questions — is called 'inference.' Training is expensive; inference is what you use every time you chat.

question: Some AI MAKES new things — text, images, music. Other AI just SORTS existing things into categories. What's the made-new-things kind called?
answer: Generative AI
choices: Generative AI
Stored AI
Frozen AI
Sleeping AI
context: Generative AI produces new outputs — text, images, audio, video. ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion are generative. Other AI just classifies — 'is this email spam?' — without producing anything new. The 2022 ChatGPT moment was about generative AI going mainstream.

question: When a chatbot reads or writes text, it doesn't process whole words — it processes small pieces called:
answer: Tokens
choices: Tokens
Pixels
Folders
Pages
context: LLMs work with 'tokens,' which are subword pieces. 'Unbelievable' might be split into 'un,' 'believ,' and 'able.' This is why models sometimes spell words strangely or miscount letters — they aren't really seeing letters, they're seeing token chunks.

question: A chatbot can only 'see' so much of your conversation at once before older parts get forgotten. The limit on how much it can see is called the:
answer: Context window
choices: Context window
Quiet zone
Login screen
Hot key
context: The context window is the maximum chunk of text the model can consider in one go — usually measured in tokens. Modern chatbots have large windows but they aren't infinite. If a conversation gets very long, the model may lose track of what was said earlier.

question: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok are all examples of which general kind of AI?
answer: Chatbot assistants
choices: Chatbot assistants
Music players
Photo editors
Video games
context: Chatbot assistants are programs you can have a back-and-forth conversation with in plain language. ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and Grok (xAI) are the main ones from major US labs. They're all built on different underlying LLMs.

question: DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and Midjourney all do the same general thing. What is it?
answer: Generate images from text descriptions
choices: Generate images from text descriptions
Translate spoken English to French
Fix broken phone batteries
Block spam in your email
context: These are image generators — you type a description ('a knight riding a robot horse') and the AI produces a picture. DALL-E is from OpenAI, Stable Diffusion is open-source, Midjourney is a separate company. They've made image-faking far easier than before, which is why image-verification skills matter.

question: When you talk to Siri or Alexa, the AI first has to do one big job before anything else. What is it?
answer: Turn your speech into text
choices: Turn your speech into text
Charge its battery
Find your photos
Update its software
context: Voice assistants use speech-recognition AI to turn your spoken words into text. Then a separate system handles the request. Whisper (OpenAI), Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant all do this. The technology has gotten very good — but it also means the microphone has to be listening.

question: Programmers can use AI tools that help write computer code. GitHub Copilot is a famous one. What does it mainly do?
answer: Suggest code as you type
choices: Suggest code as you type
Power the office lights
Run your printer
Order new keyboards
context: Code-assistant tools (Copilot, Cursor, others) read what a programmer is writing and suggest the next lines. They speed up routine work, but they can also suggest buggy or insecure code. The programmer still has to read and check what's offered.

question: YouTube's 'Up Next' video, TikTok's For You feed, and Netflix's home page all use AI to pick what to show you. Together these are called:
answer: Recommendation systems
choices: Recommendation systems
Calendar reminders
Voice assistants
Spell checkers
context: Recommendation systems use AI to decide what content to put in front of you. They're trained on what you (and people like you) clicked on, watched, or shared. They're usually optimized for engagement — keeping you on the app — not for accuracy or your wellbeing.

question: Some AI models can be downloaded by anyone and run on a regular computer. Llama (from Meta) and Mistral are examples. What's this kind of model called?
answer: Open-source / open-weight models
choices: Open-source / open-weight models
Sealed-source models
Hidden-only models
Pay-by-minute models
context: Open-weight models have their weights (the trained numbers) freely available. Anyone can download them, run them on their own computer, study them, or build on them. Llama (Meta), Mistral, DeepSeek, and Qwen are major examples. Closed models like GPT-4 or Claude are only available through their company's website or API.

question: A chatbot writes you an essay draft. Whose job is it to fact-check the claims before turning it in?
answer: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
choices: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
The chatbot's — it knows facts
Nobody's — drafts don't need checking
Your friend's — chatbots are infallible
context: Even when an LLM writes well, it can confidently include false claims, made-up dates, and invented quotes. The user is responsible for checking. Treat AI output as a draft from a clever friend who sometimes makes things up — useful, but never the final word.

question: An AI tells you a fact that sounds important. What's the safe habit to build BEFORE you share it with others?
answer: Verify it against a trusted source first
choices: Verify it against a trusted source first
Send it to ten friends fast
Memorize it word for word
Trust it because chatbots are smart
context: AI 'trust but verify' is even more important than human 'trust but verify.' Chatbots produce fluent, confident-sounding text whether or not it's true. Get into the habit of checking specific claims — especially names, dates, statistics, and quotes — in a trusted source before you pass them on.

question: A chatbot tells you something completely wrong but sounds totally sure. What's important to remember about how LLMs work?
answer: They can be confidently wrong
choices: They can be confidently wrong
They never make mistakes
They feel guilt when wrong
They warn you of all errors
context: LLMs don't 'know' when they're wrong. They generate plausible-sounding text. A wrong answer often sounds just as confident as a right one. The fluency of the writing is no clue at all to its accuracy. This is the most important habit-shifting fact about LLMs.

question: Some chatbot output has telltale signs — overuse of em-dashes, phrases like 'delve into' or 'tapestry of.' What general skill does noticing those build?
answer: Spotting AI-written text
choices: Spotting AI-written text
Spotting fake medicines
Spotting good handwriting
Spotting bird species
context: AI-generated text has subtle patterns: certain favored phrases, overuse of em-dashes, repetitive sentence structures. Spotting these is a useful skill — it tells you when something was likely written by AI rather than a person. The skill is recognition, not condemnation.

question: Many AI-generated images have a giveaway: hands sometimes have the wrong number of fingers. What general lesson does this teach?
answer: Even modern AI images often have flaws
choices: Even modern AI images often have flaws
Hands are always perfect in AI art
AI never makes images of hands
Photos always show six fingers
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce images with characteristic flaws: wrong finger counts, garbled text, jewelry blending into skin, asymmetric eye details. Learning to spot these flaws is a useful defense skill — you can tell a fake from a photo more often than you might think.

question: A 'deepfake' is a video AI-altered to make someone appear to speak. What's the right first move when you see a shocking clip?
answer: Pause and check before believing it
choices: Pause and check before believing it
Share it right away to your friends
Trust it because the face looks real
Save it as true and tell everyone
context: Deepfakes can put words in real people's mouths. Telltales: mouth-sync drifts, weird blinking, edge fuzziness around the face, voice mismatches. But the safest habit is broader — before you believe or share a shocking clip, check whether trustworthy news sources are reporting it.

question: You're shown text and asked: human-written or chatbot-written? What's the single most useful thing to know about how to tell?
answer: Look for AI's typical phrases and structure
choices: Look for AI's typical phrases and structure
Count how long it took to write
Smell the paper it was printed on
Ask what zodiac sign it has
context: AI text often has telltale rhythms: certain favorite phrases ('delve into,' 'tapestry of'), repetitive sentence structures, overuse of em-dashes, an over-balanced tone. Real people write more roughly, with stronger opinions and stranger phrasings. Reading lots of AI output and lots of human writing builds the eye.

question: A general chatbot is sometimes adjusted to be especially good at one job — say, helping with cooking questions. The extra adjusting is called:
answer: Fine-tuning
choices: Fine-tuning
Spell-checking
Streaming
Reblogging
context: Fine-tuning means taking a pre-trained model and giving it extra training on a specific task or in a specific style. The base model already knows English; fine-tuning teaches it to be a careful cooking helper, a polite customer-service bot, or whatever the company wants. It's cheaper than training a new model from scratch.

question: The way you phrase your question to a chatbot really affects the answer you get. Carefully crafting your input is sometimes called:
answer: Prompt engineering
choices: Prompt engineering
Promise keeping
Spell casting
Star charting
context: Prompt engineering means writing your input in a way that's likely to get a useful output. Specific instructions, examples, and structure all matter. It isn't magic — it's just careful writing. The same model can give very different answers to a sloppy question versus a clear one.

question: You need to draft a short story. You also need to look up today's weather. Which tool fits which job?
answer: Chatbot for drafting; search for weather
choices: Chatbot for drafting; search for weather
Search for drafting; chatbot for weather
Both jobs go to the calculator
Both jobs go to the photo app
context: Match the tool to the job. Chatbots are great at drafting, brainstorming, and reshaping text. They're bad at 'what's happening right now' because they don't see live data by default. Search engines crawl the live web for current facts. Use each for what it's actually built for.

question: Some AI can listen to a few seconds of a real person speaking and then say new sentences in that exact voice. This is called:
answer: Voice cloning
choices: Voice cloning
Voice fasting
Voice exiting
Voice trimming
context: Voice-clone AI (ElevenLabs is a well-known company) can copy a voice from a small audio sample — a voicemail, a podcast clip, a social-media video. This is the technology behind 'grandparent scams,' where a caller sounds exactly like a relative. Knowing it exists is the first step in not being fooled.

question: You hear someone mention 'a large language model' that powers a chatbot. In plain words, what is that model trained to do?
answer: Predict the next word in a text
choices: Predict the next word in a text
Steer a self-driving car
Diagnose engine problems
Solve crossword puzzles only
context: An LLM is a program trained to predict the next word (or token) in a sequence of text. When you 'chat' with it, it's just predicting words one at a time, given the conversation so far. That single mechanism — guess the next word — is what powers all modern chatbots.

question: Voice clones can sound exactly like a real person from just seconds of recorded audio. What habit best protects your family?
answer: Set a family safe word in advance
choices: Set a family safe word in advance
Trust every familiar-sounding call
Pay any urgent request fast
Always speak only in whispers
context: A 'family safe word' is a short phrase only family members know. If someone calls sounding like a relative and asks for money or help, you ask for the safe word. A voice clone can't know it. The FBI publicly recommends every family set one up — it's the simplest defense against the new voice-clone scam class.

question: A chess program 'beats' a grandmaster. Does it actually WANT to win?
answer: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
choices: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
Yes, it gets excited like a person would feel
Yes, it cheers up right after every victory
Only if you tip it some money for trying
context: A chess engine has no wanting, hoping, or feeling. It evaluates moves and picks high-scoring ones. The word 'wins' is just a label for what happened — the program didn't experience victory. Capability isn't the same as consciousness. This is the most basic distinction kids need to keep clear about AI.

question: Two friends ask the same chatbot the same question. They get slightly different answers. What does this reveal about how chatbots work?
answer: Answers are generated, not retrieved
choices: Answers are generated, not retrieved
Chatbots have human moods
One friend has bad internet
The chatbot was sleeping
context: Chatbots generate text by sampling from probabilities — there's randomness involved. Ask the same question twice and you can get different wordings, sometimes different content. They aren't pulling fixed answers from a database. This is one more reason to verify — there's no 'canonical' answer, just one of many possible generations.

question: Your phone has an 'always-listening' assistant — Siri, Alexa, or Google. To activate it, you say a special word like 'Hey Siri.' What's that word called?
answer: A wake word
choices: A wake word
A welcome bell
A start key
A boot button
context: Smart speakers and phones use a wake word — a short phrase the device listens for. The microphone is on, listening locally for that word. After the wake word, audio is sent to the cloud for processing. It's worth knowing that the device IS always listening, even if it's only supposed to act on the wake word.

question: Out of these four chatbot names, which one is NOT actually real?
answer: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
choices: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
ChatGPT from the company OpenAI
Claude from the company Anthropic
Gemini from the company called Google
context: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), and Gemini (Google) are the main chatbots from major US AI labs as of the 2020s. 'ChatBuddy-X9' is invented. When you see a chatbot name in the news, it's worth checking whether the model is real — confident articles sometimes cite chatbots that don't exist.

question: Out of these four, which is NOT a real AI image generator?
answer: PixelMaster-Z
choices: PixelMaster-Z
DALL-E
Midjourney
Stable Diffusion
context: DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (a separate company), and Stable Diffusion (open-source) are the main text-to-image generators of the 2020s. 'PixelMaster-Z' is invented. Knowing real-tool names helps you spot fabrications — both human and AI-written articles sometimes invent plausible-sounding product names.

question: A chatbot answers 'I think the sky is blue.' Is the chatbot actually 'thinking'?
answer: No, it is producing words it learned from training
choices: No, it is producing words it learned from training
Yes, chatbots think exactly like a human brain
Maybe, it depends on the weather outside today
Only when nobody is currently watching the screen
context: When a chatbot writes 'I think,' those are just words. There's no thought, deliberation, or belief underneath — only word-prediction. Chatbots will produce 'I feel,' 'I believe,' 'I think,' and 'I worry' because their training data is full of those phrases. The phrases aren't reports about inner states. There are no inner states.

question: When people say 'deep learning,' the 'deep' refers to:
answer: Many layers stacked in the network
choices: Many layers stacked in the network
Deep undersea data centers
Deep meaning in the answers
Deep voices in the speech
context: A neural network is 'deep' when it has many layers stacked between input and output. Each layer transforms the data a bit further. The deep-learning revolution after 2012 was about making much deeper networks practical — and they turned out to handle much harder problems.

question: By default, when you ask a basic chatbot a question, where does the answer come from?
answer: Patterns learned during training
choices: Patterns learned during training
A live web search just now
A human typing the reply
A satellite link in space
context: An LLM by itself has no internet. The answer comes entirely from patterns the model learned during training. Some chat products bolt on search tools as a feature — when they do, they usually tell you ('searched the web'). The pure model alone is just predicting from training patterns.

question: You hear someone call a chatbot 'the world's smartest friend.' What part of that is most misleading?
answer: It's a tool, not a friend
choices: It's a tool, not a friend
It's smart in every subject
It uses the internet to think
It is friends with other AIs
context: A chatbot isn't a friend. It has no skin in the game, no care for you, no memory of you across chats by default. It's a useful tool when you want a draft, a summary, or a starting point. Calling it a friend invites a kind of trust that the tool isn't built to deserve.

question: You ask a chatbot to multiply two 5-digit numbers. The chatbot answers immediately. What's the smart move next?
answer: Check the result with a real calculator
choices: Check the result with a real calculator
Trust it because chatbots do perfect math
Multiply the answer by zero to verify
Ask a friend to guess if it sounds right
context: LLMs are bad at multi-step arithmetic because they predict text, not numbers. They can be confidently wrong on 5-digit multiplication. Always verify chatbot math with an actual calculator. Some chatbot products bolt on a calculator tool — when they do, the math is reliable. Without it, don't trust it.

question: ChatGPT was released to the public in late November of which year?
context: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. It reached 100 million users in two months — the fastest any consumer product had ever grown. The launch is widely treated as the moment when the modern AI era went mainstream and showed up in every classroom and newsroom.

question: The company that released ChatGPT in 2022 was originally founded as what kind of organization?
answer: A non-profit research lab
choices: A non-profit research lab
A high-school tutoring chain
A breakfast cereal startup
A used-car dealer franchise
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab with a stated mission of ensuring AGI benefits humanity. It later restructured to a 'capped-profit' company so it could raise the billions of dollars needed for the compute behind GPT-3 and GPT-4. ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022.

question: ChatGPT hit 100 million users faster than any consumer product before it. About how long did that take?
answer: Two months
choices: Two months
Two days
Two years
Twelve years
context: ChatGPT reached 100 million monthly active users in roughly two months after its November 30, 2022 launch — faster than TikTok, Instagram, or any prior internet product. The speed of adoption is part of why the moment felt seismic to so many.

question: A British mathematician proposed in 1950: if you can't tell a machine apart from a human in a typed conversation, the machine should count as intelligent. Who was he?
answer: Alan Turing
choices: Alan Turing
Albert Einstein
Henry Ford
James Watt
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' proposed what's now called the Turing test. Turing had broken the Enigma code at Bletchley Park during WWII. He's considered a founder of computer science. He died in 1954, two years after being chemically castrated by the British government for being homosexual.

question: Alan Turing proposed a famous test in 1950. The idea: if a person can't tell a typed conversation apart from a human's, the machine has passed. What's the test usually called?
answer: The Turing test
choices: The Turing test
The Newton test
The Edison test
The Darwin test
context: The Turing test was Alan Turing's 1950 thought experiment for machine intelligence. He didn't claim to have built such a machine — he argued for a way to settle the question if one ever appeared. Modern chatbots can sometimes pass simple versions; whether that counts as 'intelligence' is still debated.

question: A small summer workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956 is where the field of AI got its name. Who proposed the term 'artificial intelligence' for that meeting?
answer: John McCarthy
choices: John McCarthy
John D. Rockefeller
John F. Kennedy
Johnny Appleseed
context: John McCarthy proposed the term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project. The term stuck. McCarthy went on to invent the LISP programming language in 1958. The Dartmouth workshop is widely treated as the founding moment of AI as an organized research field.

question: AI as a research field got its name at a summer workshop at which college?
answer: Dartmouth
choices: Dartmouth
Harvard
Yale
Stanford
context: The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. John McCarthy organized it. Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester were among the attendees. They thought one summer would make significant progress on machine intelligence; it took decades.

question: AlphaGo played the ancient board game Go on a board that is how many lines on a side?
answer: Nineteen by nineteen
choices: Nineteen by nineteen
Five by five tiles
Four by ten spaces
Two by sixty cells
context: Go is played on a 19x19 grid with black and white stones. The search space is vastly larger than chess. Computer scientists had long predicted that top-human-level Go was still a decade away when AlphaGo arrived in 2016 and defeated Lee Sedol in Seoul. The match was watched by hundreds of millions of people, especially in East Asia.

question: DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the 3D structure of huge numbers of which biological molecules?
answer: Proteins
choices: Proteins
Tornadoes
Galaxies
Volcanoes
context: AlphaFold, built by DeepMind, predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino-acid sequences. It mapped roughly 200 million proteins — essentially every known protein in nature. Knowing a protein's shape is critical for drug design. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored this work.

question: Demis Hassabis is the co-founder of DeepMind, the AI lab behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold. He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in which subject?
answer: Chemistry
choices: Chemistry
Literature
Peace
Economics
context: Demis Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper (also DeepMind) and David Baker (University of Washington) for AlphaFold's protein-structure prediction work. Hassabis is a former chess prodigy who founded DeepMind in London in 2010; Google bought it in 2014.

question: In November 2023, the board of OpenAI made a sudden announcement that surprised the world. What did they do?
answer: Fired CEO Sam Altman
choices: Fired CEO Sam Altman
Hired the President of France
Banned all chatbots forever
Renamed the company OpenLab
context: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman, citing loss of confidence. Within five days, Altman was back as CEO and most of the board that fired him was gone. Microsoft (OpenAI's largest investor) and nearly every OpenAI employee had backed Altman. The episode showed how little outside control there is on the people building powerful AI.

question: Sam Altman was fired by the OpenAI board in November 2023. How many days later was he back as CEO?
answer: About five
choices: About five
About five hundred
About five thousand
Exactly one year
context: Sam Altman was fired Nov 17, 2023. Within days, Microsoft offered to hire Altman and the entire research team; nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Altman was back as CEO on Nov 22 — about five days. Most of the original board was out. It's a striking example of how fragile formal AI governance can be.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, sometimes called a 'godfather of AI' for his work on neural networks, resigned from which big tech company in 2023?
answer: Google
choices: Google
Disney
Boeing
Walmart
context: Geoffrey Hinton resigned from Google in May 2023. He cited concerns about AI safety — mass-produced disinformation, job displacement, autonomous weapons. His concerns are different from Eliezer Yudkowsky's 'shut it all down' position. Hinton helped develop backpropagation (1986) and the AlexNet ImageNet breakthrough (2012).

question: Geoffrey Hinton's 2012 ImageNet-winning team gave a huge boost to which kind of AI?
answer: Deep neural networks
choices: Deep neural networks
Spinning windmill turbines
Hot-air balloon flight
Solar panels on roofs
context: Hinton's 2012 ImageNet team (with grad students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever) won the famous image-recognition contest by a huge margin using a deep neural network trained on GPUs. The result convinced the field that deep learning worked at scale. It's often called the start of the modern deep-learning era.

question: Yann LeCun is the Chief AI Scientist at which company?
answer: Meta
choices: Meta
FedEx
Tesla
Twitter
context: Yann LeCun is Chief AI Scientist at Meta (Facebook's parent company). He helped develop convolutional neural networks for image recognition. He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio. He's one of the most prominent voices skeptical of 'AI doom' concerns — distinct from Hinton's middle-ground view.

question: Yoshua Bengio is one of three deep-learning pioneers who shared the 2018 Turing Award. He's based at a university in which Canadian city?
answer: Montreal
choices: Montreal
Madrid
Manchester
Mumbai
context: Yoshua Bengio is a professor at the University of Montreal. He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun for foundational deep-learning work. Unlike LeCun, Bengio has voiced concerns about advanced AI risk; unlike Hinton, he stayed in academia rather than leaving a big tech company.

question: Elon Musk's AI company, founded in 2023, has a short three-letter name. What is it?
answer: xAI (Musk's lab)
choices: xAI (Musk's lab)
OpenAI (a different lab)
DeepMind (Google's lab)
Anthropic (Claude's maker)
context: Elon Musk founded xAI in 2023. Its chatbot is called Grok. Musk was a co-founder and early funder of OpenAI but left its board in 2018. He has been publicly critical of OpenAI's direction since. Grok is offered through X (formerly Twitter), which Musk bought in 2022.

question: Elon Musk's company xAI makes a chatbot called what?
answer: Grok
choices: Grok
Bark
Squawk
Yawn
context: Grok is xAI's chatbot, integrated with X (formerly Twitter). The name is borrowed from Robert Heinlein's 1961 novel Stranger in a Strange Land, where 'to grok' means to deeply understand. Musk has marketed Grok as a 'rebellious' or 'anti-woke' alternative to ChatGPT, with mixed reviews on how that's actually played out.

question: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, is led by which co-founder?
answer: Dario Amodei
choices: Dario Amodei
Daniel Boone
Doc Holliday
Davy Crockett
context: Dario Amodei is CEO of Anthropic. His sister Daniela Amodei is President. Many Anthropic founders previously worked at OpenAI; they left in 2021 to start Anthropic with a focus on AI safety research. Claude is their main chatbot, competing with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok.

question: Anthropic's chatbot is called what?
answer: Claude
choices: Claude
Carl
Carlos
Calvin
context: Claude is Anthropic's chatbot. The name is reportedly a nod to Claude Shannon, the mathematician who founded information theory in 1948 (and who attended the 1956 Dartmouth AI workshop). Claude competes with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok in the major-US-chatbot lineup.

question: The 2012 ImageNet-winning network from Hinton's team is sometimes named after a grad student on the team. What's the network called?
answer: AlexNet
choices: AlexNet
MaxNet
ZackNet
PamNet
context: AlexNet, named for Alex Krizhevsky (a grad student in Hinton's lab, along with Ilya Sutskever), won the 2012 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge by a huge margin using a deep neural network trained on GPUs. The result convinced the field that deep learning worked at scale. It's often called the start of the modern deep-learning era.

question: A 2017 Google paper introduced the 'Transformer' architecture — now used in almost every chatbot. The paper has a famous short title. What is it?
answer: Attention Is All You Need
choices: Attention Is All You Need
Try Faster, Lose Slower
The Future Is Big
Speak Up Now
context: 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer — a neural network design built around a 'self-attention' mechanism. Every major chatbot (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) is built on Transformers. The paper is one of the most cited AI papers of all time.

question: GPT-3, the model that made many people first realize how good text generation could get, was released around which year?
context: OpenAI released GPT-3 in 2020. With 175 billion parameters it was much larger than its predecessors. It could write fluent essays, code, and creative fiction from short prompts. The original GPT-3 wasn't a polished chatbot — ChatGPT (built on a tuned version of GPT-3.5) is what made the technology accessible to non-experts in 2022.

question: OpenAI's GPT-4 model was released in which year?
context: OpenAI released GPT-4 in March 2023, a few months after ChatGPT made the GPT-3.5 model famous. GPT-4 was a major upgrade — better reasoning, longer context, ability to handle images as well as text. The transition from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 was the largest single capability jump of the recent chatbot era.

question: An early chatbot built at MIT in 1966 by Joseph Weizenbaum used simple pattern-matching to imitate a therapist. What was it called?
answer: ELIZA
choices: ELIZA
TARZAN
ROBIN
ARIEL
context: ELIZA, built by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in 1966, was one of the earliest chatbots. It mostly reflected the user's input back as a question ('I'm sad' → 'Why do you say you're sad?'). Weizenbaum was disturbed by how readily people opened up to it — even though they knew it was a simple program. It's an early lesson about anthropomorphizing AI.

question: After early AI excitement faded, funding collapsed for years in the 1970s and again in the late 1980s. These slumps are sometimes called:
answer: AI winters
choices: AI winters
AI summers
AI parties
AI grand tours
context: An 'AI winter' is a period when AI funding and interest collapsed because progress fell short of grand promises. The first major winter started in the 1970s after the UK's Lighthill Report. A second hit in the late 1980s after the 'expert systems' boom went bust. The modern boom started after the 2012 deep-learning breakthrough.

question: In 2011, an IBM AI system beat top humans on the TV quiz show Jeopardy! What was it called?
answer: Watson
choices: Watson
Hawking
Newton
Edison
context: IBM Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. The win showed AI could handle complex natural-language puzzles, not just classical games like chess. IBM later tried to apply Watson to medicine and other industries, with much more mixed results.

question: OpenAI was originally founded as a non-profit research lab in which year?
context: OpenAI was founded in December 2015 as a non-profit research lab. Co-founders included Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever, and others. It later restructured as a 'capped-profit' company. The mission as originally stated was to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity; whether the structure now matches that mission is a matter of ongoing debate.

question: John McCarthy, who coined the term 'artificial intelligence,' also invented a famous programming language. What was it called?
answer: LISP
choices: LISP
LUNCH
LIGHT
LIST
context: John McCarthy invented LISP at MIT in 1958. It's the second-oldest high-level programming language still in use (after Fortran). LISP was hugely influential in early AI research and introduced ideas — like garbage collection and treating code as data — that show up in most modern languages.

question: Meta (the company behind Facebook) releases an open-weight model family that anyone can download and run. What's it called?
answer: Llama
choices: Llama
Lemur
Lobster
Leopard
context: Llama is Meta's open-weight LLM family. Anyone can download the weights and run the model on their own computer or server. Versions include Llama, Llama 2, Llama 3, and so on. Llama is an important countervailing force to closed-API-only models like GPT-4 and Claude.

question: Before ChatGPT made AI famous to everyone, the 2016 AlphaGo match against world-class player Lee Sedol was watched live in which part of the world especially?
answer: East Asia (where Go is huge)
choices: East Asia (where Go is huge)
Antarctica (where chess is huge)
Greenland (where chess is huge)
Vatican City (where chess is huge)
context: AlphaGo's 4-1 victory over Lee Sedol in March 2016 was the most-watched AI breakthrough before ChatGPT. Hundreds of millions of viewers — especially in East Asia, where Go is a major game — followed the match. The win convinced many people that something fundamental had changed in machine learning.

question: OpenAI was started as a non-profit, but it later restructured to a 'capped-profit' model so it could:
answer: Raise large amounts of investment
choices: Raise large amounts of investment
Avoid paying any taxes ever
Move to a tropical island
Pay employees in board games
context: OpenAI restructured in 2019 to a 'capped-profit' model — investors can earn returns, but the returns are capped at a multiple of their investment. The move let OpenAI raise the billions needed for compute. Critics argue the change drifted the lab from its non-profit mission. The 2023 board drama partly turned on this tension.

question: A company called ElevenLabs is best known for making AI that does what?
answer: Generates realistic voices
choices: Generates realistic voices
Makes paper notebooks
Sells flower bouquets
Designs nail polish
context: ElevenLabs is a voice-AI company that became prominent around 2022-23. Its technology can clone a voice from seconds of audio. The same tech that lets actors record once and dub many languages also powers the 'grandparent scam' wave — voice fakes that sound exactly like a real relative.

question: When the OpenAI board briefly fired Sam Altman in November 2023, which major OpenAI investor pushed for his return?
answer: Microsoft (its largest investor)
choices: Microsoft (its largest investor)
Walmart (its biggest customer)
Disney World (its main partner)
The New York Stock Exchange ban
context: Microsoft, OpenAI's largest investor, immediately offered to hire Altman and the entire research team during the November 2023 board crisis. Nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Five days later, Altman was reinstated as CEO. The episode showed how fragile OpenAI's formal governance structure was against the economic pressure of its main backer.

question: DeepMind, the AI lab behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold, is based in which city?
answer: London
choices: London
Lagos
Lima
Lisbon
context: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, and Mustafa Suleyman. Google bought it in 2014 for an estimated $500 million. It's still headquartered in London and remains Google's main AI research lab alongside Google Research and Google Brain.

question: The 2018 Turing Award (sometimes called 'computing's Nobel') went to three deep-learning pioneers. Of these four people, which one was NOT among the winners?
answer: Demis Hassabis (DeepMind founder)
choices: Demis Hassabis (DeepMind founder)
Geoffrey Hinton (Toronto/Google)
Yann LeCun (NYU/Meta)
Yoshua Bengio (Montreal)
context: The 2018 Turing Award went to Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio for foundational deep-learning work. Demis Hassabis founded DeepMind and later shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold — a different prize. Knowing who is recognized for what helps you read AI news critically.

question: Geoffrey Hinton spent many years at which Canadian university before joining Google?
answer: University of Toronto
choices: University of Toronto
University of Vienna
University of Tokyo
University of Tahiti
context: Geoffrey Hinton was a professor at the University of Toronto for decades. His 2012 ImageNet team (Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever as graduate students) launched the deep-learning revolution from there. Hinton joined Google in 2013 and resigned in May 2023 to speak more freely about AI risks.

question: When Google Translate turns Spanish into English, the system underneath uses what kind of AI?
answer: A neural network
choices: A neural network
A solar panel
A wind turbine
A submarine
context: Modern translation services (Google Translate, DeepL) use neural networks trained on huge amounts of parallel text — sentences translated by humans into both languages. Quality improved dramatically after 2016 when Google switched from older statistical methods to neural machine translation.

question: Before 2016, machine translation between major languages was famously bad. What technology fixed it?
answer: Neural networks
choices: Neural networks
Old encyclopedias
Carrier pigeons
Telegraph wires
context: Until about 2016, machine translation used either hand-written grammar rules or statistical word-frequency models. Both produced stiff, awkward output. Google's switch to neural machine translation in 2016 made translation good enough that human translators noticed it changed their work. DeepL (a separate company) competes with similar quality.

question: DeepMind's AlphaGo learned to play Go partly by playing against:
answer: Itself, millions of times
choices: Itself, millions of times
Famous chess grandmasters
Tic-tac-toe champions
Bingo players in Florida
context: AlphaGo learned from a mix of human Go games and self-play — playing against copies of itself for millions of games. A later version, AlphaZero (2017), learned chess, shogi, and Go with NO human game data at all — purely self-play. Self-play turned out to be a powerful way to train game-playing AI past human level.

question: DeepMind's AlphaFold has predicted the 3D shape of about how many proteins?
answer: 200 million
choices: 200 million
200 thousand
200 billion
context: AlphaFold has predicted the 3D structure of roughly 200 million proteins — essentially every known protein in nature. The database is freely available. Knowing a protein's shape lets researchers design drugs that target it. The work won DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

question: Why is knowing the 3D shape of a protein so important for medicine?
answer: Drugs are designed to fit the shape
choices: Drugs are designed to fit the shape
Doctors mostly carve them on rocks
Hospitals use them as decorations
Pharmacies wrap pills with them
context: Proteins do almost all the work in living cells, and their shapes determine what they do. Drugs typically work by fitting precisely into a target protein, the way a key fits a lock. Knowing the shape upfront lets researchers design candidate drugs faster. AlphaFold made this once-slow lab work suddenly routine.

question: AI image-classification systems help doctors read X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs. The doctor stays in charge, and the AI mainly acts as a:
answer: Second reader catching missed details
choices: Second reader catching missed details
Vending machine for paper cups
Sleep meditation podcast host
Bouquet of fresh winter flowers
context: AI in radiology is most often used as a 'second reader' — the human radiologist reads the scan, then AI checks for things the human might have missed. The human stays responsible for the final read. This 'augment, don't replace' pattern is common across many domains where AI has been deployed in serious work.

question: Self-driving cars rely heavily on AI to make sense of cameras, radar, and lidar. Which of these companies is famous for self-driving car research?
answer: Waymo
choices: Waymo
Crayola
Lego
Hasbro
context: Waymo (a sister company to Google) operates self-driving taxi services in several US cities. Tesla offers driver-assistance software called Autopilot and a paid 'Full Self-Driving' option. Cruise (a GM subsidiary) ran similar services. Self-driving has made real progress but has also missed many predicted timelines.

question: What is a recommendation system on YouTube mostly trying to predict?
answer: What you'll watch next
choices: What you'll watch next
Where you live exactly
What you ate for dinner
Your shoe size in inches
context: YouTube's recommendation system predicts which videos you're likely to watch and watch for a long time. It's optimized for engagement — usually measured by watch time. It's NOT optimized for whether what you watch is true, useful, or good for you. Knowing what it's actually optimizing is the first step in choosing what to do about it.

question: Netflix and Spotify both use AI to pick content for you. The general name for that kind of system is a:
answer: Recommendation system
choices: Recommendation system
Recommendation library
Recommendation cafeteria
Recommendation lighthouse
context: A recommendation system uses AI to predict what content you'll like, based on what you (and people like you) clicked or watched. Netflix and Spotify made this approach famous in the 2010s. Most major content platforms now use them. They are excellent at retention; they aren't designed for your wellbeing.

question: A virtual chat agent on a customer-service website that types replies to your questions is most likely powered by:
answer: A chatbot AI
choices: A chatbot AI
A toaster oven
An old fax machine
A windmill
context: Most customer-service chat widgets are powered by chatbot AI — either off-the-shelf LLMs or specialized customer-service systems. They're often fine for routine questions and frustrating for unusual ones. Many companies hand off to a human agent when the AI can't help. Knowing you're chatting with an AI matters for what you should and shouldn't share.

question: What does GitHub Copilot help its users do?
answer: Write computer code faster
choices: Write computer code faster
Write better poetry only
Cook dinner remotely
Drive a car safely
context: GitHub Copilot is an AI tool that suggests code as a programmer types. It can complete a function from a comment, write tests, fill in repetitive code. It can also suggest buggy or insecure code, which is why programmers still have to read and review what it offers. Other tools in this space include Cursor and Tabnine.

question: An AI image generator takes what kind of input?
answer: A short text description
choices: A short text description
A song's notes
A vial of perfume
A magnet
context: Text-to-image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) take a written prompt — 'a knight riding a robot horse at sunset' — and produce a matching image. Stable Diffusion is open-source; DALL-E is OpenAI; Midjourney is its own company. They've made it much easier to generate fake-looking photos that can fool people online.

question: When you say 'Hey Siri,' your iPhone listens for that phrase locally before sending anything to Apple's servers. That phrase is called the:
answer: Wake word
choices: Wake word
Pillow word
Sleeping word
Window word
context: Voice assistants use a small on-device model to listen continuously for a wake word. Audio before the wake word is not (officially) sent to the company. Audio after the wake word goes to the cloud for processing. The microphone IS always on — that's how the local detection works.

question: Modern AI voice synthesis can produce speech that sounds like:
answer: A specific real person
choices: A specific real person
Only robotic monotones
Just one cartoon character
Only ancient Latin
context: Voice-synthesis AI has improved dramatically since around 2022. Companies like ElevenLabs can clone a voice from a short audio clip. The tech has real uses (audiobooks, accessibility, dubbing) and serious abuse cases (scam calls, fake quotes). Knowing it exists is the first step in not being fooled when you hear a familiar voice ask for money.

question: When your credit card alerts you to a suspicious purchase, an AI system has likely been:
answer: Checking your spending patterns
choices: Checking your spending patterns
Eating chocolate snacks
Tweeting from the moon
Sleeping under your desk
context: Credit-card fraud detection has used machine learning for decades — long before the chatbot era. The system watches transaction patterns and flags anything unusual: a charge in a country you've never been, a price ten times your normal, an odd merchant. It's one of the longest-running quietly-useful AI applications in everyday life.

question: AI is being used to help farmers monitor crops using:
answer: Satellite images
choices: Satellite images
Old radios
Wooden spoons
Paper kites
context: Precision agriculture uses AI to analyze satellite and drone imagery, helping farmers spot drought stress, pest damage, and yield differences across fields. Combined with sensors and GPS-guided machinery, it has changed large-farm management. It also raises questions about who controls the data and whether small farms can compete on the same terms.

question: Some AI systems can now forecast the weather. Compared to older methods, AI weather forecasters often:
answer: Run much faster
choices: Run much faster
Get sleepy in the rain
Need flat windless places
Smell coming storms
context: AI weather models (Google's GraphCast, Huawei's Pangu-Weather, others) can produce forecasts much faster than traditional physics-based numerical weather prediction. They're trained on decades of historical data. They don't replace traditional models entirely, but they've become a real complement — and faster forecasts mean more warning when severe weather is coming.

question: AI is being used in drug discovery mainly to:
answer: Speed up finding candidate compounds
choices: Speed up finding candidate compounds
Bake bread for clinical trials
Replace pharmacies entirely
Manage hospital cafeterias
context: AI in drug discovery is used to narrow the search for promising candidate compounds — sorting through billions of possibilities far faster than human chemists alone could. AlphaFold-style protein-structure prediction is one piece of this. Drug development still takes years and clinical trials, but the early-stage search has changed dramatically.

question: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok are competing chatbots from different companies. Out of these, which is from Google?
answer: Gemini
choices: Gemini
Grok
Claude
ChatGPT
context: ChatGPT is from OpenAI. Claude is from Anthropic. Gemini is from Google. Grok is from xAI (Elon Musk's company). They compete on different strengths — Gemini integrates with Google services; Claude has long context windows; ChatGPT had the biggest head start; Grok markets itself as less filtered.

question: A productive way to use a chatbot for learning math is:
answer: Ask it to walk through steps
choices: Ask it to walk through steps
Submit its answers as your own
Never check what it says
Get it to do your test for you
context: AI is genuinely useful as a learning tool when you ask it to explain step-by-step, check your work, and quiz you. Submitting its output as your own is cheating and trains you to skip the actual learning. The line: AI for explanation and review = useful. AI for replacing the work you should do yourself = makes you weaker.

question: Apple's voice assistant is called what?
answer: Siri
choices: Siri
Sandy
Sammy
Stevie
context: Apple's voice assistant is Siri, launched in 2011 with the iPhone 4S. Amazon has Alexa (with Echo devices). Google has Google Assistant. Microsoft has Cortana. All of them rely on AI for speech recognition (turning your speech into text) and natural-language understanding (figuring out what you meant).

question: Amazon's voice assistant, which lives in the Echo line of speakers, is called what?
answer: Alexa
choices: Alexa
Athena
Aurora
Aspen
context: Alexa is Amazon's voice assistant, built into Echo smart speakers and other devices. Like Siri and Google Assistant, it uses AI to recognize speech and process natural language. It's also a microphone in your house listening for the wake word 'Alexa' — worth being aware of when deciding where to put one.

question: Of these four image AIs, which is open-source — meaning anyone can download and run it themselves?
answer: Stable Diffusion
choices: Stable Diffusion
DALL-E
Midjourney
Sora
context: Stable Diffusion is open-source. Anyone can download the model and run it on their own computer. DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (its own company), and Sora (OpenAI, video) are closed — you have to use the company's website or API. Open-source models are an important countervailing force to closed model companies.

question: What does TikTok's 'For You' page mostly use to pick videos for you?
answer: A recommendation AI
choices: A recommendation AI
A randomized dice roll
Your zodiac chart only
Today's stock prices
context: TikTok's For You page is powered by an AI recommendation system that has become famous for how quickly it learns what holds your attention. It uses what videos you watch fully, what you rewatch, what you scroll past, and what you share. Knowing it's hunting your attention is the first step in not being hunted.

question: Coding assistants like GitHub Copilot can sometimes suggest code that has security bugs. What's the right habit for a programmer?
answer: Read and check what's suggested
choices: Read and check what's suggested
Use every suggestion immediately
Submit code without reading
Trust AI completely on security
context: AI code suggestions are useful drafts, not final answers. They can suggest insecure patterns, deprecated libraries, or subtly wrong logic. Programmers still need to read, understand, and test what's suggested. 'AI for speed; human for review' is the rule that keeps quality from sliding.

question: DeepL is a translation service from Germany. It competes with which other major translation service?
answer: Google Translate
choices: Google Translate
Google Calendar
Google Photos
Google Calculator
context: DeepL and Google Translate are the two best-known machine-translation services. DeepL is often praised for nuance with European languages, while Google Translate covers more languages overall. Both use deep neural networks trained on huge corpora of human-translated text. Both have moved the practical floor for cross-language communication.

question: AlphaGo's famous moment was 'Move 37' in a 2016 game against Lee Sedol. Why is the move so often remembered?
answer: It surprised top human players
choices: It surprised top human players
It was a typo of Move 38
It set the board on fire
Lee Sedol fell asleep first
context: Move 37 in game 2 of the 2016 Lee Sedol match was so unusual that commentators initially called it a mistake. Lee Sedol left the room to recover. AlphaGo won that game. Top human Go players have since incorporated similar ideas into their own play. It's the moment when an AI made a creative move that humans hadn't considered, then was vindicated by what came next.

question: Why is AlphaFold a big deal for biology?
answer: It predicts protein 3D shapes fast
choices: It predicts protein 3D shapes fast
It writes biology textbooks
It paints biology classrooms
It manages biology lectures
context: Before AlphaFold, working out the 3D shape of a single protein could take months or years of careful lab work (X-ray crystallography, NMR, cryo-EM). AlphaFold predicts the shape from a protein's amino-acid sequence in minutes. The database of ~200 million predicted structures is freely available to researchers and is now a routine starting point in molecular biology.

question: Image generators sometimes draw hands with the wrong number of fingers. Why does this kind of mistake happen?
answer: The model doesn't truly understand hands
choices: The model doesn't truly understand hands
Hands are too small to draw at all
All cameras break around hands
Hands are illegal to depict by law
context: Image generators learn patterns of pixels that statistically appear together. They don't 'understand' that a hand has exactly five fingers — they just know what hands tend to look like. When the model isn't sure, it can produce six fingers, missing fingers, or impossible joints. Hands and text in images are the two classic giveaways.

question: When a coding assistant like Copilot writes a function for a programmer, where does the suggestion come from?
answer: Patterns from training on lots of code
choices: Patterns from training on lots of code
A team of humans typing live
A satellite over the office
The programmer's lunch order
context: Coding assistants are LLMs (often specialized) trained on huge amounts of public code, including open-source repositories. Their suggestions reflect patterns in that training data. This raises real questions about licensing, attribution, and code copying — and is one reason developers still need to review what's offered before they use it.

question: AI translation is excellent between major languages but tends to be weaker for what kinds of language?
answer: Low-resource languages with little data
choices: Low-resource languages with little data
Languages with red flags
Languages spoken at high altitudes
Languages with curved letters
context: Translation AI works best when there's a lot of parallel training data — sentences translated between two languages by humans. Major languages (English, Spanish, Mandarin, French) have plenty. 'Low-resource' languages with fewer speakers or less digital text get poorer-quality translation. This is a real fairness gap in the technology.

question: AI fraud detection in banking is an example of:
answer: Old AI that quietly works
choices: Old AI that quietly works
Brand-new AI from this year
AI that nobody actually uses
AI that talks like a person
context: Credit-card fraud detection has used machine learning since the 1990s. It's an example of older 'narrow' AI that quietly works every day, far from any chatbot drama. Most of the AI in your daily life — spam filtering, recommendation, fraud detection, voice transcription — has been working for years without any fanfare.

question: Many self-driving cars use a spinning sensor on top that bounces laser pulses off the world. What is the technology called?
answer: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
choices: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
Sonar (sound-based ranging)
Radar (radio-based ranging)
Solar (sun-based ranging)
context: Lidar bounces laser pulses off objects and times the return to build a 3D map of the surroundings. Waymo and many other self-driving programs use it. Tesla famously chose to rely mostly on cameras and radar instead. Sonar uses sound, radar uses radio waves; lidar uses light. Each has different strengths for different conditions.

question: When companies use AI to read audiobooks in a celebrity's voice, the celebrity usually has to first:
answer: Give recorded samples for training
choices: Give recorded samples for training
Watch every chapter being read
Drive the audiobook truck
Pick the cover art color
context: AI voice cloning needs samples to train on. Legitimate uses (audiobooks, dubbing, accessibility) involve consent — the voice owner agrees and is usually paid. The same technology without consent powers voice-clone scams. The technology itself doesn't know the difference; that's why the law and personal habits both matter.

question: A bank's AI spots an unusual purchase pattern on your card and freezes it. What is the AI mainly looking for?
answer: Patterns that don't match yours
choices: Patterns that don't match yours
What's on your grocery list
Whether you washed your hands
How polite your texts are
context: Fraud-detection AI builds a model of YOUR normal spending — places, amounts, times — and flags purchases that don't fit. A $5,000 charge in a country you've never been is unusual. The system isn't reading your messages or judging your character; it's pattern-matching against your own past behavior.

question: DeepMind's AlphaZero (2017) was different from AlphaGo because it learned chess and Go:
answer: From scratch with no human games
choices: From scratch with no human games
By watching human players in person
From a printed book of moves
Only when humans weren't looking
context: AlphaZero learned chess, shogi, and Go using only the rules and self-play — no human game data at all. AlphaGo had used some human games. AlphaZero showed that pure self-play could match or exceed human-data-augmented training. It's a striking demonstration of how powerful self-play can be when the rules are clear and the system can play itself millions of times.

question: DALL-E and Stable Diffusion are both:
answer: Text-to-image generators
choices: Text-to-image generators
Brands of toothpaste
Sports drink flavors
Bicycle frame makers
context: DALL-E (OpenAI) and Stable Diffusion (Stability AI / open-source) are both text-to-image generators. You type a description; they produce an image. Midjourney is another in the same category. DALL-E is closed (use OpenAI's site). Stable Diffusion is open-source — anyone can run it. The technology has changed what's possible to fake.

question: Programmers using AI coding tools usually still have to:
answer: Read and test the suggested code
choices: Read and test the suggested code
Pay the AI directly with cash
Pet the AI when it works
Sing to the AI each morning
context: AI coding tools speed up routine work but they can suggest buggy, insecure, or subtly wrong code. The programmer still has to read what's offered, test it, and decide whether to use it. 'Tool that drafts; human that reviews' is the discipline that keeps quality from sliding when AI is in the loop.

question: A recommendation system on a video site optimizes for engagement. Engagement is measured by things like:
answer: Watch time and shares
choices: Watch time and shares
How loud you cheer
Your shoe brand
Your last test grade
context: Engagement is usually measured by watch time, repeat visits, likes, comments, and shares. These are easy to count. They are NOT the same as 'did this help the user' or 'is the content true.' The system optimizes whatever it's measured by, so the metric shapes what gets shown. This is one of the most important facts to know about how these systems work.

question: Geoffrey Hinton said in 2016 that AI would replace radiologists within five years. About a decade later, how has that prediction aged?
answer: Radiologists are still in demand
choices: Radiologists are still in demand
Radiologists vanished in 2017
All hospitals closed by 2018
Hospitals replaced beds with bots
context: Hinton publicly said in 2016 that medical schools should stop training radiologists because AI would replace them within five years. Nearly a decade later, radiologists are still in demand and AI is used as a second-reader rather than as a replacement. The prediction is a famous cautionary tale: confident AI job-displacement timelines have a poor track record.

question: AI tools that help radiologists catch lung nodules or skin cancers are typically used as:
answer: A second reader alongside the human
choices: A second reader alongside the human
A replacement for the human
A lunch ordering system
A waiting-room TV channel
context: AI in radiology is most often used as a 'second reader' — the human radiologist reads the scan, then AI checks for things the human might have missed. The human remains responsible for the read. This 'augment, don't replace' pattern is common across many domains where AI has been deployed in serious work.

question: Precision agriculture uses AI to help farmers do which of these?
answer: Spot crop problems early
choices: Spot crop problems early
Sing to the plants
Paint barns purple
Bake bread on the tractor
context: Precision agriculture uses AI on satellite imagery, drone footage, and ground sensors to spot drought stress, pest damage, nutrient deficiencies, and yield variation across a field. Farmers can then water, fertilize, or treat only where needed instead of treating the whole field uniformly. It's a quietly important application of AI to real-world problems.

question: Audiobook companies have started using AI to record books in voices that sound like real narrators. This raises a question for actors about:
answer: Whether they get paid for AI voices
choices: Whether they get paid for AI voices
Whether books should still be read aloud
Whether libraries should close
Whether bookstores should sell coffee
context: AI voice cloning lets companies produce many audiobooks fast, including in voices that resemble specific narrators. Voice actors' unions have negotiated rules requiring consent and payment for AI use of an actor's voice. The technology and the contracts are still settling — but the question of who controls a voice (and who gets paid for its use) is real and ongoing.

question: A student uses ChatGPT to ask 'explain this math problem step by step.' This is a use of AI that is:
answer: Helpful for learning
choices: Helpful for learning
Always cheating
Banned by every country
Only legal in winter
context: Asking AI to explain something — show steps, give analogies, quiz you — is one of the most productive uses of the technology. It's like having a patient (if sometimes wrong) tutor available any time. The line is doing your own work versus submitting AI output. Explanation-and-review = good. Submit-as-yours = bad.

question: A voice on the phone sounds exactly like your cousin and asks you to wire money fast. What's the smart first move?
answer: Hang up and call your cousin back
choices: Hang up and call your cousin back
Wire the money right away
Whisper a secret family song
Tell them your address out loud
context: Voice clones can fool family members from just seconds of recorded audio. The single best defense is to hang up and call back on a number you already know. If it was really your cousin, they'll pick up. If it was a scammer, the call ends right there. Urgency is the scammer's tool; calling back is yours.

question: Modern AI can clone a voice from how much recorded audio?
answer: Just a few seconds
choices: Just a few seconds
Twenty years exactly
Half a lifetime
Several decades
context: Voice-cloning AI like ElevenLabs needs only a few seconds of clean audio to produce a near-perfect impersonation. The source can be a voicemail, a podcast, a social-media video, even a clip from a school play. Knowing how little it takes is the first step in being careful what audio is publicly available.

question: Your family wants protection from voice-clone phone scams. What simple step should they take together?
answer: Set up a family safe word
choices: Set up a family safe word
Buy matching umbrellas
Memorize each other's pets
Always whisper on calls
context: A family safe word is a short phrase only family members know. If someone calls sounding like a relative and asks for money or help, you ask for the safe word. A voice clone can't know it. The FBI publicly recommends every family set one up. It's free, takes five minutes, and stops the entire scam class.

question: You're chatting with a free AI chatbot. Out of these four, what should you NEVER paste into the chat?
answer: Your password
choices: Your password
A song lyric
A book title
A weather forecast
context: Free chatbot services typically log your conversations. They may be used to train future models, reviewed by employees, or accessed under legal process. Never paste passwords, full credit card numbers, or sensitive medical/legal documents you wouldn't want public. Treat anything you send to a free chatbot as potentially seen by someone else.

question: A chatbot writes you a paragraph and says a famous scientist was born in 1872. The date sounds slightly off. What's the smart move?
answer: Look it up in a reliable source
choices: Look it up in a reliable source
Trust the chatbot and move on
Ask the chatbot if it's lying
Memorize the wrong date
context: Chatbots invent dates, names, and citations with confidence. The safe habit is to look up specific factual claims in a trusted source before using or sharing them. Encyclopedias, government and university websites, and major news organizations are reasonable starting points. Two different chatbots agreeing isn't enough — they often share the same training data and same errors.

question: You see a viral video of a famous person saying something shocking. Before believing or sharing, you should:
answer: Check if trusted news outlets report it
choices: Check if trusted news outlets report it
Forward it to ten people very fast
Trust it because the clip is popular
Trust it because the face looks real
context: Deepfakes can put words in real people's mouths. Telltales (mouth-sync drift, weird blinking, voice mismatch) are useful but not foolproof. The bigger defense is: if something shocking happened, trusted news organizations are usually reporting it. If the only place you see a story is a viral clip on social media, treat it with extra suspicion.

question: A photo online shows a person holding a sign with text. The text on the sign is garbled and unreadable. This is a telltale sign of:
answer: An AI-generated image
choices: An AI-generated image
Bad camera focus only
Foreign-language script
Old vintage film
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce garbled, unreadable text in images — letters that look right at first glance but spell nothing. Real photos with real signs have real text. Garbled text on signs, labels, or storefronts in an image is a strong indicator that the image is AI-generated.

question: Looking at someone's hands is a useful trick for spotting AI-generated photos. Why?
answer: AI often gets finger counts wrong
choices: AI often gets finger counts wrong
AI never draws hands at all
AI hands are always pink
AI always draws six fingers
context: AI image generators frequently produce hands with wrong finger counts, extra knuckles, impossible joints, or fingers that meld together. Real photos don't have this problem (real people have five fingers). Hands are one of the most reliable AI-image giveaways, along with garbled text and weird jewelry-skin blending.

question: In 2023, a New York lawyer filed a court brief citing six prior cases — but none of them existed. What had he used to find them?
answer: ChatGPT (made-up citations)
choices: ChatGPT (made-up citations)
An old library book (worn out)
A magic 8-ball (random reply)
A weather app (rain forecast)
context: Steven Schwartz, an attorney in Mata v. Avianca, used ChatGPT to research case law. It returned six cases that ChatGPT had completely fabricated. When opposing counsel couldn't find them, Schwartz asked ChatGPT to confirm — it confirmed they were real. The judge fined him $5,000 in June 2023. The lesson: LLMs invent confident-sounding citations. Always verify.

question: A chatbot recommends you read a book that sounds great. What's the safe move before you go buy it?
answer: Search to confirm the book exists
choices: Search to confirm the book exists
Order it immediately
Tell all your friends to buy it
Quote it in a school paper
context: Chatbots invent plausible-sounding book titles, authors, and quotes. The book may not exist; if it does, the author may not have written it; if the author did, the quote may not be in it. Always confirm a book exists (and that the relevant author wrote it) before quoting or recommending. Library catalogs and major bookseller sites are quick to check.

question: Your friend has a confusing health symptom. They ask a chatbot what's wrong. The chatbot gives a confident diagnosis. What should they do?
answer: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
choices: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
Trust the chatbot completely
Buy whatever pills it names
Use it as final medical advice
context: Chatbots can provide useful general information but they don't know your full medical history, they can't examine you, and they can be confidently wrong. For real symptoms, see a real doctor. Use the chatbot as a starting point for questions to ask, never as the final word. The same rule applies to legal advice — real lawyer for real legal issues.

question: You're doing your math homework and the chatbot gives you an answer. What's the smart step before turning it in?
answer: Check it with a calculator
choices: Check it with a calculator
Submit it without thinking
Trust the chatbot's math fully
Erase your own work entirely
context: LLMs are bad at multi-step arithmetic. They predict text patterns, not numbers. They can be confidently wrong on big numbers, long chains of operations, or unusual calculations. Always verify chatbot math with an actual calculator. Some chatbot products bolt a calculator on — when they do, the math is reliable. Without it, don't trust it.

question: When you use a free AI chatbot, the company usually:
answer: Logs your conversations
choices: Logs your conversations
Forgets them all instantly
Sells them to one shopper
Burns them with a candle
context: Most free chatbot services log conversations. Their terms of service usually grant the company rights to use that data for model training, employee quality review, and other purposes. Some paid or enterprise plans offer no-logging or no-training options. Reading the terms once for any service you use heavily is worth a few minutes.

question: Many phone apps ask for permission to use your microphone. The smart default is:
answer: Only allow it for apps that need it
choices: Only allow it for apps that need it
Allow it for every app always
Reject every app permission
Let every app record forever
context: Most apps don't actually need microphone access. A photo editor doesn't need to hear you; a flashlight app doesn't either. The smart default is 'only for apps that genuinely need it' — voice assistants, video chat, voice messaging. The same logic applies to camera, location, contacts, and other permissions. Default-off, allow on a case-by-case basis.

question: Two different chatbots give you the same wrong fact. Does the agreement make the fact more likely to be true?
answer: No — they may share training data
choices: No — they may share training data
Yes — two sources confirm it
Yes — but only on weekdays
Yes — if both replies are long
context: Two chatbots agreeing isn't independent confirmation. They were often trained on overlapping internet data and have the same common errors built in. For real verification you need a different KIND of source — a textbook, an encyclopedia, a government or university page. 'Two AIs say so' is closer to 'one AI said so twice' than to genuine corroboration.

question: A 'school essay' you read in a homework group seems to use a lot of em-dashes and phrases like 'delve into the rich tapestry.' What's a reasonable suspicion?
answer: It may have been AI-written
choices: It may have been AI-written
It was written in invisible ink
Its author is a robot truly
It was definitely Shakespeare
context: Heavy em-dash use, phrases like 'delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'navigate the complexities,' and overly balanced sentence structure are common AI tells. Real student writing tends to be rougher, more opinionated, with stranger phrasings.
