Spotting these patterns is a useful skill — both for teachers checking work and for readers checking sources online.

question: Out of these four signs, which is a typical deepfake video tell?
answer: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
choices: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
Bright sunshine in the background
A song playing on the radio
The person sitting at a desk
context: Deepfake video tells include: mouth movement that drifts slightly out of sync with the speech, weird blinking patterns, blurry or shifting hair or jewelry edges, voice that doesn't quite match the lip movement, and inconsistent lighting on the face. The technology keeps improving — so the tells keep getting subtler — but the general idea is to look for small mismatches.

question: A chatbot quotes a famous author at length. The quote sounds good but you've never seen it before. What's the safe step?
answer: Search for the exact quote first
choices: Search for the exact quote first
Use it in an essay right away
Trust it for sounding real
Get it printed on a poster
context: Chatbots invent confident-sounding quotes attributed to famous authors. The quote often sounds 'in style' but was never actually written by that author. Before using a quote in an essay, search for the exact phrase in quotation marks. If the only places it appears are AI outputs or scraped AI content, it's probably invented.

question: Out of these four, which is the WORST thing to paste into a free chatbot?
answer: Your bank account number
choices: Your bank account number
A line of a poem
A recipe for soup
A list of board games
context: Free chatbot services typically log conversations. Bank account numbers, full credit-card numbers, social security numbers, passwords, and full medical records should never be pasted into a free chatbot. Treat the chat box like a public-ish place. For sensitive use, look for enterprise-grade services or run an open-source model locally.

question: A scammer calls and the voice sounds exactly like your grandma. She's crying and needs money fast. What's the move?
answer: Hang up and call grandma directly
choices: Hang up and call grandma directly
Wire the money immediately
Promise it on a video call
Send your address to confirm
context: 'Grandparent scams' use voice cloning to mimic a real relative. Urgency and emotion are how the scam works — the victim is rushed past their better judgment. The defense is to break the urgency: hang up and call grandma back on the number you already have. If she's fine, you just dodged a scam. If something is wrong, she'll pick up.

question: The 2023 New York lawyer who cited fake court cases from ChatGPT was fined how much?
answer: About 5,000 dollars
choices: About 5,000 dollars
About 5 cents
About 500 million dollars
Nothing at all
context: Steven Schwartz was fined $5,000 in June 2023 for filing a brief citing six ChatGPT-fabricated cases in Mata v. Avianca. The story made worldwide news. It's now a standard cautionary tale — first because LLMs invent citations, and second because verifying isn't optional, especially when professional reputation or money is at stake.

question: An image online shows someone wearing glasses, but the frames seem to melt into the side of their face. This is most likely:
answer: Glasses-into-skin AI blending
choices: Glasses-into-skin AI blending
Just a low-quality phone camera
A brand-new fashion choice
A bright reflection from the sun
context: AI image generators frequently produce flaws around objects that touch skin or hair — glasses merging into the face, earrings half-disappearing, hair blending into clothing. Real photos don't have these problems (real objects have edges). Watch for these blending flaws as image-generation tells.

question: You want to share a 'fact' you read in a chatbot reply. What's the safe step first?
answer: Verify it in a trusted source
choices: Verify it in a trusted source
Share it right away to friends
Memorize the chatbot's wording
Tell everyone the chatbot said so
context: AI 'trust but verify' is a real habit, not just advice. Chatbots produce fluent, confident-sounding text whether or not it's true. Get into the routine of checking specific claims — especially names, dates, statistics, and quotes — before passing them on. A small habit prevents a lot of confidently shared bad information.

question: A chatbot tells you to read 'a famous book by C.S. Lewis about pirate octopuses.' Your gut says this book may not exist. What's the right next step?
answer: Search the internet for it
choices: Search the internet for it
Trust the chatbot anyway
Tell your teacher you read it
Order it from a bookstore now
context: C.S. Lewis didn't write a book about pirate octopuses. A chatbot can confidently invent such a title because it's pattern-completing from training data — generating something that 'sounds like a Lewis title' is well within its capability. Chatbots especially love to invent books in genres that don't quite exist. Always search before quoting or recommending.

question: You need to find out who won a sports game that ended ten minutes ago. Which tool fits best?
answer: A search engine
choices: A search engine
A basic chatbot
A calculator
A photo editor
context: Basic chatbots don't see live data. A game that ended ten minutes ago is outside any chatbot's training cutoff. Search engines crawl the live web and will find news stories about the game. Some chatbot products bolt search on as a feature; when they do, they usually tell you. For 'what just happened' questions, search is the right tool.

question: Anything you type into a free chatbot may be:
answer: Used to train future models
choices: Used to train future models
Translated into all languages
Mailed to your relatives
Posted in your school paper
context: Free chatbot services often use conversations for model training (their terms of service usually say so). Some pay-for plans or enterprise plans turn this off. Knowing this changes what you should and shouldn't paste — anything truly private, especially identifiers and credentials, doesn't belong in a free chat box.

question: A friend asks you to paste your home address into a chatbot to 'see what it knows.' Smart response?
answer: Don't paste your home address
choices: Don't paste your home address
Paste it and add phone number
Add your social security too
Add your bank password also
context: Don't paste personal identifiers — home address, phone, social security number, bank info — into free chatbot services. The conversation is logged. The data has value. It can be reviewed, repurposed, or exposed. 'Want to see what it knows about you' is a curiosity trap; the answer is rarely worth the data trail.

question: A voice clone of a famous singer is used to make a fake song. How small a sample does the technology usually need?
answer: Just seconds of clean audio
choices: Just seconds of clean audio
Hours of in-person concerts
All their albums together
Their entire life's recording
context: Modern voice-cloning AI needs only a few seconds of clean audio. Famous singers' voices are everywhere — songs, interviews, podcasts — so cloning their voice is trivial for someone with the tech. Several musicians have spoken publicly about fake AI tracks attributed to them. The technology challenges what it means to 'own' a voice.

question: Out of these four, which is the strongest way to verify a fact a chatbot told you?
answer: Check an established encyclopedia
choices: Check an established encyclopedia
Ask the chatbot again
Ask a second chatbot
Repeat it to a friend
context: Established sources — encyclopedias, government and university websites, major news organizations — are independent of any given chatbot. Asking the chatbot again or asking another chatbot doesn't give independent confirmation; they were often trained on the same data with the same errors. Real verification means a source the AI didn't draw from.

question: Heavy use of em-dashes is sometimes a telltale sign of:
answer: AI-generated writing
choices: AI-generated writing
An old printing press
A foreign translator
A very tired writer
context: Em-dash overuse is one of the famous AI writing tells, along with phrases like 'delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'navigate the complexities,' and overly balanced sentence structure. Real human writers use em-dashes sometimes; AI-generated text uses them constantly. Spotting the pattern is a useful skill for reading online text critically.

question: You see a video of a celebrity endorsing a product. The voice is a little flat and the mouth doesn't quite match. The reasonable assumption is:
answer: It may well be a deepfake
choices: It may well be a deepfake
Real videos always look like that
All endorsements are deepfakes
Celebrities can't say 'no' to ads
context: AI-generated celebrity endorsements are a fast-growing scam category. The voice is often slightly off; the lip-sync drifts; the overall feel is uncanny. If you see a celebrity 'endorsing' a product on social media — especially a get-rich-quick or crypto scheme — assume deepfake until proven otherwise. Check the celebrity's actual verified accounts.

question: A scam call uses a voice clone of your child. What's the FIRST thing to do after hanging up?
answer: Call your child directly
choices: Call your child directly
Mail them a long letter
Send a text very slowly
Send them a paper map
context: Voice-clone 'kidnapping' scams use a fake of a child's voice to claim the child is in danger and money must be sent now. The scam works through urgency. Hang up and call your child directly on the number you already have. If they pick up, the scam is over. If they don't, try other family contacts before doing anything the caller asked.

question: Your sibling wants to use a chatbot to file legal paperwork for an important matter. What's the smart caution?
answer: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
choices: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
Trust the chatbot completely
File it without reading first
Skip lawyers entirely forever
context: AI legal tools can produce documents that look professional but contain wrong citations (the 2023 New York lawyer case is famous), wrong jurisdiction-specific rules, and other errors that matter in court. For important legal matters, talk to a real lawyer. AI can help you prepare questions and understand basics; it shouldn't be your only counsel on something that matters.

question: Out of these four facts, which is MOST important to verify before relying on a chatbot's answer?
answer: A specific historical date
choices: A specific historical date
A general topic summary
The word for an idea
How to spell a common word
context: Chatbots are most error-prone on specific facts — particular dates, specific numbers, specific citations. General topic summaries are usually OK at a high level. The fine details are where hallucinations cluster. Whenever a date, statistic, or specific citation matters for what you'll do with the information, verify it.

question: An online photo of a person has earrings that don't quite match — one large, one tiny. This is most likely a:
answer: Mismatch sign of AI generation
choices: Mismatch sign of AI generation
Trendy new fashion statement
Defect of an old film camera
Sunlight playing optical tricks
context: AI image generators often produce asymmetric earrings, mismatched eye details, or other small details that don't match across left and right. Real photos of real people typically have matching pairs (or at least intentional mismatch). Asymmetric tiny details are a small but reliable AI-image tell.

question: The lesson of the 2023 New York lawyer's ChatGPT court case is mainly about:
answer: Verifying AI citations before using them
choices: Verifying AI citations before using them
Banning chatbots from courts
Lawyers retiring at age 30
Ending the practice of law forever
context: The fines and headlines were memorable; the underlying lesson is general. LLMs produce plausible citations they have no way to verify. If a chatbot cites a source — a court case, a study, a book — and you plan to use the citation, you have to confirm it exists. The lawyer skipped verification; the verification habit is what would have caught the fakes.

question: A chatbot mentions a research study supporting a claim. Before you use the study in an essay, you should:
answer: Search for it to confirm it exists
choices: Search for it to confirm it exists
Trust the chatbot's word for it
Quote it in your conclusion
Make up new claims to add to it
context: Studies, like books and quotes, get confidently invented by chatbots. The author may not exist; the journal may not exist; the conclusion may be backwards. Before citing any study a chatbot mentioned, search for it in a database (Google Scholar is a reasonable starting point), and check that the real study supports what the chatbot claimed.

question: Out of these four, which is NOT a safe defense against voice-clone scam calls?
answer: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
choices: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
Calling the person back directly
Having a family safe word
Asking a question only they'd know
context: Trusting any familiar voice on an unexpected call is exactly what scammers want. Familiar-sounding voices can be cloned. The defenses: call back on a known number, use a family safe word, ask a question only the real person would know. Each of these breaks the scammer's reliance on urgency and audio impersonation.

question: A 'deepfake' is BEST described as:
answer: An AI-altered video of a real person
choices: An AI-altered video of a real person
A typo in a movie credit
A very deep swimming pool
A song stuck in your head
context: A deepfake is a video (or audio) that has been AI-altered to make a real person appear to say or do something they didn't. The technology comes from face-swap and voice-clone AI. Deepfakes are real, they're getting better, and they're used in scams, harassment, and political disinformation. Knowing they exist is the first step in not being fooled.

question: You're helping a parent set up a new chatbot account. What's a good safety rule to share?
answer: Don't share passwords with the chatbot
choices: Don't share passwords with the chatbot
Tell it your social security
Paste your bank info to test
Type all addresses you know
context: Set the safety rule up front: no passwords, no financial account numbers, no full social security or government ID numbers, no sensitive medical records, no full home addresses. The chatbot won't 'use' the info maliciously by itself, but the conversation is logged and the data has value. Keep the high-sensitivity stuff out of free chatbot inputs.

question: AI-written text often has a pattern where every paragraph carefully presents 'on one hand' and 'on the other hand.' What's this an example of?
answer: Overly balanced AI-style writing
choices: Overly balanced AI-style writing
A new way to write essays
Strong personal opinion writing
Old-fashioned letter writing
context: AI text tends toward overly balanced, hedged, both-sides presentations — partly because it was trained to be 'helpful' and partly because that style appears safe. Real human writing usually has stronger opinions, more uneven attention, and clearer takes. The bland-balance pattern is a useful AI-text tell, especially in opinion pieces and essays.

question: You want to find out what flights are available between two cities tomorrow. Which tool fits this need?
answer: A flight search website
choices: A flight search website
A basic chatbot
A photo-editing app
A calculator program
context: Flight availability is live data — it changes every minute. A basic chatbot has no access to it. A flight search site (or airline app) queries live booking systems and gives you actual options. The general lesson: 'what's available right now' goes to a specific tool that talks to live systems. Chatbots are for drafting, summarizing, and brainstorming, not for live data.

question: A friend sends you a 'personal letter' that uses careful balance, em-dashes, and bland phrasing. What's a reasonable suspicion?
answer: The friend used a chatbot
choices: The friend used a chatbot
The friend speaks five languages
The friend was born in 1850
The friend writes in Latin only
context: AI-style polish in a 'personal letter' is a red flag — real personal letters tend to be rougher, more idiosyncratic, with stronger voice. A perfectly balanced, em-dash-heavy, 'tapestry of'-phrasing letter probably had AI help. This isn't bad in itself — but it's worth knowing when a 'personal touch' came partly from a chatbot.

question: Out of these four sources, which is LEAST suitable for verifying a fact you got from a chatbot?
answer: Another chatbot
choices: Another chatbot
A well-known encyclopedia
A government website
A university website
context: Another chatbot is the worst choice for verification — it was likely trained on overlapping data with the same errors. Encyclopedias, government sites, and university sites are independent of any given AI's training and aim for accuracy. Real verification means a different KIND of source, not the same kind under a different brand name.

question: A video shows a politician saying something they actually didn't say. What's the right defense?
answer: Search the supposed quote in real news
choices: Search the supposed quote in real news
Believe the video because it is clear
Share it before checking the sources
Trust it because it has good subtitles
context: Political deepfakes are a known and growing problem. If a clip would be major news, major news outlets are covering it. Search the politician's name and the supposed quote — if no trusted news source reports it, treat the clip with strong suspicion. Sharing first and checking later is exactly how disinformation spreads.

question: Out of these four content types, which does a chatbot most often invent?
answer: Specific quotes and citations
choices: Specific quotes and citations
Common dictionary definitions
Basic addition for small sums
Spellings of common words
context: Chatbots especially invent specifics — quoted phrases attributed to real people, citations to real-sounding studies, page numbers in real-sounding books, court cases with real-sounding names. Common dictionary definitions and basic math are usually fine. The pattern: the more specific the citation, the more verification matters.

question: Smart home devices with always-on microphones (Alexa, Google Home, Siri-on-speakers) have one general property worth knowing:
answer: The microphone is always listening
choices: The microphone is always listening
They never use any electricity
They communicate only by smell
They turn off completely at night
context: Smart speakers and voice assistants have always-on microphones listening locally for the wake word. Audio after the wake word is sent to the cloud for processing. Both Amazon and Google have had employees listening to clips for quality assurance. Recordings can be subpoenaed by law enforcement. Knowing the mic is on is part of deciding where to put one.

question: Out of these four, which is the simplest free protection against voice-clone family scams?
answer: Set a family safe word
choices: Set a family safe word
Buy more home insurance
Move to a different city
Get a new phone number
context: A family safe word is free, takes five minutes, and stops the entire scam class. It's a short phrase known only to family members. On any unexpected request-for-money call from a 'relative,' you ask for the safe word. A voice clone can't know it. The FBI publicly recommends this — it's one of the simplest defensive habits a family can adopt.

question: Out of these four tasks, which is the worst job for a basic chatbot?
answer: Multiplying two big numbers
choices: Multiplying two big numbers
Writing a poem about clouds
Drafting an outline for an essay
Brainstorming party ideas
context: Chatbots are bad at arithmetic, especially with large numbers or many steps. They're good at drafting, brainstorming, summarizing, rewording. Match the tool to the task: a calculator for the math, a chatbot for the writing. Or use a chatbot product that has a calculator tool bolted on — when it does, it'll usually tell you.

question: A chatbot is most reliable as a:
answer: Starting point for further checking
choices: Starting point for further checking
Final source on any medical issue
Final source on any legal issue
Replacement for all professionals
context: AI is a useful starting point — for questions to ask, for explaining basics, for drafting. It's not a final source on medical, legal, financial, or safety-critical questions where being confidently wrong has real costs. The discipline is to use it as a launching pad for further checking, not as the end of the road.

question: A clearest sign that text was likely written by an AI:
answer: Bland balance and overused phrases
choices: Bland balance and overused phrases
Strong opinions and odd jokes
Typos and inconsistent grammar
Personal stories with specifics
context: AI-generated text tends to be polished, balanced, and full of certain favored phrases. Real human writing has stronger opinions, occasional typos, weirder humor, and concrete personal stories with specifics. Polish + bland balance is not a guaranteed AI tell — but combined with em-dash overuse and stock phrases, it's a strong signal.

question: Out of these four, what's safer to discuss with a free chatbot?
answer: A book you're reading
choices: A book you're reading
Your full credit card number
Your social security number
Your password for the bank
context: Talking about a book you're reading is fine — the chatbot can summarize, suggest similar books, help you write a review. Credit card numbers, social security numbers, and bank passwords are sensitive identifiers that should stay out of free chatbot inputs. The chatbot itself isn't malicious; the data trail is what to watch.

question: TikTok's For You feed picks each next video automatically. What is the system mainly optimized to do?
answer: Keep you watching as long as possible
choices: Keep you watching as long as possible
Show only your friends' videos
Display only educational content
Pick a fully random video clip
context: TikTok's recommendation algorithm is built to maximize engagement, usually measured by watch time and how often you return. It's NOT optimized for accuracy, balance, or your wellbeing. Knowing what it's optimizing for is the first step in deciding what to do about it. The same is true for YouTube, Instagram Reels, and similar feeds.

question: YouTube's 'Up Next' recommendation isn't just suggesting videos — it's running an algorithm trained on what:
answer: Keeps people watching the longest
choices: Keeps people watching the longest
Brings the best news to you
Maintains world peace efforts
Charges the wifi router faster
context: YouTube's recommendation system optimizes for watch time and engagement. The algorithm doesn't 'know' or 'care' what's true — it just promotes whatever keeps people watching. When outrage holds attention longer than calm content, the system learns to surface more outrage. Recognizing this is the start of choosing what to watch deliberately.

question: In some Chinese cities, an AI-powered system scores residents on behaviors like online comments or paying bills. People with low scores can be banned from buying:
answer: Plane and train tickets
choices: Plane and train tickets
Bowls of rice ever
Outdoor blue jackets
Folded paper cranes
context: China's social-credit system is a collection of regional and corporate pilots — not one nationwide program, but real and consequential. Some people have been banned from buying plane and high-speed-train tickets based on low scores. The system uses facial recognition, online tracking, and government records. The pattern (AI as enforcement infrastructure for political compliance) is worth recognizing wherever it appears.

question: Many Chinese cities have heavy use of one particular AI technology — built into cameras everywhere. What is it?
answer: Facial recognition
choices: Facial recognition
Cake recognition
Cloud recognition
Music recognition
context: Facial-recognition cameras are widespread in many Chinese cities. They can identify individuals walking past in real time. The technology is used for many things — from finding lost children to tracking dissidents. The same tech exists in Western cities, often less integrated but rapidly expanding. The pattern of camera + recognition + database is what to watch.

question: Facial recognition AI is also used by some US police departments. One known risk is:
answer: Wrong identifications leading to arrests
choices: Wrong identifications leading to arrests
Forcing cops to wear sunglasses
Making everyone speak French
Reducing the price of coffee
context: Facial-recognition systems have higher error rates on certain demographics. Several US wrongful-arrest cases (Robert Williams in Detroit, 2020 was widely covered) traced back to bad facial-recognition matches. Some US cities have banned police use of the tech; others use it freely. The question of when and how to use it is an active policy debate.

question: A company called Clearview AI built a giant face-recognition database by:
answer: Scraping public social-media photos
choices: Scraping public social-media photos
Buying photos from museums
Drawing portraits on napkins
Tracing photos from movies
context: Clearview AI scraped billions of photos from public social-media pages to build a face-recognition database — without users' consent. The company sold the service mainly to law enforcement. Several countries (Canada, France, Italy, UK) have ordered Clearview to delete data on their citizens. The case shows what 'public' photos can be used for once scraping AI is cheap.

question: When a social-media app recommends a video that makes you angry, what is the algorithm typically rewarding?
answer: That anger gets more engagement
choices: That anger gets more engagement
Anger makes the screen brighter
Anger pays for the wifi bill
Anger feeds the algorithm trees
context: Recommendation algorithms reward engagement — clicks, comments, watch time, shares. Anger-provoking content gets more of all of these than calm content. The system learns this and serves up more. The algorithm has no preference for anger as such; it just notices that anger holds attention, and it promotes whatever holds attention.

question: When you see online ads that seem to know exactly what you've been thinking about, the technology behind it is:
answer: AI-driven ad targeting
choices: AI-driven ad targeting
Wizards reading minds
Tiny cameras in shoes
Bad luck on Tuesday
context: Ad targeting uses AI to match ads to people based on their browsing history, search queries, app usage, demographic data, and 'lookalike' modeling. The matches can feel uncannily accurate; the technology isn't reading your mind, it's pattern-matching against your behavior. Knowing how it works is the first step in noticing when it's hunting you.

question: Some schools use AI software (Gaggle, GoGuardian) to scan student chats and emails on school accounts. What's the general name for this kind of technology?
answer: Student surveillance software
choices: Student surveillance software
School cafeteria software
Math homework software
Library book software
context: Several companies (Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark) sell AI software to schools that scans student communications on school accounts for 'concerning content.' The companies say it helps prevent harm. Critics argue it normalizes surveillance, generates false positives, and chills student expression. The pattern (AI watching young people's communications) is worth being aware of, whatever you conclude about it.

question: When a website's design makes it easy to subscribe but hard to cancel, that's an example of:
answer: Dark patterns in user design
choices: Dark patterns in user design
A typo in the menu
An old printer error
A normal way to build sites
context: 'Dark patterns' are user-interface designs built to push you toward actions that benefit the company at your expense — hidden cancel buttons, pre-checked boxes, confusing wording. AI now optimizes many of these patterns at scale, A/B-testing what works on which users. Recognizing them is the first step in not falling for them.

question: When social-media platforms use AI to remove or label content, the choices reflect:
answer: Decisions made by humans behind the AI
choices: Decisions made by humans behind the AI
Pure mathematical objectivity
Random weather variations
What ducks vote for daily
context: AI moderation tools are trained on examples humans chose. The choices about what counts as misinformation, hate speech, or violations reflect the judgments of the humans doing the labeling — sometimes well-meaning, sometimes ideological. There's no value-free moderation algorithm; what looks like 'just the algorithm' is always the algorithm trained on human choices.

question: In February 2024, Google's Gemini image generator produced images of racially diverse Nazi soldiers and refused to generate white historical figures. What did Google do?
answer: Suspended the image feature
choices: Suspended the image feature
Made it the default forever
Renamed the company Genome
Closed all Google products
context: Google's Gemini image generator had been tuned to inject diversity into prompts. When applied to historical or ethnically specific prompts, the result was historically wrong outputs and refusals on certain prompts. Sundar Pichai apologized; the image feature was suspended. The episode illustrates that 'alignment' choices are choices — they reflect somebody's values.

question: Many apps are designed to maximize 'time on screen.' What's the simplest description of what this means for you?
answer: The app wants more of your attention
choices: The app wants more of your attention
The app wants a higher water bill
The app wants to know your address
The app wants to lower its volume
context: Apps that monetize attention (via ads, in-app purchases, or subscription retention) are usually optimized to maximize time on screen. The AI behind the recommendation, notification, and reward loops is hunting your attention. Knowing the goal helps you notice when you're being optimized — and decide what to do about it.

question: TikTok is owned by which kind of company?
answer: A Chinese company (ByteDance)
choices: A Chinese company (ByteDance)
An American newspaper chain
A European TV station network
A Canadian magazine publisher
context: TikTok is owned by ByteDance, a Chinese company headquartered in Beijing. Chinese law gives the government broad access to data held by Chinese companies. This is the basis of US security concerns about TikTok and the various attempts to force a sale or ban. It's also a recognition question: knowing who runs the platforms you use is part of being a literate user.

question: School software that scans student writing for 'concerning content' tends to produce many:
answer: False alarms about innocent text
choices: False alarms about innocent text
Hidden treats in the lunchbox
Surprise birthday parties
Discounted cafeteria meals
context: Surveillance software trained to flag 'concerning' content tends to produce many false positives — innocent text flagged as worrying. Students learn to write more cautiously, which has its own costs to honest expression. Critics argue that the rate of true catches doesn't justify the chilling effect; defenders point to specific saves. The debate is real on both sides.

question: Recommendation systems on big platforms tend to push viewers toward more extreme versions of their interests. This pattern is sometimes called:
answer: Engagement-driven radicalization
choices: Engagement-driven radicalization
Equal-time content sharing
Educational tracking design
Family-friendly recommending
context: Recommendation systems learn that more intense, more emotional, more extreme content holds attention better. Over time the system pulls viewers toward more intense variations of whatever they started watching — sometimes called 'algorithmic radicalization.' The effects are studied and documented, though the size of the effect is debated. Worth knowing as a user.

question: During the early COVID era, some content was labeled 'misinformation' that was later shown to be at least partly true. The lesson is:
answer: Misinformation labels are not always right
choices: Misinformation labels are not always right
Labels are always perfectly correct
Misinformation labels can be eaten
Misinformation labels glow in dark
context: During 2020-21, social-media platforms labeled or removed posts on topics — masks, lab leak hypothesis, vaccine side effects — that later turned out to be at least partly correct. The lesson isn't that misinformation labels are always wrong; it's that they're applied by humans (or AI trained by humans) and reflect the moment's official consensus. Healthy skepticism toward labels is a defensible reading habit.

question: When you spend ten minutes scrolling because 'one more video' keeps appearing, the design is:
answer: An infinite scroll engagement loop
choices: An infinite scroll engagement loop
Just a coincidence of timing
A feature against your wishes
Random chance from outer space
context: Infinite scroll, autoplay, and notification-loop designs are deliberate engineering choices. They keep you in the app. AI behind them learns which combinations work best on which users. Noticing the loop is the first step in stepping out of it. Some phones now offer screen-time controls that can interrupt the loops — but the underlying design is built to be hard to leave.

question: Some police departments have used AI to predict where crimes are more likely to occur. A real concern with these systems is:
answer: Bias from past arrest data
choices: Bias from past arrest data
Sleepy patrol officers only
Too many traffic cones in town
AI eating police donuts
context: Predictive policing systems are typically trained on past arrest data. If past policing was biased toward certain neighborhoods, the AI learns to send more police there, which produces more arrests, which trains the AI to focus there more. The loop amplifies existing biases. Some cities (Stop LAPD Spying coalition is one example) have organized against these systems.

question: Big platforms remove some videos during health crises. A lesson worth remembering is:
answer: Removed isn't the same as false
choices: Removed isn't the same as false
Removed always means false
Removed videos vanish from clouds
Removed means everyone agrees now
context: Platforms remove content for many reasons — policy violation, government request, internal decision, advertiser pressure. 'Removed' doesn't mean 'proven false' in the scientific sense; it means the platform decided to take it down. Sometimes the decision ages well, sometimes it doesn't. Treating 'this was banned' as evidence about truth is a mistake either way.

question: Facial recognition systems have been used in:
answer: Several US police investigations
choices: Several US police investigations
Wedding cake decoration only
Picking restaurant menu items
Choosing bowling alley colors
context: Several US police departments have used facial recognition to identify suspects in investigations. Some use is uncontroversial (matching a suspect to a known person of interest); some has led to wrongful arrests when the match was wrong. A handful of US cities have banned police use. The debate about when and how to deploy the technology is ongoing.

question: Why does TikTok's algorithm seem to learn what you like so quickly?
answer: It learns from many small signals
choices: It learns from many small signals
It reads your secret diary
It interviews your old friends
It checks your school grades
context: TikTok's For You algorithm learns from watch time per video, rewatches, scroll-past behavior, shares, and pauses — many small signals every minute you scroll. Compared to a 'like button' alone, this gives the AI vastly more data, vastly faster. The speed of learning is a feature for the platform and a hazard for the user, depending on what's being learned.

question: An app that adds little 'badges,' streaks, or rewards for daily use is using a pattern called:
answer: Gamification to drive engagement
choices: Gamification to drive engagement
Random chocolate distribution
Reverse pizza ordering
Quiet whistle blowing
context: Gamification — borrowing game-design elements (badges, streaks, points, rewards) — gets users to return. Combined with AI that learns which rewards work on which users, it can be very effective at building daily habits. It's not inherently bad (some apps gamify good habits like learning), but recognizing the pattern helps you decide whether it's serving your goals or the app's.

question: Some companies use AI to track employees' computer activity — keystrokes, mouse movement, screenshots. The general name is:
answer: Workplace surveillance software
choices: Workplace surveillance software
Workplace coffee machinery
Workplace lunchtime services
Workplace party planners
context: AI-powered workplace surveillance (Microsoft Productivity Score, Hubstaff, and others) tracks employee activity in detail. The trend grew during remote-work years. Critics argue it pressures employees to look busy rather than be productive; defenders say it helps managers identify problems. Knowing about it matters when choosing employers and when negotiating terms.

question: Some big employers use AI to filter job applications before any human sees them. A common concern is that the AI:
answer: Inherits biases from training data
choices: Inherits biases from training data
Reads applications upside down
Refuses to work on Mondays
Eats applications for breakfast
context: AI applicant screening (HireVue, Pymetrics, and others) is trained on past hiring data. If past hiring favored certain backgrounds, the AI learns to favor them too. Amazon famously scrapped one such system in 2018 after it was found to penalize résumés from women. The technology can be reformed, but knowing how it works affects how applicants prepare.

question: Dating apps are optimized for one main thing — but it might not be what users assume. What is it usually?
answer: Keeping users on the app
choices: Keeping users on the app
Finding lifelong partners fast
Reducing the divorce rate
Helping users delete the app
context: Dating apps are usually optimized for engagement and subscription retention — which means keeping users on the platform. A user who finds a lasting partner and leaves stops paying. The business model and the user's stated goal are partly aligned (some matches are needed to keep users hopeful) and partly opposed (long-term success means losing the user). Worth knowing.

question: Sports-betting and online-gambling apps use AI to:
answer: Maximize how much users bet
choices: Maximize how much users bet
Stop users from losing money
Send users to bed early at night
Print physical sports newspapers
context: Online gambling apps use AI to maximize total bets — sending personalized promotions, adjusting offers to recover lapsing users, A/B testing what works on which behaviors. The science of variable-reward schedules is well-understood in psychology, and the apps deploy it intentionally. Knowing the optimization target helps explain why these apps are so sticky.

question: Banks and lenders use AI to score loan applications. A real concern is that the AI:
answer: Inherits patterns of past discrimination
choices: Inherits patterns of past discrimination
Charges extra fees in cash
Refuses to lend on Tuesdays
Reads applications backward
context: Lending AI is trained on past lending decisions. If past lending was biased against certain neighborhoods or groups, the AI learns those patterns and continues them — sometimes called 'algorithmic redlining.' The AI doesn't 'intend' to discriminate, but it inherits the patterns in its training data. Regulations have started to address this, with mixed effectiveness.

question: Open-source AI models like Llama and Mistral are an important countervailing force to:
answer: A small number of closed-model companies
choices: A small number of closed-model companies
Public libraries everywhere
Open-source cooking recipes
Free outdoor playgrounds
context: If only a few large companies control AI models, those companies hold huge influence over what AI is allowed to do, who can build with it, and what gets censored. Open-source models (Llama from Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek) let anyone run AI on their own computer with no central gatekeeper. This isn't unconditionally good — but it's a real countervailing force to concentration.

question: Apps that use AI to maximize your attention typically design notifications that:
answer: Pull you back to the app
choices: Pull you back to the app
Tell you to take a long nap
Remind you to read books
Order delivery from a bakery
context: Notifications are tuned by AI to be exactly attention-grabbing enough to pull you back into the app. They aren't designed to inform — they're designed to interrupt and return. Most phones now let you turn off non-essential notifications. The simplest defense is to default-off and re-enable only when you genuinely want the alert.

question: Chinese internet censorship uses AI to:
answer: Filter and block certain content
choices: Filter and block certain content
Send free birthday cards
Time clocks in shopping malls
Print travel posters in parks
context: China's 'Great Firewall' uses AI-augmented systems to block certain websites, filter messages on Chinese platforms, and detect attempts to bypass the filters. The technology is mature and constantly evolving. Other countries (Russia, Iran, parts of the Middle East) operate similar systems at different scales. Recognizing that AI can serve as censorship infrastructure is part of being literate about its uses.

question: If you find yourself scrolling without intending to, the simplest first defense is:
answer: Set time limits or turn off the app
choices: Set time limits or turn off the app
Buy yourself a faster phone
Get a louder pair of headphones
Subscribe to extra paid features
context: Recognizing that you've been pulled in is the first step. Most phones let you set daily time limits per app. Turning off notifications for the worst offenders is another simple step. Some people delete apps and use them only via the browser, which is less optimized. The defense is choosing deliberately rather than being chosen for.

question: When a recommendation system shows you something you didn't ask for, the algorithm is making:
answer: A bet about what holds your attention
choices: A bet about what holds your attention
A guess about your shoe size
A poem about the weather
A snack for the developer team
context: Every recommendation is a bet — based on your past behavior and others like you — about what will hold your attention next. The algorithm doesn't know what you want; it has a statistical guess. Sometimes its guess is helpful (a song you love); sometimes it's manipulative (a video designed to outrage). Knowing it's a bet, not a judgment, changes how you respond.

question: Out of these four, which is the BEST description of what recommendation algorithms optimize for?
answer: Engagement (clicks, watch time, shares)
choices: Engagement (clicks, watch time, shares)
Truth, fairness, and accuracy
User long-term wellbeing only
Educational depth above all else
context: Recommendation algorithms optimize for what they're measured on — usually engagement, sometimes ad revenue, occasionally a custom 'quality' signal. They are not optimized for truth, balance, or user wellbeing. Some companies have experimented with adding wellbeing signals, with limited results. The default state of the technology is attention-hunting, not user-serving.

question: The single most important fact to know about an app whose business depends on time-on-screen is that it:
answer: Is designed to be hard to leave
choices: Is designed to be hard to leave
Recharges your phone battery
Filters spam from your mail
Mails a postcard to your home
context: Apps that monetize attention are designed to be hard to leave. Autoplay, infinite scroll, push notifications, streaks, badges, and personalized recommendation are all deployed to keep you. This isn't a moral failing of the apps; it's the rational design given the business model. Knowing the design is the first step in choosing how much of your attention to give.

question: A friend says chatbots like ChatGPT 'know' the answer the way a teacher does. What is the chatbot actually doing one piece at a time as it writes?
answer: Predicting the most likely next piece of text, then the next, then the next
choices: Predicting the most likely next piece of text, then the next, then the next
Searching a large library of saved replies and copying the closest match
Translating your question into formal logic and proving the answer step by step
Looking up the question in a giant database the company keeps current daily
context: An LLM has no library of saved replies, no live search, and no formal logic engine underneath. It works by predicting the next token from everything before. Token by token, it builds up a reply. That is the single most important fact about how chatbots work.

question: At dinner your cousin asks how ChatGPT works. The shortest honest answer is one sentence. Which sentence is correct?
answer: It guesses the next word in a sentence, again and again, based on what came before
choices: It guesses the next word in a sentence, again and again, based on what came before
It looks each question up on the internet and writes a careful summary in plain English
It thinks the way a person does, using common sense and quietly weighing what is right
It runs a program your teacher wrote that knows the answer to common school questions
context: ChatGPT's mechanism, plainly stated: predict the next word (token) given the conversation so far. No internet lookup, no human-style thinking, no curated answer file. This is why chatbots are good at writing fluent text and bad at facts they were never trained on.

question: You watch a chatbot's reply appear left to right on the screen. What is the model finishing before showing each new piece?
answer: A guess at the most likely next chunk of text given everything written so far
choices: A guess at the most likely next chunk of text given everything written so far
A request to the web for the next sentence from a trusted news website
A check against an internal fact database before each word is allowed to appear
A vote between three different language models all running in the same room
context: The streaming, typewriter-style effect you see is the model picking one token at a time. It samples each one from a probability distribution over its full vocabulary, then sends it to your screen. Then it does the same thing again for the next token.

question: Your friend believes ChatGPT works by reasoning out the steps of a problem. Closer to the truth, what is it doing?
answer: Generating words that LOOK like reasoning by predicting what reasoning text usually sounds like
choices: Generating words that LOOK like reasoning by predicting what reasoning text usually sounds like
Running formal mathematical proofs that always check out from the first step to the last step
Calling a separate logic engine its programmers built in to solve every kind of problem cleanly
Asking three other chatbots in parallel and showing whichever set of steps the majority picked
context: Modern LLMs can produce 'chain-of-thought' style replies — they list steps that look like reasoning. The model isn't reasoning the way you do; it has learned the shape of reasoning text from its training data. Sometimes the steps add up; sometimes they look correct but the conclusion is wrong. This is why verifying chains of reasoning matters, especially for math and law.

question: An LLM is called 'large' for one specific reason — not because of the company that built it. What is that reason?
answer: The model has a huge number of internal numbers (parameters) and is trained on a huge amount of text
choices: The model has a huge number of internal numbers (parameters) and is trained on a huge amount of text
The chatbot's window takes up the whole screen on most laptops once the user opens it
The data center where it runs covers more floor space than any other building in the area
The reply messages are larger than what older chatbots could write before this generation
context: 'Large' in Large Language Model refers to two things scaled up: parameters (the model's adjustable internal numbers, counted in billions) and training data (the text it learned from, measured in trillions of tokens). The combination is what made modern LLMs work as well as they do compared to predecessors from a decade ago.

question: Strip away the chat interface and the suggestion buttons. What is the one thing an LLM was trained to do?
answer: Take a passage of text and predict the most likely next piece of text that follows
choices: Take a passage of text and predict the most likely next piece of text that follows
Read the user's mind by analyzing typing speed and word choice during the conversation
Browse the internet for facts and rewrite whichever paragraph the user asks about
Carry out a step-by-step plan its programmers wrote out for it before any user typed
context: Underneath the friendly chat wrapper, an LLM is a next-token predictor. The chat behavior, the helpfulness, the refusals — all of those are layered on top through training tricks. The core machine takes text in and predicts text out, one piece at a time. Understanding this one fact resolves most beginner confusions about chatbots.

question: Modern LLMs are trained on truly large amounts of text. Which rough number is in the right ballpark for the training data of a frontier model?
answer: Trillions of words drawn from books, websites, code, and other sources
choices: Trillions of words drawn from books, websites, code, and other sources
About one thousand carefully chosen sample sentences from a school reading list
Roughly one full set of any encyclopedia, copied page by page, plus a small dictionary
Only the most recent year of news articles, with everything older deliberately removed
context: Frontier LLMs are trained on huge text corpora — typically trillions of tokens, drawn from web pages (Common Crawl is a common source), books, code repositories, and other written material. The scale is part of why the results work as well as they do, and it is also why the data the model saw is impossible for any one human to audit by hand.

question: A neighbor asks 'What does LLM stand for, and what is the L there for?'  Your one-sentence answer should mention which two facts?
answer: Large Language Model — and the 'large' refers to the model's size in parameters and training data
choices: Large Language Model — and the 'large' refers to the model's size in parameters and training data
Live Language Module — and the 'live' refers to its always-on connection to the open internet
Logical Learning Machine — and the 'logical' refers to formal proofs built in by programmers
Long-form Listening Mode — and the 'long' refers to how patient it is when waiting for input
context: LLM = Large Language Model. The 'large' captures both the model's number of internal parameters (in the billions for frontier systems) and the amount of training text (trillions of tokens). When the field talks about 'scaling up' an LLM, it means making both those numbers bigger.

question: Neural networks are sometimes called 'brain-inspired.' Why is that a LOOSE description, not a literal one?
answer: Real neurons are far more complex than the simple math units in a neural network
choices: Real neurons are far more complex than the simple math units in a neural network
Brains are made of metal but neural networks are made of biological living cells
Real brains do not use any layers at all, while neural networks always use exactly two
Neural networks contain a small bit of brain tissue, donated by volunteers, in each layer
context: The name 'neural network' comes from a 1940s idea of loosely modeling a brain neuron with a small math unit. Real neurons are chemically and electrically far more complex — and biological brains do not have neat layers or a backpropagation algorithm. The inspiration is real; the literal correspondence is not.

question: The word 'deep' in 'deep learning' refers to a specific design choice. Which one?
answer: Many layers stacked between input and output, instead of just one or two
choices: Many layers stacked between input and output, instead of just one or two
Deep involvement of human reviewers reading every output the model ever produces
A deeper meaning that the model is trying to find behind every word the user types
Deep-blue paint on the outside of the data-center building where the model is running
context: A 'deep' network has many layers — that is all the adjective means. Shallow networks have one or two. Modern frontier models can have dozens or hundreds. The depth (combined with scale and good training tricks) is what powers modern AI. Deep learning is just neural networks with more layers.

question: An AI model lives two distinct stages of life. What are they called and what is the difference?
answer: Training — where weights are learned from data; and inference — where the trained model is used to answer
choices: Training — where weights are learned from data; and inference — where the trained model is used to answer
Sleeping — where the model rests and saves power; and waking — where it gets to work for users
Drafting — where the model writes a rough reply; and editing — where it polishes the same reply
Reading — where the model takes in user input; and writing — where it outputs the new reply
context: Training and inference are the two phases. Training is expensive, slow, and done once (or a few times) by the company building the model — billions of weights get adjusted to fit the data. Inference is what you do every time you chat — the trained weights stay frozen, and the model just runs forward to produce a reply.

question: Training a frontier language model costs a company tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. Once it is done, what about that cost?
answer: It is paid one time; afterwards each user reply costs only a small inference cost on top
choices: It is paid one time; afterwards each user reply costs only a small inference cost on top
It is paid daily; the model has to be fully retrained from scratch at the end of every day
It is paid each time a user logs in; the model trains fresh for each new account that opens
It is paid by users; every user pays a share of the original training bill before they get a reply
context: Training a frontier LLM is a one-time (or sometimes a few-times) capital cost. Once the weights are set, inference — running the trained model to answer questions — is cheap per request. This is why frontier AI is so capital-heavy upfront, and why open weights matter: once weights are released, anyone can run inference cheaply.

question: You type a message to ChatGPT and get a reply two seconds later. The work happening during those two seconds has a specific name. Which?
answer: Inference — running the already-trained model forward to produce the reply
choices: Inference — running the already-trained model forward to produce the reply
Training — adjusting weights based on the new message before the reply can be made
Compiling — turning the user's words into a special programming language for the model
Backups — saving the conversation in case the model needs to learn from it tomorrow
context: Inference is the technical word for using a trained model. Each chat reply you get is an inference call. It is fast (often seconds) and uses far less compute than training. Most of the cost of running a chatbot at scale is inference — millions of users making millions of inference calls.

question: Frontier LLMs are described in 'billions of parameters.' One way to picture this number: if each parameter were a marble, how big a container would 175 billion marbles fill?
answer: Roughly a small swimming pool's worth — enough to make the count hard to picture
choices: Roughly a small swimming pool's worth — enough to make the count hard to picture
Roughly a tea cup's worth — about right for a small modern student's school bag
Roughly a thimble's worth — these counts sound bigger than they really are in practice
Roughly the volume of an entire small country — the units are simply that astronomical
context: 175 billion marbles at 1 cm each would be roughly 175 million liters — about a small swimming pool worth. The point isn't the exact volume; it is that 'billions of parameters' is an inhumanly large number, and that scale is part of why modern AI works and part of why it is expensive.

question: A token is NOT the same as a letter and NOT exactly the same as a word. Roughly, how many English words equal one token on average?
answer: Slightly less than one — about three-quarters of an English word per token, on average
choices: Slightly less than one — about three-quarters of an English word per token, on average
Exactly twenty — one token covers a whole standard paragraph of English text in practice
Exactly one letter — each letter is one token regardless of where it sits in the word
Exactly one full sentence — each token is one complete subject-verb-object sentence
context: Rule of thumb: in English, 1 token is roughly 0.75 of a word (or about 4 characters). The relationship varies by word. 'Cat' is one token. 'Antidisestablishmentarianism' might be six or more. Most punctuation is its own token. Non-English languages often use more tokens per word.

question: Picture a chatbot's context window as a sliding window over your conversation. What slips out of view as the chat grows longer?
answer: The oldest messages — they leave the window first as new ones come in at the other end
choices: The oldest messages — they leave the window first as new ones come in at the other end
The most recent messages — the model deliberately forgets the latest ones to save room
Nothing ever slips out — the window simply grows along with the conversation forever
Random messages from the middle — the model drops one at random whenever it needs room
context: When the chat outgrows the window, the model can only see the most recent tokens that fit. The oldest messages drop out (first-in-first-out). Some chatbot systems compensate by summarizing or storing earlier content elsewhere; vanilla LLMs just lose the early material.

question: An LLM writes a confident sentence containing facts that are simply not true. What is this common failure called?
answer: A hallucination — the model inventing plausible-sounding content with no real basis
choices: A hallucination — the model inventing plausible-sounding content with no real basis
A typo — a fixable small character error easily corrected by the user before sharing
A bug — a software error in the chatbot interface that the company will patch tonight
A virus — a malicious code injection from outside that has compromised this one chat
context: 'Hallucination' is the field's name for the LLM-specific failure where the model produces confident, fluent, completely fabricated content. Fake citations, invented book titles, made-up court cases, wrong dates — all hallucinations. It's not a bug to be patched; it is downstream of how next-token prediction works.

question: Which kind of fact is an LLM especially likely to hallucinate?
answer: Specific dates, names, and citations — exactly the things that need to be looked up
choices: Specific dates, names, and citations — exactly the things that need to be looked up
General opinions about taste in food — these the model gets exactly right every time
Statements about how to spell common English words — these are uniformly accurate
Definitions of common everyday objects — these are never wrong, even at the edges
context: Hallucination shows up especially on facts that require precision — dates, names, page numbers, court case citations, scientific paper titles. The model produces something that sounds right because the words around it sound right. Always verify dates and named references from a chatbot against a trusted source before using them.

question: Your AI essay quotes a study that you cannot find anywhere online. What's the right move?
answer: Treat the study as likely invented — leave it out unless you can verify it from another source
choices: Treat the study as likely invented — leave it out unless you can verify it from another source
Use the study anyway — chatbots are too smart now to invent something out of thin air
Ask the same chatbot if the study is real — its confirmation is enough for a school essay
Cite the chatbot itself as the source — that way the teacher can decide if it counts or not
context: When you cannot find a study, book, or court case the AI cited, the most likely explanation is that the model made it up. Asking the chatbot 'is this real?' rarely helps — the model has no way to check. The reliable move: verify any citation from an LLM against a trusted source. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

question: Your dad asks 'Can I use ChatGPT instead of Google to find current news?' What is the honest answer?
answer: No — a basic LLM has no live web access, so news is the wrong job for it
choices: No — a basic LLM has no live web access, so news is the wrong job for it
Yes — chatbots and search engines do exactly the same job underneath the hood
Yes — ChatGPT is a search engine; the chat interface is just an alternate version of Google
No — search engines are slower than chatbots, so chatbots are the better choice for current news
context: An LLM is a pattern-completion engine, not a search engine. A vanilla chatbot has no internet access and no fresh data. Some chatbots (including newer versions of ChatGPT) have search tools attached as separate features, but the base model is still pattern completion. For news, weather, sports scores — use a search engine or a news app.

question: Search engines and chatbots LOOK alike in the chat box, but they do different things underneath. Which sentence captures the key difference?
answer: A search engine finds existing web pages; an LLM produces new text by predicting tokens
choices: A search engine finds existing web pages; an LLM produces new text by predicting tokens
A search engine works only in the United States; a chatbot is available anywhere on Earth
A search engine costs money for every query; a chatbot is always free in every country today
A search engine ranks results by popularity; a chatbot ranks results by user politeness only
context: A search engine indexes the web and returns existing pages. An LLM generates new text. Different mechanisms, different strengths. Use search for 'find me this real page' and 'what's currently happening.' Use chatbots for drafting, summarizing pasted text, asking explanatory questions on settled topics, and brainstorming.

question: ChatGPT writes you a poem. Stable Diffusion paints you a picture. What kind of model are both?
answer: Generative — they produce new content, whether words, images, or audio
choices: Generative — they produce new content, whether words, images, or audio
Discriminative — they sort each user request into a fixed list of topic categories
Reinforcement — they receive a score from a teacher after every response they make
Symbolic — they apply hand-written rules to come up with the words or paint colors
context: Both ChatGPT (text) and Stable Diffusion (images) are generative — they output new content. 'Generative AI' is the umbrella term, and it covers text, image, audio, video, code, and more. The recent boom in AI products is mostly generative. Behind the scenes, discriminative AI is still humming along (your inbox spam filter, your bank's fraud detection).

question: Your email's spam filter sorts each new message into 'spam' or 'not spam.' What kind of model is doing this?
answer: A discriminative classifier — it labels existing email as belonging to one of two categories
choices: A discriminative classifier — it labels existing email as belonging to one of two categories
A generative model — it writes a brand-new spam version of each message you receive
Neither one — spam filters use a different family of method that has nothing in common with ML
Reinforcement learning — the filter is being rewarded for catching each spam message it labels
context: Spam filtering is a classic discriminative task. The model takes an email and outputs a label (spam, not spam, or sometimes finer categories). It does not write new content. Spam filters were one of the early commercial wins for ML — a quiet but very useful application that ran for years before the generative-AI boom.

question: In 1950, a British mathematician published a paper asking 'Can machines think?' His proposed test became one of the most-cited ideas in AI. Who was he?
answer: Alan Turing, who proposed an imitation game between a human and a machine
choices: Alan Turing, who proposed an imitation game between a human and a machine
John von Neumann, the Hungarian-American architect of early stored-program computers
Norbert Wiener, the MIT mathematician who coined the term 'cybernetics' in 1948
Claude Shannon, the Bell Labs founder of modern information theory
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' opened with 'I propose to consider the question, can machines think?' He answered by proposing the imitation game — what is now called the Turing test. Turing had also broken the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during WWII and is widely considered a founder of computer science.

question: Turing's 1950 paper had a specific title that is still cited today. Which one?
answer: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — published in the philosophy journal Mind
choices: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — published in the philosophy journal Mind
'On Thinking Machines' — published in the journal of the Royal Society in London
'The Imitation Game' — a popular pamphlet distributed by the British government in 1950
'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' — published at Bell Labs in 1948 by Shannon
context: Turing's paper was titled 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' and appeared in Mind, a philosophy journal. The choice of venue is interesting — a working mathematician publishing a careful philosophical argument. The paper proposed the imitation game, anticipated several objections, and gave thoughtful responses. It is still readable today and remains a starting point for thinking about machine intelligence.

question: Before his 1950 paper, Turing had already done important wartime work that helped defeat Nazi Germany. What did he work on?
answer: Breaking the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II
choices: Breaking the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II
Designing the first American rocket engine for the V-2 weapons program in California
Translating intercepted radio broadcasts at the British embassy in Stockholm during 1942
Writing speeches for Winston Churchill at the prime minister's wartime offices in London
context: Turing's wartime work at Bletchley Park helped break Enigma — the German military's main cipher system. The Bombe machine he co-designed automated parts of the codebreaking process. Estimates suggest the work shortened the war in Europe by months or years and saved many lives. The work was classified for decades; Turing's role was not widely known until the 1970s.

question: When people today say 'a chatbot passed the Turing test,' which kind of evidence are they usually pointing to?
answer: Human judges could not reliably tell the chatbot's writing from a real person's in conversation
choices: Human judges could not reliably tell the chatbot's writing from a real person's in conversation
The chatbot won a chess tournament against ten human players in a row at one event
The chatbot earned a passing grade on a standardized school math examination test
The chatbot received a degree from a respected university for its public writing samples
context: The classic Turing test is about conversation: can a hidden machine fool a human judge into thinking it is also human? Modern LLMs do often pass casual versions of this test. Turing himself thought the test would be passed by the year 2000; the actual date is debatable but probably around the early 2020s for everyday conversation. Note: passing the test isn't proof of consciousness — it's proof of conversational imitation.

question: Why is Alan Turing considered a founder of computer science as well as a founder of AI?
answer: His earlier 1936 work on the 'Turing machine' is one of the foundations of modern computing
choices: His earlier 1936 work on the 'Turing machine' is one of the foundations of modern computing
He founded the world's first computer company in Cambridge with profits from his book sales
He invented the first commercial computer language in 1959 with his colleagues in London
He patented the integrated circuit in 1957, becoming the inventor of the modern computer chip
context: Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' described what we now call a Turing machine — a simple theoretical device that could compute anything a modern computer can. This abstract model became the foundation for computer science. Layered with his wartime codebreaking and the 1950 imitation game, Turing's contributions span both computing and AI.

question: Claude Shannon, one of the four 1956 Dartmouth organizers, is famous for an OTHER landmark work eight years earlier. Which one?
answer: His 1948 paper founded information theory, including the concept of the 'bit' as a unit
choices: His 1948 paper founded information theory, including the concept of the 'bit' as a unit
His 1948 paper introduced the first commercially successful computer language ever made
His 1948 paper announced the first transistor at Bell Labs to the wider public scientific world
His 1948 paper was the first to describe the design of a working artificial neural network
context: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' founded information theory. It introduced the bit (binary digit) as a unit of information, defined channel capacity, and gave us tools that underlie modern digital communication, compression, and error correction. Shannon, working at Bell Labs, was already a legend by 1956 when he co-organized the Dartmouth meeting.

question: Marvin Minsky, co-organizer of the 1956 Dartmouth meeting, went on to co-found which famous AI lab?
answer: The MIT AI Lab, which he co-founded with John McCarthy in 1959
choices: The MIT AI Lab, which he co-founded with John McCarthy in 1959
The Stanford AI Lab, which became the West Coast hub for early AI research in the 1960s
The IBM Watson Research Center, which would later build the Jeopardy-winning system
The Bell Labs AI Lab, the early industrial leader through the 1960s for AI research
context: Marvin Minsky co-founded the MIT AI Lab with John McCarthy in 1959. McCarthy then left for Stanford in 1962 and founded the Stanford AI Lab. The two labs were the East Coast and West Coast hubs of US AI research for decades. Minsky stayed at MIT for his whole career and was an influential thinker — sometimes a skeptic of the very neural-network methods that would later dominate.

question: Why did John McCarthy coin the new term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 workshop instead of using an existing term?
answer: To distance the new work from Norbert Wiener's earlier 'cybernetics' tradition
choices: To distance the new work from Norbert Wiener's earlier 'cybernetics' tradition
Because the US Department of Defense would only fund research with that exact name
Because Alan Turing had banned the use of the word 'intelligent' from all of his papers
Because the British Royal Society had already trademarked the term 'machine thinking'
context: McCarthy later explained that he wanted to mark the new field as different from Wiener's cybernetics — the earlier postwar movement that studied feedback systems and intelligence in animals and machines together. By coining 'artificial intelligence,' McCarthy carved out a research program focused specifically on machines that perform tasks requiring intelligence. The new term stuck — and seventy years later, almost everyone in the field uses it.

question: The Dartmouth proposal asked for funding for a single summer's research. What was their actual stated goal?
answer: To make a significant advance in machine intelligence over two months of summer work
choices: To make a significant advance in machine intelligence over two months of summer work
To finish a complete artificial brain by the end of the summer for the US Air Force
To translate the entire Bible into a computer language by the end of August in one go
To prove that machines could never be intelligent, so the field could be shut down again
context: The Dartmouth proposal — read with hindsight — was wildly optimistic. The organizers thought significant progress could be made over a single summer if a small group of bright researchers worked together. Seventy years later, the deeper problems they identified are still being worked on. The optimism wasn't wrong about the importance of the questions — only about how soon they could be solved.

question: Looking back from today, what's the most important thing the 1956 Dartmouth workshop accomplished?
answer: It launched AI as a named, organized research field that grew steadily for the next 70 years
choices: It launched AI as a named, organized research field that grew steadily for the next 70 years
It built the first working chatbot, which was demonstrated at the end of the eight-week meeting
It produced a single mathematical proof that solved most outstanding problems in computer science
It convinced the US Congress to pass the first ever law regulating computer-based machinery
context: Dartmouth 1956 didn't produce specific big technical results that summer. Its real legacy was launching AI as an organized research field with a name, a community, and an ambition. The participants left to found labs at MIT, Stanford, CMU, and IBM that would dominate the field for decades. Most of what AI accomplished in the next 70 years can be traced back through those labs to that summer.

question: In 1958, John McCarthy invented a programming language that would shape AI research for decades. What was it called?
answer: LISP — designed for symbolic computation and built around lists of expressions
choices: LISP — designed for symbolic computation and built around lists of expressions
BASIC — invented for teaching, with simple line-numbered statements throughout
COBOL — designed for business data processing on early commercial computers
Pascal — built for teaching structured programming to college students worldwide
context: LISP — short for List Processing — was designed by McCarthy for symbolic AI work. Its lists-of-lists structure and code-as-data approach made it ideal for writing programs that could examine and modify other programs. LISP dialects (Common Lisp, Scheme, Clojure) are still in use today. Many ideas from LISP — garbage collection, dynamic typing, first-class functions — became standard in later languages.

question: LISP is famously one of the OLDEST programming languages still in use today. Which one is older?
answer: Fortran, designed at IBM in 1957 for scientific and engineering computation
choices: Fortran, designed at IBM in 1957 for scientific and engineering computation
Python, designed by Guido van Rossum in the 1990s for general-purpose programming
C, designed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972 for system programming work
Algol, designed by an international committee in 1958 but never gained wide commercial use
context: Fortran (1957) is the oldest high-level programming language still in widespread use. LISP (1958) is the second-oldest. The two were designed for different audiences — Fortran for scientific number-crunching, LISP for symbolic AI work — but both shaped the field. Most languages students learn today inherit ideas from one or both.

question: Backpropagation is the algorithm that lets a neural network learn from its mistakes. In plain words, what does it do?
answer: It computes how much each weight contributed to the error and nudges it in a helpful direction
choices: It computes how much each weight contributed to the error and nudges it in a helpful direction
It backs the model up to the previous task whenever it makes a mistake during training
It runs the training data backwards through the network to test the model's memory of it
It deletes the layer that was responsible for the worst predictions during this round of work
context: Backpropagation answers the question 'which weight should I change, by how much, to reduce my error?' It does this layer by layer, working from the output backward to the input. Combined with gradient descent, it powers almost all modern neural-network training. The 1986 paper turned backprop from a niche idea into a practical tool — kickstarting the long path that led to today's deep learning.

question: Geoffrey Hinton is sometimes called a 'godfather of AI.' He shares that informal title with two other researchers who won the 2018 Turing Award with him. Who?
answer: Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio — together honored for deep-learning contributions
choices: Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio — together honored for deep-learning contributions
John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky — both already passed away before the Turing Award arrived
Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis — leaders of OpenAI and DeepMind at the time of the prize
Alan Turing and Claude Shannon — both posthumous winners as recognized founders of AI
context: Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award (the 'Nobel of computing') for their work on deep neural networks. The three had championed neural-network research during years when it was unfashionable. The award marked the moment when deep learning's success was widely acknowledged as the foundation of modern AI.

question: Before backpropagation became widely used in 1986, neural networks had a reputation problem. What had pushed them out of fashion?
answer: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' pointed out limits of single-layer networks
choices: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' pointed out limits of single-layer networks
A US Senate hearing in 1969 voted to ban all neural-network research at federal universities
Neural networks were tested in court in 1969 and ruled unsafe by a panel of judges in California
All neural-network code was lost when a major university lab burned down in late 1969
context: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' showed that single-layer networks could not learn certain simple functions (like XOR). The book was technically correct but was widely read as discrediting neural networks overall. Funding dried up — part of the first 'AI winter.' Backpropagation revived the field by showing multi-layer networks could learn things single-layer ones could not.

question: In May 1997, an IBM computer became the first to defeat a reigning world chess champion in a full match. Which year and event was this?
