Their phone battery drains faster because AI uses a lot of phone power
context: Skill is built by doing the work. When AI does the math, the outlining, the summarizing, your own brain doesn't practice. Over a school year, the gap shows up — first in tests you can't use AI on, then in any real-world task that depends on the skill. AI is useful as a second brain that comments on your work; outsourcing the work to AI is the trap. Same logic applies to adults learning new skills.

question: Which of these claims from a chatbot deserves the strongest verification before you act on it?
answer: A specific date, name, number, or citation
choices: A specific date, name, number, or citation
A general description of what photosynthesis does in plants
A definition of a common word you already partly know
A summary of what a fairy tale is generally about overall
context: Hallucinations cluster on specifics. Dates, named people, exact numbers, citations to real-world sources — these are the hot zones for confident fabrication. Broad descriptions of well-known concepts (photosynthesis, fairy tales, basic math) are usually safer because the answer is overdetermined by training data. Spend your verification effort on the specifics.

question: A friend asks a chatbot for legal advice on a custody dispute and is ready to act on the answer. What should you tell them?
answer: Use it to prepare questions for a real lawyer, not as a substitute
choices: Use it to prepare questions for a real lawyer, not as a substitute
Trust the chatbot because it has read every legal book ever
Have the chatbot represent the friend at the actual custody hearing
Skip the lawyer because the chatbot is faster and cheaper to consult
context: Legal and medical advice from a chatbot is risky for the same reason. The chatbot is producing plausible-sounding text, not consulting a real case or applying real judgment to your situation. Worse, it has no skin in the game — bad advice doesn't cost it anything. Use AI to orient yourself, draft questions, and learn vocabulary. Decisions go through a human professional with credentials and accountability.

question: A kid wants to use AI as a tutor for fractions. What's a productive approach?
answer: Ask the AI to explain steps and check the kid's work, not do the work
choices: Ask the AI to explain steps and check the kid's work, not do the work
Have the AI do the homework so the kid can move on to other shows
Use the AI to mock the kid when they get a problem wrong on purpose
Have the AI tell the kid that fractions are too hard to learn forever
context: AI is a useful tutor when it explains, checks, and asks Socratic questions — but the kid is doing the actual work. Having the AI solve problems while the kid watches builds nothing. Productive prompts: 'Explain the steps for adding fractions with different denominators' or 'Here's my answer; what did I do wrong?' Many kids' tutoring apps now have AI built into this Socratic frame on purpose.

question: A free app on your phone wants permission to use the microphone, camera, location, and contacts. The app is a flashlight. What should you do?
answer: Deny the permissions or choose a different flashlight app
choices: Deny the permissions or choose a different flashlight app
Grant all four because permissions don't matter on free apps
Buy the paid version of the flashlight to get even more permissions
Trust the app because the icon on your phone looks professional
context: A flashlight needs the LED. It doesn't need your microphone, your camera, your location, or your contacts. Apps that ask for more than they need are typically harvesting data to sell. The rule: grant only what the app actually needs to do its stated job. If the permissions list doesn't match the function, choose a different app. Both iOS and Android let you review and revoke permissions any time.

question: A browser extension promises to 'add AI to every website' for free. What's a fair concern before installing it?
answer: It may be reading and sending the content of every page you visit
choices: It may be reading and sending the content of every page you visit
It might slow your computer's keyboard response by a tiny amount
It could change the color of the buttons on your favorite website
It might make your laptop fan run louder when you scroll quickly
context: A browser extension with 'access to all websites' permission can read every page you load — including your email, your banking screens, your private messages. Some 'free AI' extensions exfiltrate that content to their servers. Before installing, look at what the extension is allowed to do and who built it. Established companies with skin in the game are safer than unknown developers. If a permission seems wide, it probably is.

question: A student uses ChatGPT to write their entire history essay and submits it as their own. What outcome is realistic?
answer: The teacher likely spots the AI tells, and the student didn't learn the material
choices: The teacher likely spots the AI tells, and the student didn't learn the material
The student gets a perfect grade and full mastery of the topic for free
The chatbot delivers the essay to the teacher with the student's name
The student is automatically expelled from every school in the country
context: Teachers see AI-written work all the time now. The em-dashes, the 'delve into,' the bland-but-correct argument structure, the suspicious consistency — they add up. Detection isn't perfect (and some innocents get accused), but it's good enough that the strategy fails often. And even when it succeeds, the student learned nothing. Use AI as a tutor or editor, not as a ghostwriter.

question: A chatbot writes a glowing description of a small town that mentions a historic battle there. You've never heard of the battle. What's the move?
answer: Search the battle name; if no real source comes up, treat it as invented
choices: Search the battle name; if no real source comes up, treat it as invented
Add the battle to your essay because the chatbot sounds authoritative
Ask the chatbot to confirm and quote its second answer as proof
Tell your teacher you found a hidden battle the textbooks don't list
context: Chatbots often invent small details to make text more vivid — a battle, a famous resident, an old factory that gave the town its name. The invented detail sounds plausible because the model has seen many real ones like it. Defense: any specific historical claim from a chatbot gets verified before you use it. If the search produces nothing real, the chatbot made it up. The whole town might be real; the colorful detail often isn't.

question: By default, an ordinary chatbot doesn't actually browse the live web. What does that mean for current events?
answer: It can't tell you about events from this week or yesterday
choices: It can't tell you about events from this week or yesterday
It downloads the entire internet again every twenty-four hours
It checks the live web after every message you send to be sure
It refuses to discuss any topic that occurred in the last decade
context: A vanilla chatbot has no live web access — it knows only what was in its training data. Some chatbot products add a 'browse the web' tool you can enable. Many free versions don't. When you ask 'what happened today,' the model either says it can't say or invents something. Trust currentness only when the chatbot explicitly says it just searched. Otherwise, for fresh information, use search.

question: When should you use a chatbot, and when should you use a search engine?
answer: Chatbot for explanation and drafting; search engine for current facts and primary sources
choices: Chatbot for explanation and drafting; search engine for current facts and primary sources
Chatbot for everything because search engines are outdated technology
Search engine for everything because chatbots are never right anywhere
Whichever loads faster at the moment you happen to need an answer
context: The two tools are best at different things. Chatbots are great at explaining a concept, drafting a paragraph, brainstorming, or summarizing a passage you paste in. Search engines are better at finding current facts, primary sources, and authoritative pages on specific topics. Using them together — chatbot to orient, search to verify — is stronger than either alone. The trap is using a chatbot as a search engine and getting confidently wrong answers.

question: A grandparent receives a tearful voicemail in their grandchild's exact voice asking for bail money. The defense before this happened was supposed to be set up when?
answer: Earlier, calmly, before any crisis call, when the family picks a safe word together
choices: Earlier, calmly, before any crisis call, when the family picks a safe word together
Right now in the panic, while the scammer is still on the line
Only after several family members have already lost money first
Whenever the bank requires it during a transfer authorization form
context: The whole point of a safe word is that it's agreed in advance, in calm conditions, before any scammer applies pressure. In a real emergency, the family member just says it — and you know it's them. If you wait until the call comes to start figuring out a defense, the scammer has already won the framing. This is why families that have read about voice-clone scams should set the safe word at the next family dinner.

question: An employee uses a free chatbot to summarize a confidential company report. What risk does the company face?
answer: The chatbot company may store the report and possibly train on its contents
choices: The chatbot company may store the report and possibly train on its contents
The chatbot will email the report directly to competing companies
The chatbot will refuse and post the report on social media platforms
The chatbot will translate the report into German for no reason
context: Free chatbots typically log conversations and may train on them. When an employee pastes a confidential document, that document leaves the company's control. Several large firms (Samsung, banks, hospitals) have publicly banned employee use of free chatbots for this reason. Companies that want to use AI on confidential data buy enterprise plans with contractual no-training, no-logging terms — or run open-weight models on their own hardware.

question: A chatbot answers a question with confident bullet points and a clean summary. Does the polished format mean the answer is correct?
answer: No — fluent and confident output can still be wrong
choices: No — fluent and confident output can still be wrong
Yes — chatbots format clearly only when they are certain
Yes — the formatting is generated by a separate fact-checking program
Yes — bullet points indicate the chatbot ran a database query first
context: Chatbots produce fluent, formatted, confident text by default. The formatting is part of the generation, not a sign of correctness. A wrong answer with bullet points reads just as authoritatively as a right one. The fluency is a deception trap — humans subconsciously trust well-formatted text more. Train yourself to separate 'looks polished' from 'is accurate.' Always verify specifics before you act on them.

question: Why is a person's ear sometimes a giveaway in AI-generated photos?
answer: Ears have complex folds that AI tools often render asymmetrically or with wrong details
choices: Ears have complex folds that AI tools often render asymmetrically or with wrong details
Ears are larger in real photos than in AI photos by exactly twenty percent
AI tools refuse to draw ears and always cover them with hair
Ears glow in AI photos because the model adds light to every face
context: Ears have intricate folds and ridges that vary subtly between people. AI image models often slip on them — ears that don't match each other (asymmetric), missing folds, fused edges, or unusual shapes. Plus, jewelry, hair, and earrings interact with ears in ways that confuse the model. Photographers' tip: zoom in on the ears of any suspicious image. It's a low-glamour but reliable tell.

question: Two AI text tells are 'delve into' and 'tapestry of.' What about them is the giveaway?
answer: They appear too often, in the wrong contexts, like a tic
choices: They appear too often, in the wrong contexts, like a tic
They are words that don't actually exist in any English dictionary
They are spelled wrong every time an AI model uses them
They are translated from a language no human speaker uses today
context: 'Delve into' and 'tapestry of' are real English phrases. Humans use them. The tell is overuse — they show up at the start of paragraphs, in conclusions, in casual contexts where a human would just say 'look at' or 'mix of.' The frequency and contexts are the signal, not the phrases themselves. Same with 'navigate the landscape,' 'in the realm of,' 'multifaceted.'

question: You stop using a chatbot service and decide to remove your account. What's a reasonable next step?
answer: Request account deletion through the service's settings or contact form
choices: Request account deletion through the service's settings or contact form
Change your computer's wallpaper and consider the account fully deleted
Move to a different country so the service can no longer find you
Wait for the service to notice you've left and delete you on its own
context: EU users have a legal right to deletion under GDPR; California residents have similar rights under CCPA. Most services worldwide now offer some kind of account deletion in settings — though they may keep some data for legal compliance. Deletion of past chat logs is a separate request. If you've shared sensitive content, deletion is a partial defense but not perfect (already-trained models retain whatever they learned).

question: Why does AI-generated text inside images often look like letters but spell nothing?
answer: The model renders letter shapes without truly understanding spelling
choices: The model renders letter shapes without truly understanding spelling
The model deliberately scrambles text to protect against copying
The image was photographed through a fogged camera lens carefully
The text is written in a language that doesn't have any words yet
context: Image generation models learn what letters look like — strokes, curves, density — without an internal 'spelling' module. They reproduce the visual texture of writing. The result: signs, labels, and book titles inside generated images look like letters at a glance but don't spell anything real when you read them. Newer models do better on short, common words. Long phrases on a sign in the background are still a strong tell.

question: An AI gives a confident answer that contradicts what your teacher said in class today. Whose judgment wins?
answer: Yours, after thinking carefully, and probably your teacher's first
choices: Yours, after thinking carefully, and probably your teacher's first
The AI's, because computers are more accurate than human teachers
Whichever sounds longer, because length means more research
Your friend's, because they were sitting closer to the screen earlier
context: AI as tool, not authority. A chatbot can be wrong even when it's confident; a teacher can be wrong even when they're certain. Your job is to think about it. In subjects with established consensus (math, science, history dates) check primary sources or textbooks. In contested topics, AI and teacher are both inputs. Don't outsource the conclusion. Disagreement between authorities is an invitation to think, not a tie-break by who has more letters after their name.

question: Which kind of question is a chatbot most likely to answer reliably without you needing to check?
answer: Definitions and explanations of well-established ideas
choices: Definitions and explanations of well-established ideas
Specific dates and citations to particular books and articles
Statistics and rankings for very recent events this week
Lists of named people who said particular sentences once
context: Chatbots are most reliable on broad, well-documented topics — what photosynthesis is, what a metaphor is, how an electric motor works. The training data covers these many times in many sources. They're least reliable on specifics: dates, citations, statistics, exact quotes, recent events. Spend your verification effort on the specifics; trust broad explanations more, but stay alert if the topic is unfamiliar to you.

question: TikTok's For You page, YouTube's recommendations, and Instagram's Reels all share one main goal. What is it?
answer: Maximize the time you spend on the platform
choices: Maximize the time you spend on the platform
Show only news verified by independent fact-checkers worldwide
Show only educational videos that teach a single new skill daily
Display videos in strict alphabetical order by uploader name
context: Recommendation systems are optimized for engagement — time spent, sessions per day, shares, return visits. They are NOT optimized for whether what you watch is true, balanced, or good for you. The simplest fact about how these systems work, and the most important one to internalize. The system isn't your friend; it isn't your enemy; it's measuring time-on-platform and surfacing whatever increases it.

question: If outrage-driving content gets more engagement than calm content, what does an engagement-maximizing system learn?
answer: To surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards
choices: To surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards
To filter out the outrage because designers prefer calm content
To rotate evenly between calm and outrage minute by minute always
To switch off completely whenever any outrage is detected on screen
context: Optimization systems do exactly what they measure. If outrage holds attention longer than agreement, the system learns to feed you outrage. If fear is more sticky than reassurance, fear wins. The effects are documented at scale — Frances Haugen's 2021 Facebook disclosures, Jonathan Haidt's research on adolescent mental health. The fix isn't 'better AI'; it's recognizing what the system is doing and choosing not to be optimized.

question: China has piloted systems in several cities that score residents based on things like jaywalking, bill payment, and online comments. What are these systems usually called?
answer: Social credit systems
choices: Social credit systems
Citizen confidence ratings
Behavioral pension plans
Civic patience awards
context: China's social credit system isn't one unified nationwide program — it's a collection of regional and corporate pilots. Some are real and consequential. In documented cases, people with low scores have been banned from buying plane and high-speed-train tickets. The system uses facial recognition, online tracking, and government records. Western coverage sometimes exaggerates centralization, but the core pattern (AI as enforcement infrastructure for political compliance) is documented and worth recognizing.

question: In China's social credit pilots, what kind of penalty has actually been documented for people with low scores?
answer: Being banned from buying plane or high-speed-train tickets
choices: Being banned from buying plane or high-speed-train tickets
Being forced to change their name to something the state picks
Being painted on the side with a colored mark for life
Being sent into outer space on a one-way rocket trip
context: Documented social credit penalties have included travel restrictions — bans on buying high-speed rail tickets, plane tickets, certain hotel stays — for people on judicial blacklists. Other reported penalties include slower internet speeds, loss of access to certain jobs, and naming-and-shaming displays. The system is patchier and less centralized than some Western descriptions, but the documented penalties on real people are not exaggerated.

question: In many large Chinese cities, facial recognition cameras are widespread. What everyday activity has been gated by them in some places?
answer: Entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings
choices: Entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings
Buying a loaf of bread anywhere in any small village ever
Watching the morning sun rise from a hilltop with friends
Choosing what to plant in a private home garden each spring
context: China has deployed facial recognition at enormous scale. Documented use cases include subway entry, school check-in, residential access in some compounds, store payments, and policing. Cameras are integrated with government identity databases. The build-out is uneven across regions and has met some resistance. Recognition: surveillance infrastructure is a deployment decision, not a property of AI itself — the same tools can be built and not deployed, or restricted by law.

question: Clearview AI is a US company that built a face-search tool. Where did the photos in its database come from?
answer: Billions of images scraped from public social media without consent
choices: Billions of images scraped from public social media without consent
A single small contract with one police department's archive
Permission forms voluntarily signed by every person in the system
A children's drawing book purchased from an art-supply store
context: Clearview AI scraped billions of photos from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and other public sources to build a face-recognition database. The company sells access mostly to police and government clients. Several lawsuits in the US and Europe have resulted in fines and bans on selling to private companies. The basic recognition: if your photo is anywhere public, it likely sits in a face-search database somewhere now — and there's no easy way to opt out.

question: Why did Clearview AI become a major lawsuit target in the US and Europe?
answer: It built a face database from social-media photos without asking the people pictured
choices: It built a face database from social-media photos without asking the people pictured
It published every face in its database on a free open website
It only sold its service to children's birthday party planners
It refused to take any photographs of celebrities for any reason
context: Clearview AI faces lawsuits in the US, Canada, UK, Italy, France, Germany, and Australia for scraping public photos and building a searchable face database without consent. Some courts have fined the company and ordered it to stop selling to private clients. The bigger lesson: 'public photo' on social media doesn't mean 'consenting to be in a face-search index.' The legal frameworks are still catching up to the scraping technology.

question: When a free app shows you ads that seem oddly specific to your interests, what's the basic mechanism?
answer: The platform tracks your behavior and sells access to people who match a profile
choices: The platform tracks your behavior and sells access to people who match a profile
The platform reads your mind through the camera at the top of your screen
The platform asks every advertiser to guess what each user might want
The platform shows the same three ads to every user in the world
context: Targeted advertising is built on behavior tracking — apps used, searches made, locations visited, items bought. Platforms build profiles and sell advertisers the ability to target by combinations: 'parents in this zip code who bought baby food this month.' The level of targeting can be uncannily specific. The deal is that the service is 'free' because you are the product. Recognizing this is the first step toward making it a choice.

question: Advertisers can ask platforms to target people who fit a 'lookalike audience.' What's that?
answer: People whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers
choices: People whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers
People who physically resemble the advertiser's CEO in photographs
People whose names start with the same letter as the brand name
People who own the exact same model of phone in the same color
context: 'Lookalike audiences' are an advertising tool offered by Facebook, Google, TikTok, and others. The advertiser uploads their existing customer list; the platform finds users whose behavior pattern resembles those customers and serves them ads. It's effective for the advertiser and uncanny for the user — you start seeing ads for things you didn't know you'd want. Behind the magic: tracking + statistical similarity, scaled across billions of profiles.

question: Most frontier AI models in 2025 are built by a small group of large American companies. Which five are usually named?
answer: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft
choices: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft
Spotify, Netflix, Disney, Hulu, and Discord
Visa, Mastercard, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citi
Adobe, Autodesk, Slack, Zoom, and Salesforce
context: The frontier-AI 'big five' commonly listed in 2025 are OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google DeepMind (Gemini), Meta (Llama), and Microsoft (heavily invested in OpenAI, also building Phi). All US-based. The compute, data, and capital required to train frontier models has produced concentration. Open-source releases from Meta, Mistral (France), DeepSeek (China), and others provide a countervailing force. Recognizing concentration is half the politics of AI.

question: Meta releases its Llama models with weights downloadable. OpenAI keeps GPT weights private. What kind of pressure does open-weight release create?
answer: It limits how much a small group of companies can control the technology
choices: It limits how much a small group of companies can control the technology
It forces every Llama user to pay Meta a small fee for every word
It deletes all the closed models from every server worldwide
It guarantees that all AI uses are safe and ethical for everyone
context: Open-weight models — Llama (Meta), Mistral, DeepSeek, Falcon, Qwen — let anyone with hardware run powerful AI locally. That breaks the monopoly that closed-API companies would otherwise have. You can use the technology without sending every query to OpenAI or Google. The trade-off is that open weights also lower the barrier for misuse. The bank's stance: open source is a major countervailing force to concentration, on balance worth defending.

question: Mistral is a French company that competes with American AI labs. What kind of models does it ship?
answer: Open-weight large language models that anyone can run locally
choices: Open-weight large language models that anyone can run locally
Television sets with built-in AI for European cable customers
Robot vacuum cleaners that translate languages in real time
Wireless routers that block all AI traffic by default everywhere
context: Mistral, founded 2023 in Paris by former Meta and DeepMind researchers, ships open-weight LLMs that anyone can download and run. Mixtral (a mixture-of-experts variant) and Mistral Large are widely used. Mistral is one of Europe's two best-known frontier-AI labs (along with the UK's DeepMind, owned by Google). Their open-weight approach makes them an important counterweight to closed American labs.

question: DeepSeek is a Chinese AI lab that surprised Western researchers in 2024-25. What was the surprise?
answer: Their open-weight models matched leading Western models at much lower training cost
choices: Their open-weight models matched leading Western models at much lower training cost
They built a model that worked entirely without a single computer chip
They claimed to have created a chatbot that could read minds remotely
They abandoned AI entirely to focus on selling printed paper books
context: DeepSeek's V3 and R1 models, released 2024-25, performed competitively with US frontier models at a fraction of the reported training cost. The team released open weights, letting anyone verify the work. The release rattled US AI markets — partly on cost questions, partly because it broke the assumption that frontier AI requires the absolute newest chips. Western export controls on chips to China have shaped the playing field in complicated ways.

question: TikTok is owned by a company called ByteDance. Why does TikTok face political pressure in the US?
answer: ByteDance is based in China, where laws can require data sharing with the government
choices: ByteDance is based in China, where laws can require data sharing with the government
ByteDance refuses to translate any video into the English language
ByteDance makes the same videos appear on Instagram by accident
ByteDance charges users a daily fee to access the For You page
context: ByteDance, TikTok's parent, is headquartered in Beijing. Chinese national security laws (notably the 2017 National Intelligence Law) require Chinese companies to assist intelligence work when asked. US officials worry that data on hundreds of millions of American users — and the algorithm shaping what they see — could be accessible to Chinese authorities. ByteDance disputes this; the US has pursued forced-divestiture legislation. The recognition: who owns the algorithm matters, especially across jurisdictions.

question: In late 2022 and 2023, journalists were given internal Twitter documents about content moderation. What did the documents show, broadly?
answer: US government officials had been coordinating with the platform on content decisions
choices: US government officials had been coordinating with the platform on content decisions
Twitter had been giving free coffee to its 100 most active users daily
Twitter had no employees at all and was run entirely by volunteers
Twitter posts were translated into Mandarin in random batches each week
context: After Elon Musk acquired Twitter in October 2022, he gave selected journalists access to internal documents — the 'Twitter Files.' The releases (December 2022 onward) documented patterns of US government officials requesting content actions, including during the 2020 election and COVID period. Some requests went through normal trust-and-safety channels; others looked more direct. Lawsuits like Missouri v. Biden built on the documents. The recognition: content moderation isn't always purely a platform decision.

question: During the COVID-19 period, social platforms labeled some posts as 'misinformation' that later turned out to be defensible claims. What does this pattern suggest?
answer: Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid
choices: Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid
Labels never affect what users see or share on social media at all
Labels are applied randomly by computer with no human review involved
Labels only existed for one week during the pandemic and never returned
context: During COVID, several claims were labeled 'misinformation' on major platforms that later gained mainstream credence — including discussion of the lab-leak hypothesis (later treated seriously by the FBI and Department of Energy) and certain vaccine side-effect discussions. The pattern matters for AI literacy: content-moderation labels are not neutral verdicts; they're decisions made by a team using a policy at a moment in time. Recognition: the label shapes what users see. Question the label.

question: In February 2024, Google's Gemini image generator produced unusual results — like racially diverse Nazi soldiers — and was suspended. What does the episode show about AI alignment?
answer: Tuning choices made by developers can override historical accuracy
choices: Tuning choices made by developers can override historical accuracy
Image generators don't work on any historical figures from any period
Google deliberately set out to rewrite all of history through its product
The product worked correctly and was suspended for unrelated technical reasons
context: Google's Gemini image generator was tuned to inject diversity into prompts by default — apparently to counter training-data bias. When applied to historical and ethnically specific requests, it produced anachronisms (diverse Nazi soldiers, refused white historical figures). Sundar Pichai apologized; the image feature was suspended. The episode shows that 'alignment' isn't value-neutral — it's a series of choices made by people. Recognizing alignment as a value vector is core AI literacy.

question: What was the Google CEO's public response after the Gemini image-generation controversy of February 2024?
answer: Sundar Pichai apologized and the image feature was suspended
choices: Sundar Pichai apologized and the image feature was suspended
Google denied any issue and ran the same product unchanged
Google's CEO refused to comment for the entire calendar year
Google handed all image generation to a different company within hours
context: After widespread criticism in February 2024, Google CEO Sundar Pichai called the Gemini image-generation outputs 'completely unacceptable.' Google suspended Gemini's people-image generation feature and worked on changes before re-enabling later. The episode became a case study in alignment-as-ideology: a well-intentioned diversity adjustment, layered on top of an opaque pipeline, produced outputs that even the company found indefensible. Useful recognition for any AI product team.

question: In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman. What happened in the next five days?
answer: He was rehired and most of the board members who fired him were gone
choices: He was rehired and most of the board members who fired him were gone
He retired permanently and started a coffee shop in Vermont
He moved OpenAI's headquarters from California to Japan that week
He gave the company to the United Nations to run as a non-profit
context: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired Altman, citing loss of confidence. Within hours, Microsoft (OpenAI's largest investor) offered to hire him and the team. Nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Five days later, Altman was back as CEO; most of the original board was out. The episode showed that formal governance (a non-profit board overseeing a capped-profit company) had little real power against the people building the technology.

question: OpenAI was originally founded as one kind of organization and is being restructured into another. What's the shift?
answer: Founded as a non-profit research lab; later restructured toward for-profit
choices: Founded as a non-profit research lab; later restructured toward for-profit
Founded as a for-profit corporation; later restructured into a museum
Founded as a government agency; later restructured into a private school
Founded as a labor union; later restructured into a sporting league
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit with a stated mission of safe AI development. In 2019 it added a capped-profit subsidiary to raise the capital needed for large-scale training. As of 2024-25, restructuring discussions have included further moves toward a more conventional corporate form. The original non-profit governance structure was tested and largely overridden in November 2023. The pattern (mission-driven nonprofit drifting toward for-profit) is common in fast-growing tech sectors.

question: Researchers have studied how the YouTube recommendation column shapes what people watch. What pattern have they found?
answer: It often nudges viewers toward more extreme or emotionally charged content
choices: It often nudges viewers toward more extreme or emotionally charged content
It always shows calm educational content to every viewer equally
It shows the same five videos every day to every single user
It only recommends videos in the language of the country flag chosen
context: Studies of YouTube's recommendation system have found patterns of escalation — viewers who start with a mildly partisan video are nudged toward more emotionally charged versions, and so on. YouTube has updated its system multiple times in response. The underlying issue isn't politics; it's that emotional content tends to drive more engagement, and an engagement-optimizing system will surface it. Recognition matters more than blame: the metric shapes the output.

question: In 2022, the US Department of Homeland Security announced a 'Disinformation Governance Board.' How long did it last?
answer: It was disbanded within months after public backlash
choices: It was disbanded within months after public backlash
It is still operating today with the original staff in place
It expanded into a cabinet department under a new name
It was sent to the United Nations to operate worldwide
context: DHS announced the Disinformation Governance Board in April 2022. Critics called it a 'Ministry of Truth' echoing Orwell's novel. The board was paused within weeks and formally disbanded by August 2022. The episode illustrates how content-moderation infrastructure looks different depending on who runs it — and how public backlash can curb expansion. Recognition: the line between 'fighting misinformation' and 'speech control' depends entirely on who decides what counts as misinformation.

question: Some US schools use software like Gaggle or GoGuardian to monitor student communications on school accounts. What do these tools do?
answer: Scan student emails, documents, and chats for flagged keywords using AI
choices: Scan student emails, documents, and chats for flagged keywords using AI
Lock students out of school accounts after exactly five hours each day
Translate student work into Spanish without anyone asking them to
Show students cartoon clips during free periods on Fridays
context: Tools like Gaggle, GoGuardian, and Bark scan content created on school accounts — Google Docs, school email, browser activity — looking for flags like self-harm keywords, threats, or 'inappropriate' content. Schools defend the tools as safety measures; critics argue they normalize surveillance and produce false positives. The wider recognition: AI-powered content scanning is increasingly built into platforms used by minors. Students and parents may not know what's monitored.

question: Robert Williams was arrested by Detroit police in 2020 after a facial-recognition match. What was wrong?
answer: The match was wrong, so he wasn't the person in the surveillance image
choices: The match was wrong, so he wasn't the person in the surveillance image
The arresting officers had forgotten to bring handcuffs that morning
Williams had been arrested by mistake on a parking ticket from 1990
Williams had been arrested for jaywalking in a different state
context: Robert Williams, a Black man in Detroit, was arrested in January 2020 after facial-recognition software wrongly matched him to a shoplifting suspect. He was held for 30 hours before being released. His was one of the first publicly documented wrongful arrests from facial recognition in the US — several more have followed. The recognition: face-match systems have higher error rates on dark-skinned faces, and 'the computer matched' is not the same as 'we have the right person.'

question: Some police departments have used 'predictive policing' software that suggests where crime is likely to happen. What's the recurring concern?
answer: The model learns from past patrol patterns, so it sends police back where they already went
choices: The model learns from past patrol patterns, so it sends police back where they already went
The software requires officers to wear special glasses at all times
The model demands a fee from every citizen who appears on its map
The software runs only on rotary phones from the 1970s era
context: Predictive policing tools (PredPol and similar) draw on past crime data to suggest where to patrol. The recurring concern is feedback: more patrols in a neighborhood produce more recorded incidents, which the model reads as confirmation. The cycle can entrench existing patterns of over-policing. Several cities (Santa Cruz, New Orleans) have ended their programs. The recognition: 'data-driven' doesn't mean neutral if the data already reflects choices.

question: In 2013, Edward Snowden's leaks revealed an NSA system that could search internet activity at huge scale. What was it called?
answer: XKeyscore
choices: XKeyscore
Cleanview
Argus Net
Echelon One
context: XKeyscore was one of the NSA programs revealed in 2013 by contractor Edward Snowden. Internal documents described it as letting analysts search 'nearly everything a user does on the internet' through a searchable interface. The Snowden disclosures triggered global debate about surveillance, encryption, and oversight. They also drove adoption of HTTPS and encrypted messaging. AI-era recognition: large-scale surveillance infrastructure existed before the AI boom; AI makes it cheaper and faster to scale.

question: App designers sometimes call certain features 'nudges' — small design choices that push users toward a particular behavior. Why does AI matter here?
answer: AI can personalize nudges to each user, making them more effective
choices: AI can personalize nudges to each user, making them more effective
AI replaces every nudge with a physical poke on the user's shoulder
AI deletes all nudges from every app within a single afternoon
AI confuses nudges with sneezes and removes them automatically
context: 'Nudge' design comes from behavioral economists Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein — small choices in how options are presented that steer behavior. AI lets nudges be personalized: the timing, framing, and content adjust to what works on each user. That's powerful when used for the user's benefit (medication reminders, savings) and concerning when used against it (manipulative checkout flows, gambling dark patterns). The recognition: feature-by-feature, ask who the design serves.

question: Dating apps want to make matches. They also want you to keep using the app. Can those two goals point in different directions?
answer: Yes — if you find a partner and leave, the app loses a user
choices: Yes — if you find a partner and leave, the app loses a user
No — the apps are charities with no incentive to keep anyone
No — finding a partner triggers a free lifetime membership for everyone
Yes — but only on Tuesdays, when the app is open to non-members
context: Dating apps face a real conflict between their users' goal (find a partner and stop using the app) and their business goal (keep users engaged). The result, critics argue, is interfaces optimized for engagement and matches — not necessarily for relationships. Whether this is a fair description depends on the app and the user. The recognition matters generally: when a service's success metric differs from your success metric, expect friction.

question: Many large companies now use AI to screen job applications before any human reads them. What's a typical concern?
answer: The AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed
choices: The AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed
The AI will offer every applicant a guaranteed job at the company
The AI charges each applicant a fee for sending in a resume electronically
The AI prints a paper copy of every resume that is filed forever
context: AI-based applicant screening (HireVue, Pymetrics, and many in-house systems) sifts resumes and sometimes scores video interviews. Concerns include opacity (rejected candidates often get no explanation), shifting criteria the model learned from past hires (which may encode past bias), and difficulty of appeal. Some jurisdictions now require disclosure when AI is used in hiring. The recognition: when you apply for a job, a model may decide whether a human ever sees you.

question: Microsoft introduced a 'Productivity Score' feature for businesses some years ago. Why did it draw criticism?
answer: It scored individual employees in ways that felt like surveillance
choices: It scored individual employees in ways that felt like surveillance
It refused to load on any computer made before the year 2020
It deleted spreadsheets that were too long for any human to read
It changed employee passwords every fifteen minutes for safety
context: Microsoft's Productivity Score, launched 2020, tracked workplace behavior with employee-level identifiers. Critics — including digital-rights advocates — argued it amounted to surveillance of individual workers. Microsoft removed the user-level identifiers after public pushback. The recognition: even productivity tools can become surveillance infrastructure when the data is fine-grained enough to identify individuals. AI scaling makes more such tools possible across more employers.

question: You can now run a capable open-weight language model on a high-end laptop with no internet. Why is that significant?
answer: Your prompts never leave your computer, so no company logs them
choices: Your prompts never leave your computer, so no company logs them
The model can fly between countries to find new information for you
The model erases all data on your hard drive when you start it up
The model invents new languages each time you ask it a question
context: Open-weight models — Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Phi — can be downloaded and run locally with tools like Ollama or LM Studio. A modern laptop can run a competent model. Local models mean prompts never leave your machine: no logging, no training on your conversations, no cloud bill. The trade-off is that local models lag the latest frontier in capability. For privacy-sensitive work, that trade is often worth it.

question: An ad platform offers 'psychographic' targeting. What does that mean?
answer: Targeting people by personality traits, values, or attitudes inferred from behavior
choices: Targeting people by personality traits, values, or attitudes inferred from behavior
Targeting people who happen to be photographers by profession only
Targeting people who live in cities with names that start with P
Targeting people who type in cursive script on touch screens daily
context: Psychographic targeting goes beyond age and zip code: it tries to reach people by inferred personality and attitude (openness, conscientiousness, anxiety, partisan lean). The Cambridge Analytica episode (2016-18) made the term famous and triggered global scrutiny. Modern platforms don't sell psychographic categories directly but do offer 'interest' and 'behavior' targeting that approximates similar groupings. Recognition: the ad you see may not be about who you are — but about which lever the advertiser thought worked on you.

question: China's 2017 National Intelligence Law applies to Chinese companies. What does it say about cooperation with intelligence work?
answer: Chinese organizations and citizens must support, assist, and cooperate when asked
choices: Chinese organizations and citizens must support, assist, and cooperate when asked
Chinese companies are completely exempt from any government request ever
Only state-owned companies must cooperate; private companies are free
The law has been formally repealed and is no longer in effect now
context: China's National Intelligence Law (2017) requires organizations and citizens to support and cooperate with national intelligence work. This is the central legal basis for US concerns about Chinese tech companies (TikTok/ByteDance, Huawei) and their data. Beijing argues the law has limits and oversight; US officials and many analysts read it as compelling cooperation. The recognition isn't about TikTok specifically — it's that ownership jurisdiction shapes who can access platform data.

question: Major social platforms used 'misinformation' labels on certain COVID-related posts. Who decided what counted as misinformation?
answer: Platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities
choices: Platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities
A single global committee elected by all internet users in a fair vote
The author of the post got to decide if it was labeled or not
An independent court system designed for this single purpose alone
context: Each major platform had its own trust-and-safety team making labeling decisions, often in consultation with public-health authorities (WHO, CDC) and government agencies. The Twitter Files (2022-23) documented some of this coordination during COVID and the 2020 election. The general recognition: 'misinformation' labels are not neutral verdicts from above. They're decisions made by people, under pressure, on contested topics, in real time.

question: A friend says they can't stop scrolling on a particular app. What's the recommendation system doing?
answer: Surfacing exactly the content shown to hold their attention longest
choices: Surfacing exactly the content shown to hold their attention longest
Showing them random clips from people they have never heard of
Helping them finish quickly so they can get back to other tasks
Charging them extra for every five minutes spent scrolling daily
context: The infinite-scroll feed plus the engagement-optimized recommendation system is a powerful combination — the platform's whole job is to find the next clip you won't be able to stop watching. The pull is real, not weak willpower. The recognition: feeling out of control on these apps doesn't mean you're broken; the system was tuned to produce that feeling. Useful counter-moves: timers, scheduled use, removing the app at certain times, choosing what to watch deliberately.

question: Meta is one of the biggest AI labs, and yet it releases its main Llama models with open weights. What does Meta say it gains?
answer: Wider adoption, faster outside improvement, and a counterweight to closed competitors
choices: Wider adoption, faster outside improvement, and a counterweight to closed competitors
Meta has no business reason and releases the weights by accident yearly
Meta hopes to be sued by the largest open-source projects on earth
Meta gives away its models to drive its only product, which is bicycles
context: Meta's open-weight strategy with the Llama family has several rationales: wider adoption means more people building on Meta's stack; outside researchers improve the models for free; an open ecosystem checks the market power of closed competitors like OpenAI. Mark Zuckerberg has framed it as similar to Meta's earlier open-source contributions (React, PyTorch). The bank's stance: open weights are a major counterweight to concentration, and worth defending.

question: After Elon Musk acquired Twitter in 2022, he gave selected journalists access to internal documents. What were these releases collectively called?
answer: The Twitter Files
choices: The Twitter Files
The Big Blue Tapes
The Bird Box Papers
The Engagement Archives
context: The 'Twitter Files,' published December 2022 through 2023, were a series of releases by journalists including Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, and Michael Shellenberger. They drew on internal Twitter documents to describe content-moderation decisions, government coordination, and trust-and-safety practices during the Trump era and COVID. Different observers read them differently — but the underlying documents are public. The recognition: platform moderation is not always the platform alone deciding.

question: In November 2022, the cryptocurrency exchange FTX collapsed. Why did the collapse matter for AI policy debates?
answer: Its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him
choices: Its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him
The exchange was secretly developing the world's largest language model
FTX was the only company that hosted the OpenAI website on its servers
The crash made everyone forget about AI for the entire next decade
context: Sam Bankman-Fried built FTX into one of the largest crypto exchanges before its November 2022 collapse. He had publicly tied himself to Effective Altruism and longtermist AI-safety advocacy, funding nonprofits in that space. The implosion revealed that a substantial portion of AI-doomer advocacy had been funded by a fraud-built fortune. SBF was convicted of fraud in November 2023. The recognition: follow the money, even on 'safety' causes.

question: A privacy-focused user wants to use AI without any conversation leaving their computer. What setup helps?
answer: An open-weight model running locally through software like Ollama
choices: An open-weight model running locally through software like Ollama
A free cloud chatbot with the user's home address removed from the profile
An app that emails every prompt to the user before sending it on
A version of the chatbot only available between midnight and dawn
context: Local-model setups — Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp — let you download an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and run it on your own machine. Your prompts never leave the computer. The trade-off is that local models trail the frontier in capability, and large ones need significant RAM. For sensitive work, a local model that knows 80% of what a frontier model knows is usually a better deal than the frontier model logging everything.

question: A teen falls into a long streak of intense political videos on YouTube. What's the simplest first counter-move?
answer: Clear watch history or use a fresh session to break the recommendation pattern
choices: Clear watch history or use a fresh session to break the recommendation pattern
Watch the same video on a louder speaker for several extra hours
Send the videos to ten friends so they share the same recommendations
Send the YouTube CEO an email asking them to make a personal change
context: The recommendation system learns from your watch history. If you've been pulled into a rabbit hole, clearing history (or switching to incognito) resets the model's picture of you. Conscious choice from a fresh start lets you set new patterns. Other moves: subscribe explicitly to channels you trust so subscribed-content competes with recommendations, use 'not interested' on intense clips, watch on a schedule, or take a few days off the platform entirely.

question: The biggest social platforms remove the side-rail clock and timestamp markers from the feed. Why might this design choice matter?
answer: Without time cues, users lose track of how long they've been scrolling
choices: Without time cues, users lose track of how long they've been scrolling
Designers think clocks are ugly and don't fit the aesthetic of the feed
Time cues are illegal under federal regulations for all social apps
Users prefer to guess what time it is rather than read a clock
context: Hiding time cues — clocks, timestamps, day-of-week markers — is a known design move that lengthens session times. Without anchors, time blurs. Other engagement-extending designs: autoplay, infinite scroll, variable-interval rewards (like slot machines), red-dot notifications. Recognizing these patterns is the start of pushing back. Set a watch nearby, use the phone's screen-time tools, and pick app exits deliberately rather than waiting to feel done.

question: Compared to a frontier closed-API model, what's a typical downside of running an open-weight model on your laptop?
answer: Capabilities tend to lag the very latest frontier model by some margin
choices: Capabilities tend to lag the very latest frontier model by some margin
Open-weight models charge fees per question, unlike closed models
Open-weight models can only respond in Latin or Ancient Greek
Open-weight models share every answer with your internet provider
context: Open-weight models you can run locally are powerful but typically trail the absolute frontier in capability. The frontier labs invest enormous compute in their newest closed models. Open releases (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) often lag by 6-12 months — sometimes less. For many tasks, that lag doesn't matter. For privacy-sensitive use, the trade is often worth it. The picture is fluid; capability gaps close and open as new releases ship.

question: Why is it expensive to start a new frontier-AI company in 2025?
answer: Training a leading model needs huge compute, huge data, and huge capital
choices: Training a leading model needs huge compute, huge data, and huge capital
The US government charges a flat fee of one dollar to register a company
Each new AI company must build a satellite before training any model
The university system refuses to teach AI to anyone under thirty years old
context: Training a frontier model takes tens of thousands of high-end chips, massive curated datasets, energy, and engineering talent — typically hundreds of millions to billions of dollars per training run. Only a handful of companies and governments have the resources. The result is concentration. Open-weight releases lower the barrier to using a strong model but don't change the cost of training a new frontier one. Recognition: cost shapes who builds the technology and whose interests it serves first.

question: TikTok's recommendation algorithm is widely considered the most effective of any social platform. What does 'most effective' mean in practice?
answer: It captures and holds user attention faster and longer than competitors
choices: It captures and holds user attention faster and longer than competitors
It only shows videos that have been verified by independent fact-checkers
It runs entirely without a single computer chip anywhere in the company
It guarantees every user a small cash bonus for using the app daily
context: TikTok's algorithm is widely described as the standout in the engagement-optimization industry. The combination of short clips, autoplay, and fine-grained signal collection (watch-time, rewatches, scroll pauses) lets the model converge on what holds your attention quickly. Internal TikTok documents reported by the Wall Street Journal in 2021 described the system in similar terms. The recognition isn't 'TikTok is bad' — it's 'this is what engagement optimization at the current state of the art looks like.'

question: Why is it risky for a platform to permanently delete posts labeled 'misinformation' rather than just label them?
answer: Some 'misinformation' calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record
choices: Some 'misinformation' calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record
Deletion creates more storage space, which is illegal in many countries
Deletion always requires the platform to refund the post's author cash
Deletion is impossible because the posts are stored on indestructible disks
context: Permanent removal forecloses debate. If a 'misinformation' label later proves wrong — as happened with several COVID-era claims, including the lab-leak hypothesis — labeled posts can at least be re-examined. Deleted posts vanish from the record, and the wrong call can't easily be revisited. The general lesson for AI-augmented moderation: errors will happen at scale; design systems so errors can be corrected, not buried. Transparency over erasure.

question: Several US cities have passed laws restricting police use of facial recognition. What's the usual concern?
answer: False matches plus the chill effect on protest and public life
choices: False matches plus the chill effect on protest and public life
Facial recognition cameras break too easily in rainy weather
Cameras refuse to work on people with brown eyes specifically
The technology is illegal anywhere in the world without exception
context: San Francisco (2019), Boston, Portland, and other US cities have passed laws restricting government facial recognition. The two main concerns: documented false-match errors (Robert Williams Detroit 2020 and other cases) plus the broader chilling effect on lawful public activity — protest, assembly, attending a place of worship. The recognition isn't anti-AI; it's that deployment decisions are political, and 'we have the technology' is not the same as 'we should use it everywhere.'

question: TikTok says it stores US user data on US servers (a project called 'Texas'). Why don't critics consider this a full answer?
answer: Where data is stored is only one of several access pathways the company controls
choices: Where data is stored is only one of several access pathways the company controls
Texas is too far from the user, so the data takes hours to load
Storage location doesn't matter at all on any social media platform
The data is stored in a language only Texans can read clearly
context: TikTok's 'Project Texas' moved US user data storage to Oracle servers in the US, with claimed restrictions on access. Critics point out that storage location is only part of the picture: engineering, model training, content recommendation, and corporate ownership remain with ByteDance. Internal investigations have surfaced cases of mainland-China-based ByteDance staff accessing US data. The recognition: privacy promises must be evaluated against the full system, not just the storage server's address.

question: What's the difference between a feed that 'shows what your friends posted' and a feed that 'shows what an algorithm thinks will hold you'?
answer: The second one optimizes for your attention, not for your social circle
choices: The second one optimizes for your attention, not for your social circle
The two feeds are identical because they show the same friends always
The first feed is illegal in all countries under privacy regulations
The second feed shows only old posts from many years in the past
context: Early social media was chronological — what your friends posted, newest first. Modern feeds are algorithmic — what a recommendation system thinks will hold you. The shift made the platforms more addictive and lower-cost (the platform doesn't depend on your friends being interesting). Most platforms now offer chronological or 'following' modes as an option you have to find. Switching back is one of the simplest counter-moves available.

question: Stability AI released Stable Diffusion with open weights in 2022. What was the result for the broader AI image-generation field?
answer: Anyone could build new tools, fine-tunes, and apps on top of the model
choices: Anyone could build new tools, fine-tunes, and apps on top of the model
Stable Diffusion was banned the same week it was released
No one ever used Stable Diffusion because closed models stayed cheaper
Image generation became impossible without explicit government approval
context: Stable Diffusion's August 2022 release with open weights triggered an explosion of derivative work — fine-tunes, web apps, plug-ins for creative tools, custom models trained for specific art styles. The pattern shows the open-source dynamic: a powerful base model, released freely, enables a much broader ecosystem than any single company would build alone. The same dynamic plays out for language models (Llama, Mistral) and other modalities. Worth defending.

question: Your friend says 'my YouTube feed reflects my interests.' What's a more accurate way to put it?
answer: Their feed reflects what the algorithm thinks holds their attention
choices: Their feed reflects what the algorithm thinks holds their attention
Their feed reflects videos uploaded by people in their zip code
Their feed reflects the official curated picks of YouTube's editors
Their feed reflects a complete archive of every video in their language
context: What feels like 'my interests' on an engagement-maximizing platform is a mix of your actual interests and what the system can use to hold your attention. The two overlap but aren't identical — emotionally charged versions of your interests usually do better than calm versions, so the feed drifts toward intensity. The reframe matters: 'this is what the algorithm thinks works on me' opens up the question 'am I OK with that?' in a way 'this is who I am' doesn't.

question: What's the simplest reason a major fraud's collapse should make people re-examine the causes it funded?
answer: Funding shapes which voices get heard, and major funding by a fraudster bent the conversation
choices: Funding shapes which voices get heard, and major funding by a fraudster bent the conversation
Causes funded by frauds become automatically correct once the fraud is exposed
Once a funder collapses, every funded research result is automatically deleted
Funding has no effect on which arguments reach a wide public audience
context: Money chooses which think tanks get staffed, which papers get written, which conferences get held, which journalists get briefed. Sam Bankman-Fried's giving to AI-safety nonprofits and Effective Altruism in the years before FTX's 2022 collapse helped shape that conversation. Re-examination doesn't mean automatically rejecting funded work — it means asking what the conversation would look like if it hadn't been bent by one funder's resources. Good intellectual hygiene applies symmetrically to every funded cause.

question: A school's monitoring tool flags a student's essay for a self-harm-related word. What's the school's claim about why the tool exists?
answer: To intervene early when a student may be in danger
choices: To intervene early when a student may be in danger
To embarrass the student in front of their classmates by default
To delete all writing the school does not personally agree with
To grade the essay automatically and notify the parent of a low score
context: Schools defend tools like Gaggle, Bark, and GoGuardian as safety measures — automated scanning for self-harm signals, threats, or signs of abuse. The defense is real: in some cases the tools have flagged students in crisis. Critics raise three issues: false positives that scar the student, normalization of surveillance, and the trade-off between safety and privacy. The recognition: 'for your safety' framings cover real cases and real costs. Worth being precise about both.

question: A budgeting app uses AI to nudge you toward saving more. A casino-style app uses AI to nudge you toward betting more. What's the same and what's different?
answer: Same technique with opposite goals, where one serves your interest and the other serves the platform's
choices: Same technique with opposite goals, where one serves your interest and the other serves the platform's
The two apps are literally the same product in different colors only
The casino app is technically illegal, so the comparison doesn't matter
The budgeting app uses paper, not computers, so AI doesn't apply
context: The technology is morally neutral. The deployment is not. Personalized nudges from a budgeting app, fitness app, or medication reminder can serve the user well. The same technique inside a gambling app, dark-pattern checkout, or attention-maximizing feed serves the platform at the user's expense. Recognition: every nudge has a beneficiary. Ask, feature by feature, who actually benefits. Same tools, different ethics.

question: A short, clear sign of an engagement-maximizing system at work in any app: what to watch for?
answer: Autoplay and infinite scroll with no clear stopping point built into the design
choices: Autoplay and infinite scroll with no clear stopping point built into the design
A clear progress bar showing exactly when the content ends today
A friendly reminder to take a break after every fifteen minutes
A simple homepage that lists today's content in alphabetical order
context: Autoplay (the next video starts automatically) and infinite scroll (there's no bottom of the feed) are the architectural signatures of engagement-maximizing design. Both remove natural stopping points. Most users don't choose stops; they fall out when fatigued. Spotting these features is a useful signal: 'the makers of this app want me to keep going.' Counter-moves: timers, screen-time tools, picking apps that have clear endpoints — newsletter-style updates, podcasts you have to start manually, books.

question: Why does it matter that frontier AI is built mostly by a handful of US companies in 2025?
answer: A small group of companies has unusual power to shape how the technology is used
choices: A small group of companies has unusual power to shape how the technology is used
There is no effect, because concentration of any technology never matters at all
A handful of companies always ensures the lowest possible prices to users
A small group means each company can update its model only once a decade
context: Concentration of any major technology — railroads, telecoms, search, social media — has historically shaped how the technology is used and who it serves. Frontier AI is highly concentrated: a handful of US labs build the models everyone else uses. That gives those companies — and the governments that regulate them — outsized influence over what AI can and can't do. Open-weight releases, distributed compute, and international competition (Mistral, DeepSeek) all push back. Recognition is the first step.

question: After the Twitter Files were published in late 2022 and 2023, what general kind of question did they raise about content moderation?
answer: How much government influence shapes platform decisions about what users can say
choices: How much government influence shapes platform decisions about what users can say
Whether Twitter ever paid its employees their full salaries on time
Whether bird-themed icons are protected by US copyright in court
Whether the company should expand into selling physical coffee mugs
context: The Twitter Files documented patterns of government officials requesting content actions through trust-and-safety channels, especially during the 2020 election and COVID period. Lawsuits like Missouri v. Biden (later renamed) built on the documents to argue First Amendment concerns about government 'jawboning' of platforms. The Supreme Court ruled on a related case in 2024. Whatever one thinks of any specific case, the wider recognition stands: platform moderation is sometimes shaped from outside the platform.

question: What's a useful general principle for thinking about surveillance technology in any country?
answer: Build the infrastructure carefully, because future leaders may use it for purposes you didn't imagine
choices: Build the infrastructure carefully, because future leaders may use it for purposes you didn't imagine
Build any infrastructure as fast as possible because speed is all that matters
Avoid building any infrastructure because all technology is bad for everyone
Build whatever the current government in power requests with no debate at all
context: Surveillance infrastructure outlasts the leaders who build it. Capabilities created for 'safe' reasons under one administration become available to the next, and the next. The general lesson — drawn from history, not from a particular political view — is to be cautious about creating capabilities you would not want any future leader to have. Recognition matters more than partisan framing: who you trust today is not who will hold the keys tomorrow.

question: Ask a chatbot 'What's the capital of France?' and it writes 'Paris.' It feels like the model looked the answer up. What is the model actually doing on the inside, token by token?
answer: Predicting which word is most likely to come next, then doing it again for the next word, and again.
choices: Predicting which word is most likely to come next, then doing it again for the next word, and again.
Querying a hidden database of country facts that is shipped with the model and updated every week.
Running a small encyclopedia search inside the model that returns one matching article each time.
Calling a private Wikipedia API behind the scenes whenever it sees a question about a country.
context: This is the single most important fact about how chatbots work. An LLM is a next-token predictor. It does not look anything up, search the web, or query a database — unless it is hooked up to those tools separately. 'Paris' came out because, in the model's training data, that token was the overwhelmingly likely continuation of 'The capital of France is.' Recognition skill: when an LLM answers a question, ask yourself what it could possibly be doing besides predicting the next word.

question: A chatbot writes a paragraph about a famous court case. It includes a precise-sounding citation: 'Smith v. Jones, 421 F.3d 893 (9th Cir. 2008).' That case does not exist. The model invented it. What's the mechanism that made this happen?
answer: The model produced text that looks statistically like real legal citations and never checked anything against a real database.
choices: The model produced text that looks statistically like real legal citations and never checked anything against a real database.
The model deliberately fabricated a citation to test whether the user would catch it before submitting.
The model copied a real citation but accidentally typed one digit wrong while transcribing it.
The model was hacked by an attacker who injected fake legal references into its response stream.
context: Citations have a predictable shape — 'Name v. Name, NUMBER F.Nd PAGE (CIRCUIT YEAR).' An LLM trained on legal text learns that pattern. When asked for a citation, it generates text matching the pattern. The pattern looks right; the case may not exist. This is the same mechanism behind made-up book titles, fake URLs, and invented quotes. The defensive habit: any specific reference an LLM gives you must be verified against a real source before you use it.

question: Think of a chatbot generating a reply as a person guessing one word at a time, with no plan and no memory of guessing the previous word — only the visible result so far. Why does this picture explain the way LLMs sometimes 'change their mind' mid-paragraph?
answer: Each token is chosen based on the text so far, not a fixed answer the model committed to at the start.
choices: Each token is chosen based on the text so far, not a fixed answer the model committed to at the start.
The model has a long-term goal and adjusts the goal whenever a new sentence begins in the paragraph.
A second model checks the first model's answer halfway through and forces a correction at that point.
The chatbot service routes the conversation to a different backend after every two or three sentences.
context: There's no internal 'planning' step inside a vanilla LLM — the next token is generated, added to the text, and then the model is asked again for the next token. Drift between sentences is just the predictor following a different statistical path now that more words are in front of it. Newer 'reasoning' models add explicit steps that look more like planning, but underneath, the basic mechanism is still token-by-token generation.

question: An LLM is asked 'What's 23,847 times 6,019?' It confidently answers '143,571,693' — and it's wrong. Why does the model fail at a problem any calculator app does instantly?
answer: It predicts a number that looks plausible from training text, instead of running the actual multiplication algorithm.
choices: It predicts a number that looks plausible from training text, instead of running the actual multiplication algorithm.
It rounds the answer to the nearest hundred million by default to save processing time on big numbers.
It refuses by design because labs program LLMs to give intentionally-wrong arithmetic to discourage cheating.
It returns the answer to an unrelated multiplication problem because the question used unfamiliar digits.
context: An LLM has no built-in arithmetic engine. When it sees '23,847 × 6,019 =' it generates a number that looks statistically plausible — usually right magnitude, often right last digit, almost never exactly right. Modern chatbots get around this by handing math problems to a calculator tool when one is available. The recognition habit: never trust an LLM for arithmetic; verify with a calculator, or ask the model to write code that does the math.

question: A friend says, 'I asked ChatGPT what time the football game starts tonight, and it gave me a real-looking answer.' You know that vanilla ChatGPT has no live internet access. What probably happened?
answer: The model produced a plausible-sounding time based on training-text patterns about football schedules, and that guess is almost certainly wrong.
choices: The model produced a plausible-sounding time based on training-text patterns about football schedules, and that guess is almost certainly wrong.
OpenAI silently added live sports data to every ChatGPT account after a recent quiet rollout last week.
ChatGPT secretly checks a real sports website but does not tell users it is checking outside sources.
The model paused the conversation, waited a few seconds, and asked another LLM to look up the kickoff.
context: Without an explicit web-browse tool, an LLM has no way to know today's schedule. It will still answer — because the prompt says 'a question was asked,' so the predictor produces a continuation. The continuation will look factual. It almost certainly is not. The defensive habit: never use a vanilla chatbot for current events. Use a real search engine, or ask only models with explicit live-web access (and verify those too).

question: A common phrase for ChatGPT-style models is 'stochastic parrot' — a parrot that talks by patterning on what it heard, picking words probabilistically. Why is the metaphor useful even though it leaves things out?
answer: It captures the core mechanic of repeating statistical patterns from training data, without claiming the model 'understands' what it says.
choices: It captures the core mechanic of repeating statistical patterns from training data, without claiming the model 'understands' what it says.
It captures that LLMs are limited to bird-sized vocabularies of two or three hundred words at most.
It captures the fact that all chatbots are physically housed in zoos near major university campuses.
It captures how chatbots specifically mimic the tone of any animal-themed text they have ever seen.
context: Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru, and coauthors used the 'stochastic parrot' label in a 2021 paper to push back on hype framing LLMs as 'thinking.' The metaphor leaves out useful work the models can do — translation, code, brainstorming — but it correctly names what an LLM is not: it is not searching, reasoning, or comprehending. Recognition skill: when a chatbot impresses you, ask whether the work depended on understanding or only on producing the right kind of text.

question: If an LLM is just predicting the next word, why does it still produce essays that hang together — paragraphs that stay on topic and arguments that build?
answer: The model attends to every earlier word when picking the next one, so each prediction is shaped by the whole conversation so far.
choices: The model attends to every earlier word when picking the next one, so each prediction is shaped by the whole conversation so far.
The model writes a complete essay plan internally before it produces a single output word for the user.
The model has a long-term memory module that stores key points across multiple chat sessions over time.
The model rewrites its earlier sentences silently as it goes, keeping later paragraphs lined up with them.
context: The transformer architecture's self-attention is why LLM output reads coherently. Every new token's prediction looks at all the earlier tokens at once. Stay on topic at word 200 is downstream of attending to words 1 through 199. There is no separate planning module in a vanilla LLM. The coherence is an emergent property of attention plus next-token prediction at scale.
