Voice assistants for telephones that were widely deployed in the early 1980s before retreating.
context: Expert systems were the AI flagship of the early-to-mid 1980s. The idea: interview a human expert (a doctor diagnosing, a geologist locating oil), turn their reasoning into a giant set of if-then rules, and run the rules as a program. MYCIN diagnosed infections; XCON configured computer orders. The systems worked in narrow domains but were brittle outside their hand-coded knowledge, and updating them as the world changed was painful. By the late 1980s the expert-systems wave broke and a second AI winter followed.

question: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project — a major government-backed AI program launched in 1982 — set ambitious goals for machine reasoning and natural language. By 1992, what had happened?
answer: The project was largely judged a failure since it didn't produce the breakthroughs it promised and was wound down.
choices: The project was largely judged a failure since it didn't produce the breakthroughs it promised and was wound down.
The project succeeded so well that Japan became the world AI leader and held the title through the 2000s.
The project transferred its results to the US and is the direct ancestor of modern American AI labs.
The project was extended and is still running today as the main source of modern Japanese chatbot research.
context: Japan's Fifth Generation project, launched 1982, was a high-profile bet on logic-programming and parallel computers for AI. Western governments saw it as a competitive challenge and responded with their own initiatives. By the early 1990s, the project had not produced the predicted breakthroughs and was quietly wound down. The episode contributed to the second AI winter and reinforced a pattern: top-down government AI mega-projects often underdeliver compared to bottom-up academic and industrial research.

question: Compared to the first AI winter of the 1970s, the second AI winter of the late 1980s and early 1990s had a different flavor. What was different about the disappointment this time?
answer: Expert systems had actually been deployed in companies, so the disappointment hit real budgets and real users, not just labs.
choices: Expert systems had actually been deployed in companies, so the disappointment hit real budgets and real users, not just labs.
Researchers in the 1980s had not made any bold claims, so the funding cuts came from nowhere.
Computer hardware in the 1980s was so cheap that nobody noticed when AI projects failed and faded.
AI in the 1980s was already being merged with biotech, so the field continued under a different name.
context: The first winter (1970s) followed mostly academic disappointment. The second winter (late 1980s) followed industrial disappointment — companies had bought expert systems, hardware vendors had built specialized 'LISP machines' for them, and the wave broke. When budgets get cut by the people who paid actual money, recovery takes longer. Some scholars argue the second winter set deep learning back too: by the time backpropagation was being scaled up, AI had reputational baggage that newer researchers had to work around.

question: In 1989, a researcher named Yann LeCun, then at Bell Labs, built a convolutional neural network called LeNet. It had a specific real-world job. What did LeNet do?
answer: It read handwritten ZIP codes on mail for the US Postal Service.
choices: It read handwritten ZIP codes on mail for the US Postal Service.
It played checkers at the world-champion level for AT&T's research demonstrations.
It detected spam in early electronic mail before commercial email was widespread.
It transcribed phone-call audio into text for AT&T's customer-service department.
context: LeNet (the early versions in 1989, then LeNet-5 in 1998) was a convolutional neural network — a CNN — trained to recognize digits. Bell Labs deployed it to read handwritten ZIP codes on mail. By the late 1990s, CNN-based systems were reading a meaningful share of US mail. LeCun's work was a proof-of-concept for deep learning on images that predated the modern boom by 20 years. Recognition skill: the deep-learning revolution wasn't an overnight breakthrough — it was a slow gathering of techniques that finally clicked at scale in 2012.

question: Yann LeCun's 1989 LeNet was a convolutional network — a CNN — designed to be good at images. What's the central idea of the CNN architecture that makes it well-suited to vision?
answer: The network slides small filters across the image, learning patterns that work the same way anywhere they appear.
choices: The network slides small filters across the image, learning patterns that work the same way anywhere they appear.
The network memorizes every image it has ever seen and matches new images against the memorized set.
The network requires images to be hand-labeled at every pixel before training, with no exceptions.
The network refuses to process any image larger than 64 by 64 pixels regardless of available computing power.
context: Convolutional neural networks use small learnable filters that slide across the input image. The same filter applied at every position means the network can recognize the same pattern (an edge, a corner, an eye) wherever it appears. This 'translation invariance' is a natural fit for visual data and is why CNNs dominated computer vision from the 1990s into the 2010s. Vision Transformers have since matched or exceeded CNNs on many tasks, but the CNN idea — local filters, shared weights — was the foundation.

question: After two decades at Bell Labs and a university career, Yann LeCun took a role in 2013 that placed him at the center of modern AI. What position did he take?
answer: Chief AI Scientist at Meta (then Facebook), where he founded the company's AI research lab.
choices: Chief AI Scientist at Meta (then Facebook), where he founded the company's AI research lab.
Chief Technology Officer at Google, where he replaced the existing engineering leadership.
Chairman of the United Nations AI Council, a permanent international AI advisory role.
CEO of Microsoft, where he oversaw the company's pivot from desktop software to cloud computing.
context: LeCun joined Facebook (now Meta) in 2013 to found FAIR — Facebook AI Research. He's been Meta's Chief AI Scientist since. He's also a vocal critic of AI-doomer arguments — distinct from Geoffrey Hinton's middle-ground concerns — and a champion of open-source AI, including Meta's release of Llama with downloadable weights. The career arc — Bell Labs CNN pioneer → academic professor → industry research lead → public AI voice — is one of the field's distinctive trajectories.

question: In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo played a five-game match against world champion Lee Sedol in Seoul. The result was a watershed for AI. How did the match end?
answer: AlphaGo won four games to one, and Lee Sedol's single win in game 4 was the last time a top human ever beat a top AI in Go.
choices: AlphaGo won four games to one, and Lee Sedol's single win in game 4 was the last time a top human ever beat a top AI in Go.
Lee Sedol won four games to one, with the AI being beaten across the match by careful human strategy.
The match ended in a five-game tie that has never been broken in any subsequent computer-vs-human Go event.
AlphaGo was disqualified after game three for using a tactic that the rules of Go specifically banned.
context: AlphaGo won 4-1 in Seoul in March 2016. Lee Sedol's lone win in game 4 — featuring an extraordinary 'wedge' move at move 78 — was the final time a top human ever beat a top Go AI. After AlphaGo came AlphaGo Zero (no human data, learned from self-play), then AlphaZero (chess, shogi, Go in one). Go had been considered out of reach for AI for decades. The match's cultural impact in Korea and Japan, where Go is a tradition, was profound.

question: In game two of the 2016 AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol match, AlphaGo played move 37 — a shoulder hit on the fifth line. The professional commentators initially called it a mistake. Why is move 37 now legendary in Go history?
answer: It was a creative move no human had considered, and AlphaGo went on to win the game.
choices: It was a creative move no human had considered, and AlphaGo went on to win the game.
It was a forced move that any beginner would have played because the rules left no other choice.
It violated the rules of Go and the game was restarted after a fifteen-minute referee discussion.
It accidentally triggered a memorized opening trap from one of Go's classic 18th-century games.
context: Move 37 was so unusual that top professionals called it a mistake. AlphaGo's internal probability said only one in ten thousand human players would consider that move. AlphaGo won game 2 anyway. Top Go players have since studied move 37 and incorporated similar ideas into their play. The move is the canonical example of what AI capability looks like: pattern-finding by a system trained on millions of self-play games surfacing moves no human had tried.

question: Lee Sedol — the human grandmaster who played AlphaGo in 2016 — retired from professional Go in 2019. He named one specific reason. What did he give as the reason?
answer: He felt no longer at the top because AI had surpassed humans, and even being the world's best wasn't 'best' anymore.
choices: He felt no longer at the top because AI had surpassed humans, and even being the world's best wasn't 'best' anymore.
He had injured his hand and could not place stones on the Go board with the right precision anymore.
He had been hired by DeepMind in London and was no longer permitted to play professional Go matches.
He had been banned from Korean Go tournaments for using a smartphone during competitive play.
context: Lee Sedol announced his retirement in November 2019 at age 36. In interviews, he cited AI's dominance as the reason: 'Even if I become the number one, there is an entity that cannot be defeated.' The reaction in the Go world was complex. Some treated Lee's framing as fatalistic; others took it as honest. The cultural impact of an AI surpassing top humans in a tradition centuries old is real — and was felt as a loss by a particular kind of master.

question: AlphaGo, the 2016 system, was followed by AlphaGo Zero in 2017 — a version that learned Go from scratch using no human games at all. Then came AlphaZero, also in 2017. What did AlphaZero add?
answer: It learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch with the same algorithm, using no human data, just self-play in each game.
choices: It learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch with the same algorithm, using no human data, just self-play in each game.
It was the first version that humans could download and run on their own laptops at home for free.
It added a chat interface so users could discuss their losses with the AI after a match was over.
It included a built-in calculator that let users check their work on multiplication problems during games.
context: AlphaZero (December 2017) generalized AlphaGo Zero's approach to chess and shogi (Japanese chess). With the same core algorithm and no domain-specific human data, it learned each game from scratch through self-play. It then beat the previously-leading specialist programs at each. The result was a kind of proof: the self-play reinforcement-learning idea wasn't a Go-specific trick. AlphaZero is one of the most-cited demonstrations of game-playing AI capability — and a window onto how reinforcement learning scales across structured tasks.

question: In 2018, Google released a model called BERT — Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Before BERT, most language models read text left to right. What did BERT do differently?
answer: It looked at words on both sides at once, the 'bidirectional' part of its name, letting it understand context better.
choices: It looked at words on both sides at once, the 'bidirectional' part of its name, letting it understand context better.
It could only read text written in ancient Greek and Latin, which made it useful for classical studies.
It refused to process any text longer than a single sentence, which made it impractical for documents.
It worked entirely offline and was the first AI model that did not need an internet connection at all.
context: BERT was the first widely-used transformer-based model that took attention beyond left-to-right reading. The 'bidirectional' approach — looking at the full sentence at once — made BERT especially good at understanding tasks like classification, sentiment analysis, and question-answering on a passage. Within a year, BERT-style models became the standard for tasks where you need to understand existing text, while GPT-style models became the standard for generating new text. Both styles are transformers; they differ in training objective.

question: BERT (2018) and GPT (also a transformer line, starting 2018) are both transformer-based but used for different jobs. How does the typical job split work between them?
answer: BERT-style models analyze existing text; GPT-style models generate new text.
choices: BERT-style models analyze existing text; GPT-style models generate new text.
BERT-style models work only in English; GPT-style models work only in non-English languages.
BERT-style models are old and unused; GPT-style models have entirely replaced them everywhere.
BERT-style models cost more money to run; GPT-style models are always free for everyone everywhere.
context: BERT is an 'encoder-only' transformer — it reads text and produces a representation, useful for classification, search, and analysis tasks. GPT is a 'decoder-only' transformer — it generates text token by token, useful for chat, completion, and writing. The two architectures coexist: search engines and analytics often use BERT-style models behind the scenes; consumer chatbots use GPT-style. Both are transformers; the difference is which job the architecture is shaped for.

question: In 2020, OpenAI released GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters — far larger than any previous publicly-described language model. What was the surprising property GPT-3 showed off?
answer: Few-shot learning — give the model a couple of examples in the prompt, and it could do the task without further training.
choices: Few-shot learning — give the model a couple of examples in the prompt, and it could do the task without further training.
Self-awareness — the model could describe its own thought process in real time during inference.
Multi-modal vision — the model could process images alongside text from day one of its release.
Live-web access — the model could browse the internet to look things up while answering questions.
context: GPT-3's 2020 paper was titled 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners.' The headline result: at the scale of 175B parameters, the model could do new tasks just from a few example pairs in the prompt — no gradient updates needed. Translation, classification, math word problems, code generation, all from in-context examples. This 'few-shot' or 'in-context' capability was a surprise. It's the foundation of prompt engineering: showing a model what you want, then asking it to do the same thing.

question: GPT-3 (2020) was not a consumer product. To use it, you needed API access from OpenAI. So what was its biggest impact?
answer: Developers built early products on top of GPT-3, like Jasper, Copy.ai, and Codex, proving demand and pointing to a chat-ready future.
choices: Developers built early products on top of GPT-3, like Jasper, Copy.ai, and Codex, proving demand and pointing to a chat-ready future.
GPT-3 was a complete commercial failure and OpenAI nearly went bankrupt funding its development.
GPT-3 was deployed by the US government as the primary tool for processing tax returns nationwide.
GPT-3 was banned from civilian use and was available only inside military research laboratories.
context: GPT-3 was available through OpenAI's API starting in 2020. The first wave of LLM-powered startups built on it: Jasper and Copy.ai for marketing copy; Codex (later GitHub Copilot) for code; many smaller experiments. These products showed real demand and revealed which use cases worked well. Two years later, ChatGPT (a chat-tuned descendant) would be the consumer product that brought LLMs mainstream. The GPT-3 era is the bridge between research curiosity and consumer wave.

question: GPT-3 (2020) had 175 billion parameters. By comparison, GPT-2 (2019) had 1.5 billion. Why was the order-of-magnitude jump in parameters consequential?
answer: At the new scale, capabilities emerged that weren't there at the smaller size, including few-shot learning from prompt examples.
choices: At the new scale, capabilities emerged that weren't there at the smaller size, including few-shot learning from prompt examples.
The new scale was just a marketing claim, and every later evaluation showed GPT-3 was actually smaller than GPT-2.
The new scale shifted GPT-3 from being a language model to being a calculator with exact arithmetic skills.
The new scale meant GPT-3 used less electricity than GPT-2 because larger models are always more efficient.
context: GPT-3's scale wasn't a marketing flourish — it produced qualitatively different behavior than smaller models. Few-shot learning in particular emerged with scale; smaller models couldn't do it well. This 'emergent capabilities at scale' phenomenon became one of the central observations driving the scaling hypothesis: keep growing models and unexpected new capabilities will appear. The hypothesis has been debated since (some claimed 'emergence' may sometimes be an artifact of evaluation choices) but the GPT-3 results were the original evidence for it.

question: On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT — a chat interface built on a GPT-3.5 base. By January 2023, it had hit a milestone no consumer product had ever reached before. What was the milestone?
answer: 100 million users in two months — the fastest a consumer product had ever reached that number in any field.
choices: 100 million users in two months — the fastest a consumer product had ever reached that number in any field.
10 billion in revenue in two months — the fastest a consumer product had ever made that much money.
100 patents filed in two months — the fastest a tech company had ever filed that many patents.
1,000 lawsuits in two months — the fastest a tech company had ever been sued that many times.
context: ChatGPT's growth was unprecedented. For context: TikTok took nine months to hit 100 million users; Instagram took two and a half years. ChatGPT did it in two months. The product itself was relatively simple — a chat interface on top of an existing language model. What made it land was the combination: capable underlying model, easy interface, novelty of being able to 'talk to AI.' November 30, 2022 is widely treated as the start of the modern Gen-AI moment.

question: ChatGPT (Nov 2022) was built on a GPT-3.5 model that had existed before — what's the version of the model OpenAI added that made the chat interface work well?
answer: Instruction tuning and RLHF, where the model was fine-tuned to follow user instructions and rated by humans for quality.
choices: Instruction tuning and RLHF, where the model was fine-tuned to follow user instructions and rated by humans for quality.
A completely new neural network architecture invented just for the chat interface, replacing the transformer.
A live internet connection that let the model look up the latest news every time a question was asked.
A separate vision module that let the model handle images, which had not been possible in any earlier model.
context: ChatGPT's special sauce was the instruction-tuned, RLHF-aligned variant of GPT-3.5 sitting behind it. The base model could already produce coherent text; instruction tuning made it follow specific user requests; RLHF made it produce responses humans rated as helpful and harmless. The combination is what made it feel useful instead of merely impressive. The chat interface itself was simple. The underlying training was what made the interaction work.

question: ChatGPT (Nov 2022) wasn't free for long. By 2023 OpenAI had launched a paid tier called ChatGPT Plus. What change did the paid tier mainly offer at launch?
answer: Priority access during high-traffic times and access to newer models before they reached the free tier.
choices: Priority access during high-traffic times and access to newer models before they reached the free tier.
A guarantee that the model would never make any mistakes in any answer, with a refund if it did.
A live human typing answers behind the scenes for any question the AI could not handle correctly.
An offline mode that let the user download the model and run it locally on their home computer.
context: ChatGPT Plus launched at $20/month in early 2023. The pitch was practical: priority access when servers were busy, and earlier access to GPT-4 when it launched in March 2023. The free tier continued and remains important — but the paid tier started OpenAI's transition from API-only business to consumer-subscription business. The paid-consumer-AI model has since spread across the industry: Claude Pro, Gemini Advanced, Perplexity Pro, and so on.

question: In March 2023, OpenAI released GPT-4. It was a step up from GPT-3.5 in several ways. What was one notable new capability GPT-4 shipped with?
answer: Multimodality — GPT-4 could accept images as input and discuss them, not just text.
choices: Multimodality — GPT-4 could accept images as input and discuss them, not just text.
Live internet access — GPT-4 could automatically search the web for any question users asked.
Voice synthesis — GPT-4 could read its answers aloud through any speaker without any extra tools.
Self-improvement — GPT-4 could rewrite its own weights during conversation as it learned new facts.
context: GPT-4 launched March 14, 2023. Multimodality — the ability to process images — was a headline feature, though it rolled out gradually. GPT-4 also improved on GPT-3.5 in reasoning, in following complex instructions, and in resisting some kinds of jailbreaks. It passed standardized exams (bar exam, AP tests, GRE) at percentile rankings that drew media attention. The combination of capability gains and timing — four months after ChatGPT — drove a sense that LLM progress was rapidly accelerating.

question: GPT-4 (March 2023) made headlines partly because it passed standardized tests humans take. Why was that framing somewhat misleading?
answer: Test-taking measures one slice of human capability, so passing one doesn't mean the model matches humans across other tasks.
choices: Test-taking measures one slice of human capability, so passing one doesn't mean the model matches humans across other tasks.
GPT-4 was actually cheating, because OpenAI had loaded the answers into the model before each test was run.
GPT-4 passed by being slow, since its answers took hours while humans were given strict short time limits.
GPT-4 only took tests in Spanish and Italian, not in English, so the comparison wasn't really valid at all.
context: GPT-4 reportedly scored in the 90th percentile on the bar exam, 99th on the GRE, and well on various AP tests. The headlines often read 'AI matches lawyers' — but exams measure one slice of human capability. They don't measure judgment, client relationships, the ability to act in the world, or the legal-strategic instincts that distinguish working lawyers. The exam result is real; the broader claim isn't. Recognition skill: when AI capability is announced via a single benchmark, ask what the benchmark does and doesn't measure.

question: GPT-4 (2023) was the first OpenAI model that the company did not disclose much about — they didn't publish the parameter count, the training data, or detailed architecture. Why was that decision controversial?
answer: OpenAI was founded with a research-sharing mission and many researchers saw the shift to secrecy as a departure from it.
choices: OpenAI was founded with a research-sharing mission and many researchers saw the shift to secrecy as a departure from it.
OpenAI was legally required to publish all details and the missing information meant the model was a fake.
OpenAI was secretly using parameters from Llama and didn't want Meta to know about it across the industry.
OpenAI was running on government computers, so the secrecy meant a national-security classification existed.
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab dedicated to making AI safe and broadly beneficial — with a strong publication tradition through 2019. The GPT-4 technical report in 2023 explicitly declined to disclose 'architecture, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, training method, or similar' details. The shift away from open research, combined with the move to a capped-profit structure, was widely noted as a turn in the company's character. Recognition skill: institutional missions drift; check what an organization actually does, not what its name suggests.

question: AlphaFold, built by DeepMind, solved a problem biologists had worked on for fifty years: predicting the 3D shape of a protein from its amino-acid sequence. In what year did AlphaFold's results first stun the biology community?
answer: 2020 — at the CASP competition, where its accuracy was far ahead of any other approach.
choices: 2020 — at the CASP competition, where its accuracy was far ahead of any other approach.
1998 — when the original AlphaGo team built it as a side project during their early DeepMind years.
2024 — at the Nobel ceremony, where it was first announced as a working protein-folding system.
2010 — when Geoffrey Hinton's MIT lab released it as part of his original ImageNet research effort.
context: AlphaFold 2 entered the CASP14 protein-structure-prediction competition in 2020 and produced results so far ahead of other methods that biologists called the protein-folding problem effectively solved. AlphaFold 2's accuracy on most targets matched what experimental methods could produce, in a fraction of the time. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry would later honor Demis Hassabis and John Jumper (DeepMind) for AlphaFold — and David Baker (UW) for designing new proteins from scratch.

question: In October 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for AI-driven protein work. Two of the recipients were Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, both at DeepMind. Who was the third recipient?
answer: David Baker, at the University of Washington — for designing entirely new proteins from scratch.
choices: David Baker, at the University of Washington — for designing entirely new proteins from scratch.
Yann LeCun, at Meta — for inventing the convolutional neural network used in AlphaFold's design.
Geoffrey Hinton, formerly of Google — for inventing backpropagation, used to train every modern AI.
Yoshua Bengio, at the University of Montreal — for early work on attention mechanisms in language.
context: The 2024 Nobel Chemistry prize was split between two related leaps: Hassabis and Jumper for AlphaFold's prediction of natural protein structures, and David Baker for computational design of entirely novel proteins (proteins that don't exist in nature — drug candidates, vaccines, sensors). Baker's lab at the Institute for Protein Design at UW had been working for years on this. The Hinton/Bengio/LeCun trio shared the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning — a different prize, in a different year, for foundational AI work generally.

question: AlphaFold's free protein-structure database — launched in 2021 — contains predicted shapes for about 200 million proteins. Roughly what fraction of all known proteins is that?
answer: Essentially every protein in nature that's been catalogued — almost all of them, available to any researcher for free.
choices: Essentially every protein in nature that's been catalogued — almost all of them, available to any researcher for free.
Less than one percent — the database covers only proteins in mammals, leaving plants and bacteria out.
Exactly half — only proteins beginning with letters A through M are included in the published version.
About twenty proteins — the database is small and only covers the easiest cases AlphaFold solved.
context: The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database covers almost every protein in UniProt, the standard catalogue. Before AlphaFold, the Protein Data Bank had perhaps 200,000 experimentally determined structures. AlphaFold added 200 million predicted structures, hosted with the European Bioinformatics Institute, free to everyone. Drug discovery, basic biology, vaccine design — all benefit. It's one of the clearest examples of AI capability producing concrete public benefit at scale.

question: The 'protein-folding problem' was a famous open problem in biology for half a century. DeepMind's AlphaFold cracked it in 2020. What had made protein folding so hard before AI arrived?
answer: The number of possible folded shapes for any given protein is astronomical, and predicting which one nature picks took years of experimental work.
choices: The number of possible folded shapes for any given protein is astronomical, and predicting which one nature picks took years of experimental work.
Proteins refused to fold in a laboratory setting at all, so no experimental data existed about their shapes for any species.
The shape of a protein was thought to be random and could not even in principle be predicted from its sequence.
Government regulators had banned protein-folding research as a biosecurity risk through most of the 1980s and 1990s.
context: Levinthal's paradox (1969): a small protein has so many possible 3D configurations that an exhaustive search would take longer than the age of the universe. Yet proteins fold in seconds in nature. Predicting the answer from sequence — without searching all possible shapes — was the problem. AlphaFold cracked it by learning from the Protein Data Bank's experimentally-determined structures. The win: pattern-recognition trained at scale solved a problem that had defied physics-based simulation for decades.

question: Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in London in 2010. Before becoming an AI-research leader, he had two earlier careers. What were they?
answer: Chess prodigy and video-game designer — he competed at chess, then made games before getting his PhD in neuroscience.
choices: Chess prodigy and video-game designer — he competed at chess, then made games before getting his PhD in neuroscience.
Concert pianist and surgeon — he toured Europe, then trained as a doctor before founding the AI lab.
Olympic swimmer and architect — he won medals, then designed buildings before turning to computer science.
Stand-up comedian and farmer — he toured the UK comedy circuit, then ran an organic farm before AI work.
context: Demis Hassabis was a child chess prodigy — reached master level by age 13. He then went into video games, working on Theme Park in his teens, then founding his own game company. He returned to academia for a PhD in neuroscience, studying human memory and imagination. DeepMind, founded in 2010 with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, drew on this neuroscience interest — early DeepMind work on deep reinforcement learning was framed in terms of how brains might learn. Google acquired DeepMind in 2014 for about $500 million.

question: Google acquired DeepMind in January 2014 for around $500 million. What did the acquisition agreement reportedly include that was unusual for a tech acquisition at the time?
answer: An independent ethics board that would oversee DeepMind's AI research separately from Google management.
choices: An independent ethics board that would oversee DeepMind's AI research separately from Google management.
A guarantee that no DeepMind employee would ever be required to use English in any work meeting.
A clause that DeepMind would be allowed to retain veto power over every Google product launch.
A promise that Google would relocate to London within five years of the acquisition closing.
context: The Google-DeepMind acquisition reportedly included a clause establishing an ethics and safety board to oversee how DeepMind's AI capabilities would be used. The composition and powers of that board have remained largely opaque to the public. DeepMind operated with significant independence from Google for years; in 2023 Google Brain and DeepMind were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis. The early-acquisition concern about AI governance — built into the deal — is part of the early history of AI's institutional design.

question: In 2012, a team from the University of Toronto submitted a model called AlexNet to the ImageNet competition for image classification. AlexNet won by such a wide margin that the AI field reoriented around the approach. Who were the three authors?
answer: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton.
choices: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton.
Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton.
Andrej Karpathy, Sam Altman, and Greg Brockman.
Demis Hassabis, Mustafa Suleyman, and Shane Legg.
context: AlexNet — Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012 — is widely considered the start of the modern deep-learning era. The model was a deep convolutional neural network trained on GPUs. ImageNet 2012 was won by AlexNet at 16% top-5 error, down from 26% the year before — a dramatic leap. Sutskever later co-founded OpenAI. Krizhevsky went to Google. Hinton continued as the 'godfather of deep learning' until his 2023 Google departure. The three names are inseparable from the field's modern history.

question: AlexNet (2012) didn't just win ImageNet — it changed how AI researchers thought about scaling. What was the key technical detail that made AlexNet possible at that point in time?
answer: GPUs — graphics processors built for video games turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks.
choices: GPUs — graphics processors built for video games turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks.
Faster human labelers — Toronto had hired hundreds of students to label every image in the dataset by hand.
Better cameras — newer image sensors produced cleaner pictures that older models couldn't even read.
Quantum computers — Toronto's lab had access to a working quantum machine that competitors lacked.
context: GPUs (graphics processing units) had been built for video games — they can do many simple math operations in parallel, exactly what 3D graphics need. The AlexNet team realized that neural-network training has the same shape: lots of parallel matrix multiplications. They trained AlexNet on two consumer GPUs. The result: bigger models trained faster than anyone had been able to before. NVIDIA, the leading GPU maker, became one of the most valuable companies in the world a decade later, partly on this realization.

question: After AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, and Ilya Sutskever started a small company that Google quickly acquired. What did that acquisition signal?
answer: Big tech recognized the AlexNet team as central, and the talent-war for deep-learning researchers was on.
choices: Big tech recognized the AlexNet team as central, and the talent-war for deep-learning researchers was on.
Google planned to use the AlexNet team to design new chemical formulas for industrial use.
The three researchers had given up academic work entirely and would never publish another paper.
Google was about to fold its existing search-engine business and replace it with image classification.
context: DNN Research — the company the three founded shortly after AlexNet — was acquired by Google in 2013. Hinton joined Google part-time while remaining at Toronto. Krizhevsky stayed at Google. Sutskever later left to co-found OpenAI with Sam Altman in 2015. The acquisition was a small signal of what was coming: tech-giant talent competition for deep-learning expertise that would shape the next decade. By 2023 every major tech company had a frontier-AI lab and budget to match.

question: AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet error rate was about 16% (top-5). The previous year's winner — using traditional computer-vision techniques — had been around 26%. Why was the 10-point gap considered so striking?
answer: In benchmark competitions, single-percent gains had been the norm, so a 10-point leap meant a different approach had just won.
choices: In benchmark competitions, single-percent gains had been the norm, so a 10-point leap meant a different approach had just won.
The gap was actually a measurement error, since AlexNet's true score was about the same as the prior year.
The gap meant AlexNet was now solving math problems that other vision models could not handle either.
The gap meant AlexNet had been given a different test set than every other model in the competition.
context: Year-on-year improvement on ImageNet had typically been a percent or two — the result of careful engineering. AlexNet's leap was qualitatively different. It signaled that deep learning was a new paradigm, not an incremental improvement. Within two years, virtually every competitive ImageNet entry was a deep neural network. Within five years, the entire computer-vision field had reorganized around deep learning. The 'AlexNet moment' is a canonical example of how AI fields shift when a new approach finally clicks.

question: In 2018, the Turing Award — sometimes called the 'Nobel Prize of computing' — was shared by three researchers for their work on deep learning. Who were they?
answer: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio.
choices: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio.
Alan Turing, Marvin Minsky, and John McCarthy.
Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis, and Dario Amodei.
Andrej Karpathy, Ilya Sutskever, and Alex Krizhevsky.
context: Hinton (Toronto, Google), LeCun (NYU, Meta), and Bengio (Montreal) shared the 2018 Turing Award. The citation was for 'conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing.' The three had pursued neural-network research through the lean years of the 1990s and 2000s when other approaches were favored. By 2018, deep learning dominated AI and they were widely credited as its founding figures. Hinton would leave Google in May 2023; the other two remain at their industry posts.

question: Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio — the 2018 Turing Award winners — had pursued neural-network research through the 1990s and 2000s when other AI approaches were more popular. Why is that backstory part of why the prize meant something?
answer: They kept working on an unfashionable approach until it paid off, vindicating decades of unpopular research.
choices: They kept working on an unfashionable approach until it paid off, vindicating decades of unpopular research.
They had been the only AI researchers in the world until 2018, when others finally entered the field.
They each retired immediately after receiving the prize, so it served as a career-end recognition gift.
They invented the Turing Award itself, so giving it to themselves was simply administrative.
context: Through the 1990s and 2000s, neural networks were widely seen as a dead end. Support vector machines, decision trees, and other approaches were dominant. Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio kept publishing neural-network work — improving training methods, demonstrating new architectures — when the field had largely moved on. The 2012 AlexNet result and the explosion that followed proved their bet. The Turing Award was a recognition not just of the work but of the persistence. Recognition skill: a 'dead' research direction sometimes isn't.

question: In May 2023, Geoffrey Hinton, sometimes called the 'godfather of deep learning,' resigned from Google. He cited concerns about AI safety. How are Hinton's stated concerns different from Eliezer Yudkowsky's 'shut it all down' position?
answer: Hinton's concerns are near-term harms like disinformation, autonomous weapons, and job displacement, not Yudkowsky's 'AI wipes out humanity' framing.
choices: Hinton's concerns are near-term harms like disinformation, autonomous weapons, and job displacement, not Yudkowsky's 'AI wipes out humanity' framing.
Hinton thinks AI poses no real risk and critics are exaggerating; he resigned for unrelated personal reasons.
Hinton wants to ban all neural networks globally and rewrite AI using only formal symbolic logic systems.
Hinton and Yudkowsky hold identical views; the 'difference' is a media invention with no real substance.
context: Hinton resigned from Google in May 2023. He gave interviews citing concerns about AI-generated disinformation, fake images and video at scale, autonomous weapons, and labor disruption. His position is distinct from Yudkowsky's. Hinton talks about ordinary serious harms; Yudkowsky talks about extinction. Distinguishing these positions matters: 'AI safety' is not one position, and treating it as a single thing helps the loudest voices set the terms of debate.

question: Geoffrey Hinton said in 2023 interviews that part of why he left Google was so he could speak openly about AI risks. What does that suggest about the speech constraints that come with senior tech-company positions?
answer: Senior employees often can't publicly raise concerns about their company's products without consequences for their job.
choices: Senior employees often can't publicly raise concerns about their company's products without consequences for their job.
Senior employees at Google must speak through a press office and may not give any interviews at all.
Senior employees in AI must complete a five-year non-compete period before discussing their views.
Senior employees at Google work under federal classification rules that bar all external discussion.
context: Hinton's stated reason for leaving — being able to speak openly — is itself a recognition lesson about who can speak about technology and when. Senior employees at large companies often face real constraints on public criticism of their company's products or strategy. Hinton, financially secure and recognized for his life's work, could absorb the cost of leaving in a way younger researchers can't. The pattern is wider than AI: tech-industry insider voices often emerge most clearly after the insiders have left.

question: When Hinton left Google in May 2023, several news outlets framed it as 'godfather of AI quits over AI fears.' Why is that framing a useful but partial description of what he actually said?
answer: Hinton's worries are real but specific — disinformation, weapons, jobs — not the sweeping 'AI fears' the headline implies.
choices: Hinton's worries are real but specific — disinformation, weapons, jobs — not the sweeping 'AI fears' the headline implies.
Hinton was not actually 'godfather of AI' — the title belongs to John McCarthy, who coined the term in 1956.
Hinton did not quit Google — he stayed on as an unpaid advisor and remained a full Google employee.
Hinton was not worried about AI at all — he had quit to start a competing chatbot company of his own.
context: News headlines compress. 'Godfather of AI quits over AI fears' is a clean headline, but it elides the specifics. Hinton's articulated concerns are about disinformation scale, autonomous weapons, and job displacement — concrete near-term issues. Recognition skill: when a tech-news headline frames an event in maximally dramatic terms, read the underlying interviews. The substance is usually more interesting and more specific than the headline. Hinton's careful naming of distinct concerns has been more durably useful than the 'godfather quits' framing.

question: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman. Within five days he was back in his old role. What does the five-day timeline tell us about the company's governance structure?
answer: Whatever formal power the board had on paper, the actual power was held by the people building the technology, and those people wanted Altman back.
choices: Whatever formal power the board had on paper, the actual power was held by the people building the technology, and those people wanted Altman back.
The board never actually fired Altman, since the story was a hoax planted by competitors to damage OpenAI.
The board fired Altman in protest of a planned product launch, then unanimously reversed the decision.
The board members made a clerical error in the firing notice and had to undo it within the week.
context: The Nov 2023 OpenAI board crisis was as much governance theater as governance event. The board — set up as a non-profit overseeing the capped-profit OpenAI — fired Altman citing 'loss of confidence.' Microsoft (the largest investor) immediately offered Altman a job; nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Five days later Altman was back, most of the old board was gone, and a new board took shape. The episode showed that nominal governance — board structure on paper — doesn't necessarily map to actual power.

question: During the five days Sam Altman was fired (Nov 17-22, 2023), Microsoft made a public move. What did Microsoft do?
answer: Offered Altman and the OpenAI research team jobs at a new Microsoft AI division.
choices: Offered Altman and the OpenAI research team jobs at a new Microsoft AI division.
Sued OpenAI for breach of contract and demanded $13 billion in damages within seventy-two hours.
Closed all of its existing AI products and exited the AI market entirely for a period of weeks.
Acquired Apple in an emergency deal aimed at building a new AI chatbot platform from scratch.
context: Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, publicly offered Altman and any OpenAI staff who wanted to come a home at Microsoft. The offer was credible — Microsoft had already invested billions in OpenAI and had the engineering capacity to absorb a team. Nearly 700 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they'd leave for Microsoft if the board didn't reinstate Altman. The combination — a public landing spot at Microsoft plus an employee threat to walk — collapsed the board's position within days.

question: Ilya Sutskever — OpenAI co-founder and chief scientist — was reportedly central to the November 2023 board move against Sam Altman. He left OpenAI in May 2024. What did he do next?
answer: Founded a new AI lab called Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), focused on AI safety as its sole mission.
choices: Founded a new AI lab called Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), focused on AI safety as its sole mission.
Joined Apple as the head of its Siri division and led the team rebuilding the voice assistant.
Retired completely from AI research and became a high school computer-science teacher in Toronto.
Returned to school to get a second PhD in classical literature at Oxford University in England.
context: Sutskever co-founded OpenAI in 2015, led much of its scientific work, and reportedly sided with the board in firing Altman in Nov 2023. After Altman returned, Sutskever's role became uncertain; he left OpenAI in May 2024. Soon after, he announced Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), with the explicit single goal of building safe superintelligence. The framing — one product, one mission, no consumer offerings — was different from the typical AI startup. SSI is a notable data point in the question of what 'AI safety' looks like as an institutional commitment.

question: Ilya Sutskever's Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), founded in 2024, took a different approach from most AI startups. What's the key difference in how SSI describes itself?
answer: It has no consumer product and no commercial offerings, just a single research goal of safe superintelligence.
choices: It has no consumer product and no commercial offerings, just a single research goal of safe superintelligence.
It has the largest workforce of any AI company, with over fifty thousand employees from day one.
It is owned and operated by the United Nations as an international non-profit AI safety body.
It promises to share all of its research, weights, and trained models with anyone who emails the company.
context: SSI's founding message was about focus. No chatbot product. No API. No commercial distraction. The bet: a small lab focused entirely on one research direction can outpace larger labs split between research and commercial work. Whether this turns out to be right is open. The framing — research-pure, no-consumer — is itself worth recognizing as a particular institutional bet about how to do AI safety. Recognition skill: different AI labs make different bets about how to balance safety, commercial product, and research.

question: Andrej Karpathy is one of AI's most-followed figures online. His career has moved through several labs and roles. Where did Karpathy start in the AI industry?
answer: OpenAI — he was a founding member when the lab was launched in 2015.
choices: OpenAI — he was a founding member when the lab was launched in 2015.

context: Andrej Karpathy was a founding member of OpenAI when it launched in 2015. He'd been a Stanford PhD student under Fei-Fei Li, studying computer vision. After about a year at OpenAI, he left to lead Tesla Autopilot — the team building self-driving car software. He returned to OpenAI in 2023 and left again in 2024 to start educational content. The full arc — OpenAI founding member → Tesla Autopilot lead → educator — has shaped how the public thinks about AI through his publicly-available courses and YouTube videos.

question: Andrej Karpathy left OpenAI in 2017 to lead a major industrial AI project at another company. Which project did he lead?
answer: Tesla Autopilot — the team building Tesla's self-driving car software.

context: From 2017 to 2022, Karpathy led Tesla Autopilot — the team building Tesla's self-driving car software. The work involved scaling neural-network training and inference for real-time vehicle decisions, plus the data pipeline that fed it. Karpathy returned to OpenAI in early 2023 for about a year, then left in 2024 to focus on educational content. His path is one of a small number of AI engineers who have moved fluidly between top labs and applied industrial work.

question: Andrej Karpathy is well-known for one thing besides his industry roles: producing publicly-available educational content about AI. Why has this work mattered for AI's broader visibility?
answer: His tutorials and code walkthroughs have taught a generation of developers what's actually inside a neural network.

context: Karpathy's tutorials — building a neural network from scratch, walking through a GPT, training a tokenizer — have made the internal mechanics of modern AI accessible to a wide audience of developers. His content sits at a particular sweet spot: technical enough to be real, accessible enough that motivated newcomers can follow along. The result is a small public-education contribution that has shaped how a generation of developers thinks about what AI 'is' on the inside.

question: Elon Musk was a co-founder of OpenAI in 2015 but later departed. What did Musk do in 2023 to re-enter the frontier-AI race?
answer: Founded a new lab called xAI and released a chatbot called Grok integrated with the X platform.

context: Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 along with Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever, and others. He left the OpenAI board in 2018 (citing conflicts with Tesla's AI work). After ChatGPT's late-2022 launch, Musk publicly criticized OpenAI for departing from its non-profit roots. In 2023 he founded xAI; in late 2023 xAI released Grok, a chatbot integrated with the X platform (formerly Twitter). xAI raised billions in 2024-2025 funding rounds. Musk's lawsuits against OpenAI over its commercial pivot have continued in parallel.

question: Elon Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 but later left the board and now leads a competing lab, xAI. What does Musk's trajectory illustrate about the AI-lab landscape?

Sutskever left OpenAI for SSI. Karpathy left and returned and left again. The talent moves between labs constantly — not because of betrayals but because the community is small and the work is portable. Recognition skill: the 'competition' between AI labs is genuine but the people involved have often worked together.

question: Dario Amodei led research at OpenAI through the late 2010s and helped shape the GPT line of models. In 2021, he left OpenAI to found a new AI lab. What's the lab called?
answer: Anthropic, where he is CEO and which produces the Claude family of language models.

context: Dario Amodei left OpenAI in 2021 along with several other senior researchers — including his sister Daniela Amodei — to found Anthropic. The stated motivation was a different emphasis on AI safety research as a central concern. Anthropic produces the Claude family of language models, which compete with OpenAI's GPT line and Google's Gemini at the frontier. As of the bank's training horizon, Anthropic is one of the small handful of labs producing leading-edge language models.

question: Anthropic, founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and other ex-OpenAI researchers, describes itself as an AI-safety company. What's one practical way Anthropic has tried to express that mission in its products?

Constitutional AI is part of how Claude is trained. The approach is one institutional answer to 'how do we make a useful chatbot that behaves well' — alongside OpenAI's RLHF approach and other labs' methods. The bank doesn't take a position on which approach is right; the recognition skill is knowing that different labs make different choices.

question: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic together — Dario as CEO, Daniela as President. The sibling-led structure is unusual among major AI labs. Why is the institutional structure worth noticing?

The November 2023 OpenAI board crisis showed how board-versus-CEO dynamics can fracture a lab; Anthropic's structure is less exposed to that specific failure mode. The recognition skill: institutional design matters as much as research direction in shaping how a lab handles pressure. Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, and others all have different structures — and those structures shape what they actually do.

question: In February 2011, IBM's Watson played 'Jeopardy!' against two of the show's all-time champions. The match was watched by millions and ended decisively. What happened?

context: Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on 'Jeopardy!' in February 2011. The win required parsing the show's punny clue style, retrieving relevant facts, and producing a fast, confident answer. Watson was a complex system — not a single neural network but a stack of techniques, hand-tuned for the task. The win was a watershed for AI's public visibility — though Watson's later commercial deployments in healthcare and other industries had a more mixed record. Recognition skill: a polished demo and a working product are not always the same thing.

question: In May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. The result was a landmark for AI. Why was Kasparov's loss so significant beyond the chess world?
answer: It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, a long-anticipated milestone finally crossed.
choices: It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, a long-anticipated milestone finally crossed.

It was the first time the FIDE chess federation had certified a machine as a registered player.
context: Deep Blue won the 1997 match 3.5 to 2.5 (one win each plus a draw, with Deep Blue winning the final game). The chess-vs-AI competition had been a recurring AI benchmark since Herbert Simon's 1958 prediction. Once Deep Blue won, the goalpost moved: chess was demoted from 'real AI' to 'just search.' Kasparov, who had beaten Deep Blue's predecessor a year earlier, accused IBM of unsporting conduct around the match. The episode is a canonical example of the AI-effect pattern.

question: Before transformers (2017), the leading neural-network architecture for handling sequences was the LSTM — Long Short-Term Memory. When was the LSTM invented, and by whom?
answer: 1997 — by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, then at the Technical University of Munich.

1956 — by Marvin Minsky during the Dartmouth conference that named the AI field.
context: LSTM was published in 1997 by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber. The key idea: a recurrent neural network with carefully designed 'gates' that let information flow through long sequences without vanishing. LSTMs were the workhorse for language tasks through the 2000s and 2010s — speech recognition, machine translation, sequence modeling generally. Then the transformer (2017) largely replaced them for large-scale language work. LSTMs are still used in some applications. Schmidhuber's role in deep-learning history is sometimes contested; he has often pointed out priority claims when credit is given elsewhere.

question: Fei-Fei Li, a Stanford computer-science professor, launched a project in 2007 that turned out to be foundational for modern AI. What was the project?

context: Fei-Fei Li launched ImageNet at Princeton in 2007 and continued it at Stanford. The dataset eventually contained 14 million images, each labeled by category through a massive crowdsourcing effort. ImageNet became the benchmark that drove the deep-learning revolution: AlexNet won ImageNet 2012, and the rest of the field reorganized around the dataset and the techniques that worked on it. Li has since been a prominent advocate for ethical AI development and co-founded Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI.

question: DeepMind, the London-based AI lab now owned by Google, was co-founded in 2010 by Demis Hassabis along with two others. Who were Hassabis's co-founders?

Google acquired DeepMind in 2014. Suleyman later left to co-found Inflection AI, then moved to Microsoft to head a consumer AI division in 2024. Legg remained at DeepMind throughout. The founding-trio pattern — research lead + research generalist + business/policy partner — is a model that has been repeated at other AI labs since.

question: Stanley Kubrick's 1968 film '2001: A Space Odyssey' depicted a computer called HAL 9000 that turns against its astronaut crew. What did the film's choice of name 'HAL' allegedly come from?

Clarke, who co-wrote the film with Kubrick and wrote the novel, said the name was actually meant as 'Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer.' The IBM connection is one of those persistent cultural readings that the creators officially deny but everyone remembers. Either way, HAL set a template for fictional AI gone wrong.

question: Stable Diffusion, the open-source image-generation model, was released in August 2022 by Stability AI. Why was its release notable beyond the technical quality of the model?

It was the first AI image generator that could produce images in every language other than English with high quality.
context: Stable Diffusion's August 2022 release made open-source image generation a real thing. The weights were downloadable; anyone with a decent GPU could run the model locally. The ecosystem that grew up around it — fine-tunes, LoRAs, ControlNet, custom interfaces — was a countervailing force against the closed-API alternatives. Stability AI's subsequent corporate trajectory has been less smooth, but the open-weights release shaped how creative AI works today. The pattern parallels what Meta's Llama did for text models.

question: ImageNet, the labeled-image dataset that drove the 2012 deep-learning revolution, was built by humans labeling millions of images one at a time. How did Fei-Fei Li's team get that labeling done at scale?
answer: They used Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying many low-cost human workers small amounts per image to label categories.
choices: They used Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying many low-cost human workers small amounts per image to label categories.

context: Mechanical Turk was Amazon's crowdsourcing platform for small online tasks. ImageNet's labels — 'is this picture a dog? a cat? a Siberian husky?' — were exactly the right shape for Turk: small, well-defined, paid per task. The crowd labeled millions of images for cents each. The result was the dataset that made deep-learning vision possible. The Mechanical Turk dependence is sometimes overlooked in the AI-history story; it's a reminder that 'human in the loop' has been part of how AI works at scale from the start.

question: Andrew Ng is a major figure in AI education and applied AI. His online machine-learning course at Stanford and later at Coursera reached millions of students. Which company did he co-found that brought online courses to a wide audience?

Ng has also led AI work at Google Brain (he co-founded it), at Baidu (Chief Scientist), and at Landing AI (his current venture). He's a vocal AI doomerism skeptic and one of the people who turned the academic study of AI into something many people learn online. His career is one of the field's clearest examples of researcher-as-educator at scale.

question: Mira Murati was OpenAI's Chief Technology Officer through the company's most public-facing years and briefly served as interim CEO during the November 2023 Altman crisis. What did she do in September 2024?

After Altman's return she resumed her CTO role; in September 2024 she announced her departure. Her exit was part of a broader pattern: many senior OpenAI figures (Ilya Sutskever, Jan Leike, John Schulman, others) left in 2024. The pattern of senior-employee departures from a single lab is itself a piece of AI-industry history worth tracking.

question: DeepMind's AlphaFold released 3D structures for about 200 million proteins in 2021 — essentially every known protein in nature. Before AlphaFold, mapping one took a PhD student years. Why is this a leap for medicine?
answer: A drug works by binding to a protein's shape, knowing the shape lets researchers design drugs that fit
choices: A drug works by binding to a protein's shape, knowing the shape lets researchers design drugs that fit

Pharmaceutical labs can skip clinical trials once a protein's structure has been mapped by AI
context: AlphaFold 2, from DeepMind, solved a problem biologists had worked on for 50 years: predicting how a chain of amino acids folds into a 3D shape. Drug design starts from the target protein's shape — the drug must fit precisely into it. With a database of 200 million predicted shapes, researchers can screen drug candidates much faster than waiting for traditional X-ray crystallography.

question: In October 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was split between three scientists for protein-structure work. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper got the prize for AlphaFold at DeepMind. Who shared the other half — for designing brand-new proteins from scratch?
answer: David Baker, at the University of Washington
choices: David Baker, at the University of Washington

context: The 2024 Nobel Chemistry split honored two related leaps: AlphaFold's prediction of natural protein structures (Hassabis + Jumper), and computational design of entirely novel proteins (Baker's lab at the Institute for Protein Design, UW). Baker's group designed proteins that don't exist in nature — drug candidates, vaccines, sensors. Hinton + Bengio + LeCun shared the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning, but did not win this Chemistry Nobel.

question: AlphaFold doesn't physically fold proteins. It predicts the final 3D shape from the amino-acid sequence using a neural network trained on known structures. Why is calling it 'protein folding' a bit misleading?
answer: It learned to predict the answer from many examples, it doesn't simulate the chemistry of folding
choices: It learned to predict the answer from many examples, it doesn't simulate the chemistry of folding
It physically folds the protein in a tiny lab on a chip, then photographs the result for the output
It refuses to predict any protein that hasn't already been solved by traditional X-ray crystallography

context: The Protein Data Bank holds tens of thousands of experimentally determined protein structures. AlphaFold trained on these — learning the relationship between amino-acid sequence and 3D shape. At inference time it predicts; it does not simulate the physics of folding. This is faster but means it can fail on proteins very unlike anything in its training data.

question: Before AlphaFold, working out one protein's 3D structure typically required X-ray crystallography — growing a crystal of the protein, then firing X-rays at it and inferring the structure from the diffraction pattern. About how long did a single tough structure often take an experimental lab?
answer: Years of work, sometimes an entire PhD
choices: Years of work, sometimes an entire PhD
Minutes, using a desktop X-ray machine the lab kept ready
Hours, if the lab had a robotic crystallography rig running
Days, since most proteins formed crystals quickly with the right buffer
context: Crystallography is slow because growing well-ordered protein crystals is finicky — some proteins simply will not crystallize. Many real-world targets (membrane proteins especially) resisted for decades. Cryo-electron microscopy and NMR were alternatives, also slow. The AlphaFold leap was timing: with a sequence in hand, a researcher could now have a 3D model in hours instead of years. Experimental structure determination is still essential for confirming AI predictions and resolving cases where AlphaFold's confidence is low.

question: Game 2 of the 2016 AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol match — move 37 — AlphaGo played a 'shoulder hit' on the fifth line. Commentators called it a mistake; Lee Sedol left the room for fifteen minutes to recover. Why did this single move become the most-discussed in the history of computer Go?
answer: A machine made a creative move no human had considered, and it turned out to be a winning one
choices: A machine made a creative move no human had considered, and it turned out to be a winning one
AlphaGo accidentally triggered an opening trap that human players had memorized for decades
The move violated the rules of Go and the game had to be restarted by the referees
Lee Sedol's response forced AlphaGo into an endless loop the engineers had to manually break
context: Top professionals initially called Move 37 a mistake — it broke convention. AlphaGo's internal probability estimate said only about 1-in-10,000 human players would consider that move. AlphaGo won the game. Top Go players have since incorporated similar ideas into their play. The recognition skill: this is what AI capability looks like — pattern-finding on millions of self-play games surfacing moves humans hadn't tried — not 'understanding' or 'consciousness.'

question: AlphaGo learned Go partly by playing itself millions of times — a technique called self-play. Lee Sedol won game 4 of the 2016 match (the only human win against AlphaGo in that series) by playing a single move now called 'God's Touch.' What did the move expose about AlphaGo at the time?
answer: Even superhuman systems can have unexpected blind spots in positions they trained for less
choices: Even superhuman systems can have unexpected blind spots in positions they trained for less
Self-play makes a model perfect, Sedol's move was actually a recorded engine error after all
AlphaGo was secretly being controlled by human Go experts at DeepMind during all of the games
Lee Sedol was given access to AlphaGo's training data and exploited a memorized weakness
context: Move 78 in game 4 — Lee Sedol's 'wedge' — pushed AlphaGo into a position outside its training distribution. The engine made successive misjudgments. The recognition skill: capable AI can have surprising failure modes in cases its training under-covered. This pattern keeps showing up — from AlphaGo to LLMs that confidently fabricate citations on edge cases. Robustness to out-of-distribution inputs is a real research problem, not a minor detail.

question: Before 2016, Google Translate often produced famously broken English. The output became suddenly much better that year. The breakthrough was a switch from older statistical word-frequency methods to a new approach. What was it called?
answer: Neural machine translation, deep neural networks trained on huge parallel-text corpora
choices: Neural machine translation, deep neural networks trained on huge parallel-text corpora
Hand-crafted grammar rules, Google hired thousands of linguists to write rules per language pair
A live human translator queue, Google routed every request to translators behind the scenes
A bigger dictionary, the team simply added more word pairs to a lookup table for each language
context: From roughly 2007-2016, Google Translate used statistical machine translation: a phrase-based model that picked likely translations based on word-frequency tables. Output was stilted. In 2016, Google switched to GNMT (Google Neural Machine Translation), using deep neural networks trained on huge parallel-text corpora (sentences a human had translated into both languages). Translation quality jumped suddenly. Professional translators noticed. The 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' paper — which introduced the transformer — built on this lineage. Translation is the AI success story of the deep-learning era that least overpromised.

question: A 'parallel corpus' is the fuel for modern machine translation: a huge collection of sentences a human translator already converted into a second language. EU parliament debates, the Canadian Hansards, the United Nations records, and dubbed-movie subtitle pairs are all examples. Why does the model NEED translations done by humans first?
answer: It learns by matching patterns between paired sentences, without pairs
choices: It learns by matching patterns between paired sentences, without pairs
It needs human approval, every output sentence is checked by a translator before release
It uses the human translations directly, it looks up a near-match instead of generat
Human translators added secret marks to the parallel text that the AI is trained to decode
context: Modern translation is supervised learning: the model is shown millions of (source, target) sentence pairs and adjusts its weights to map source to target accurately. The EU parliament publishes proceedings in 24 languages — a massive pre-existing parallel corpus. Hansards (Canadian parliament) gave English-French. Subtitles gave many pairs. Without these human-made pairs, the model has nothing to imitate. This is supervised learning at scale.

question: GitHub Copilot (launched 2021, built on OpenAI's models) suggests code as a programmer types — autocomplete for whole lines and functions. Programmers say Copilot is excellent at one kind of task and unreliable at another. Which combination is closest to the reality?
answer: Great at common patterns and boilerplate; unreliable for novel logic and security-sensitive code
choices: Great at common patterns and boilerplate; unreliable for novel logic and security-sensitive code
Great at everything, Copilot now writes complete production systems with zero human review
Bad at everything, every output it produces is broken code that compiles only by accident
Great at security audits and novel logic; struggles only on common patterns and boilerplate
context: Copilot was trained on huge swaths of public GitHub code. It excels at common patterns it has seen many times — typical function signatures, standard library calls, well-known algorithms. It is unreliable for novel domain logic (which it can confabulate) and for security-sensitive code (where subtly-wrong suggestions can introduce vulnerabilities). Professional programmers use it as a fast autocomplete and then review the output. Treating Copilot output as authoritative without review is the failure mode that mirrors the lawyer-cites-fake-cases failure for legal AI.

question: Cursor is an AI-powered code editor that became popular in 2023-2024. It's basically VS Code with deep LLM integration — the AI can edit files, run commands, and reason across a whole codebase. What's the trade-off compared to GitHub Copilot's per-line autocomplete?
answer: More power, more risk, broader changes that need closer review, especially across many files
choices: More power, more risk, broader changes that need closer review, especially across many files
Less power, less risk, Cursor only suggests one character at a time with full safety
More power, less risk, the deeper integration makes Cursor automatically safer than Copilot
Less power, more risk, Cursor is just a slower Copilot with no codebase awareness
context: Cursor's design gives the AI more context — it can see the whole project, find related code, refactor across files. That power scales the risk: a wrong suggestion can touch many files at once. Programmers who use Cursor well treat the AI's output as a draft pull request, reviewing line by line before accepting. Generally: as AI tooling gets more agentic, the importance of human review goes up, not down. 'AI agents will do the review' is the failure mode worth recognizing.

question: Modern AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) use 'diffusion.' The model starts with TV static and gradually removes the noise, step by step, until a clean image appears. Why does this work?
answer: Learning to clean up noise teaches the model what real images look like, so noise becomes a creative starting point
choices: Learning to clean up noise teaches the model what real images look like, so noise becomes a creative starting point
Static is actually compressed image data, and diffusion just unpacks it back into the original photo
The noise is randomly chosen from real photos, and the model is just blending those photos together
Diffusion models steal pixels from the training set and rearrange them into the requested image
context: Diffusion models are trained on a clever flip: take a real image, add noise to it step by step, then teach the network to reverse the process — predicting how to remove noise. After training, you start with pure noise and apply the network repeatedly, guided by a text prompt. Each step the image becomes a bit more like 'what the prompt described.'

question: Stable Diffusion (released August 2022 by Stability AI) was a big deal because its weights were released as a free download. DALL-E and Midjourney are API-only. What did open-weights image generation enable that closed models couldn't?
answer: Anyone can run it locally, no logs, no censorship, modifications and fine-tunes available
choices: Anyone can run it locally, no logs, no censorship, modifications and fine-tunes available
Stable Diffusion images came out in higher resolution than any DALL-E version ever could
Stability AI ran its model on every user's GPU for free, so nobody needed an account
The model could generate images that were copyright-protected by default for the user
context: Open weights = anyone can download the model file and run it on their own computer. This means no usage logs back to the company, no content-policy filters except what you choose, the ability to fine-tune on specific styles (artists, characters, looks), and a vibrant modification community. The same open-vs-closed split appears in LLMs (Llama / Mistral / DeepSeek open; GPT-4 / Claude closed). Open weights are the countervailing force against a few companies setting all the rules.

question: ElevenLabs and similar AI voice services let anyone clone a voice from a short audio sample — sometimes just 30 seconds. The technology has powerful accessibility uses (stroke survivors regaining their original voice, audiobook narration in many languages). It also enables a scam pattern. What scam grew quickly in 2023-24?
answer: Cloned-voice grandparent scams, a 'family member' calls in distress, asking for emergency money
choices: Cloned-voice grandparent scams, a 'family member' calls in distress, asking for emergency money
Cloned voices that order pizza without paying using stolen credit-card details on file
Voice clones used to read aloud private text messages between strangers in transit
AI-cloned voices that change the listener's accent during a call automatically
context: Voice cloning needs only a few seconds of clean audio — easily harvested from a voicemail, a social media video, a podcast. 'Grandparent scams' using cloned voices took off in 2023-2024. The FBI publicly recommends every family establish a safe word — a short phrase only family members know — that can be used to verify identity on calls asking for money or help. The accessibility uses are real and good: people who lost their voice to ALS can speak again in their own voice. The defensive habit: safe word, callback to the known number, verify.

question: Voice cloning has genuinely transformative accessibility uses. ALS patients have used the technology to bank their voice before disease progression takes it. Stroke survivors and people with vocal-cord damage use cloned versions of their own pre-illness recordings. What's the right way to think about the dual-use problem?
answer: The same capability enables real human good and real human harm
choices: The same capability enables real human good and real human harm
The accessibility uses are too rare to matter, the technology should be banned outright today
Voice cloning is harmless because most callers can easily tell a clone from a real voice
Only government-licensed services should be allowed to perform voice cloning at any scale
context: The accessibility uses (assistive communication, audiobook narration in your own voice, language learning) are real. Banning the tech kills those uses without stopping bad actors, who can use open-weights tools. The realistic posture: dual-use capability that calls for defensive habits — safe words, callbacks, identity verification — not bans that mostly hurt legitimate users.

question: AI-assisted mammography is now common in screening for breast cancer. The AI flags suspicious regions for the radiologist to examine more closely. Studies have shown it can catch some cancers human readers missed. What's the role the AI is actually playing in this workflow?
answer: A second reader, a different perspective that may catch things the human missed
choices: A second reader, a different perspective that may catch things the human missed
The primary diagnostician, the AI's call is sent directly to patients without human review
A patient-care planner, the AI decides which treatment options each patient receives next
A radiology educator, the AI trains incoming residents instead of human radiologists
context: AI as 'second reader' is a well-studied workflow in mammography. The radiologist reads first; the AI flags anything it sees; the radiologist re-examines those regions. Studies (the Swedish MASAI trial 2023, others) have shown improvements in cancer detection without unacceptable increases in false alarms. The human remains responsible for the final read and the clinical decision.

question: Google Health's AI flags retinal images that show signs of diabetic retinopathy. It's used as a screening tool in clinics in India and Thailand, where specialists are scarce. What does the AI specifically do in this deployment?
answer: Filters who needs to see a specialist next, most retinas are normal and the AI catches the high-risk ones
choices: Filters who needs to see a specialist next, most retinas are normal and the AI catches the high-risk ones
Treats the retinal damage directly using laser commands sent through the camera lens
