Different LLMs run at different speeds so one of them always finishes first incorrectly
Different LLMs are programmed to always agree to make AI seem more trustworthy
context: Cross-checking between LLMs catches some hallucinations: if Claude and ChatGPT give very different answers, at least one is wrong. But shared training data (much of the public internet is in every LLM's training set) means they can independently confabulate the same wrong answer. Cross-checking is a useful early filter, not a final verification. The final verification is checking the actual source — book, paper, authoritative database, expert human. Recognition: AI cross-check is a starting point, not an endpoint.

question: A teacher receives a student essay that quotes a Shakespeare line slightly wrong. Two different AI checkers flag it as 'likely AI-written.' The teacher confronts the student, who insists it was their own work. What's the defensive principle?
answer: AI-detection tools are unreliable, false-positive rates can be high, especially for non-native speakers
choices: AI-detection tools are unreliable, false-positive rates can be high, especially for non-native speakers
AI-detection tools are always right, the student is lying every time
AI-detection tools are always wrong, they should never be used in any school
AI-detection tools work fine, the misquoted Shakespeare proves the student used AI
context: AI text detectors (GPTZero, Originality.AI, others) have known false-positive problems — sometimes flagging human writing as AI, especially when the writer is non-native, very formal, or following a template they were taught. The Stanford study (2023) found notable false-positive rates on essays by non-native English speakers. Schools that base discipline solely on AI detector output have produced unjust outcomes. Defensive principle: detection is a tool for conversation, not for verdict. If you suspect AI, ask the student to explain their thinking and rewrite a paragraph under supervision.

question: You want to know what happened in the news today. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini will give you confident answers — even though their training data has a cutoff date months or years ago. What's wrong with using an LLM for current events?
answer: Training data ends at a cutoff date; anything after is invented or guessed
choices: Training data ends at a cutoff date; anything after is invented or guessed
LLMs are biased toward bad news, they cover only negative stories
LLMs cannot read the news because they don't have eyes
LLMs are programmed to never discuss current events for safety reasons
context: An LLM's knowledge ends at its training cutoff. ChatGPT might know up to early 2023 or 2024 depending on the model. Anything after is either retrieved live (if the model has a search tool) or fabricated. Asking 'what happened today' to a non-search-enabled LLM produces confident hallucination. Recognition: for current events, use a search engine or a news site — not a static LLM. Some LLM products have built-in search; these are different from the underlying model and can be reliable for current events. Know which mode you're in.

question: Some AI products combine an LLM with live web search — the LLM searches, reads results, then answers. This is much more reliable for current events than the LLM alone. What's the new failure mode this introduces?
answer: The LLM can be misled by low-quality web sources it retrieves and then quotes them confidently
choices: The LLM can be misled by low-quality web sources it retrieves and then quotes them confidently
Search-enabled LLMs charge per question, making them expensive to use
Search-enabled LLMs only work in English-speaking countries with English-language sites
Search-enabled LLMs require a special browser that no major browser company makes
context: When an LLM uses search, the answer is only as good as the sources retrieved. If the top results for a query are bad (SEO spam, content farms, factually wrong sites), the LLM can confidently regurgitate them. Some products surface their sources so you can check; others don't. Recognition: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps a lot with knowledge cutoffs and hallucination, but introduces a new dependency — the quality of the search and the sources. Check the citations the AI uses; they reveal whether the answer is grounded.

question: Browser extensions that integrate AI (summarize this page, translate this article, write this email for me) have powerful uses and a specific privacy risk. What is it?
answer: The extension can read every page you visit and may send the content to a remote AI server
choices: The extension can read every page you visit and may send the content to a remote AI server
The extension uses too much battery and slows down all of your other browser tabs
The extension only works on certain websites because of cookies blocked by your browser
The extension shows pop-up advertisements every fifteen minutes of browsing time
context: When you install a browser AI extension, you typically grant it permission to read content on websites you visit. To 'summarize this page' or 'help me write this email,' it needs to read the page content. That content typically goes to the AI provider's server. Webmail, banking, school portals — content the user assumes is private — can flow to a third party. Recognition: read the permissions before installing a browser AI extension. 'Can read and change all your data on websites you visit' is a serious permission, even when the extension is from a reputable company.

question: A browser extension claims to 'enhance your AI experience' and is offered for free. Before installing, what's the defensive principle for evaluating it?
answer: Free = your data is likely the product, read the privacy policy and permissions carefully
choices: Free = your data is likely the product, read the privacy policy and permissions carefully
Free = free, there's no catch to browser extensions in any major browser store
Free extensions are required by law to be safer than paid ones across all jurisdictions
Free extensions can never harvest data, only paid extensions have permission to do so
context: Free browser extensions have a long history of being sold or compromised — original developer sells the extension, new owner adds tracking or malware, the old install base inherits the upgrade. Even legitimately-developed free extensions need a business model: ads, data sales, or premium-feature upsell are typical. For AI extensions specifically: anything that 'reads page content' is also potentially exfiltrating it. Recognition: vet the developer, read the privacy policy, check community reviews for sketchy behavior. Treat 'free AI extension' as you'd treat 'free anything' — with healthy skepticism.

question: The C2PA standard (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) signs images and videos at the moment they're captured — by the camera or by the AI model that generated them. Why is upfront signing stronger than trying to detect fakes after the fact?
answer: A signature proves the source; detection is an arms race that AI generation keeps winning
choices: A signature proves the source; detection is an arms race that AI generation keeps winning
Signed content cannot be edited in any image editor, every change destroys the file
Signed content is automatically blocked from social media for safety reasons
Signed content is owned by C2PA, which takes a small fee for every view
context: C2PA is backed by Adobe, Microsoft, Intel, BBC, Sony, and others. Cameras sign images at capture (chain of provenance: this Nikon photographed this scene at this time). AI tools can sign generated content (this image was made by DALL-E from this prompt). Editing tools sign their changes (this image was cropped in Photoshop). The chain of custody travels with the file. Adoption is still partial. Recognition: the right defense against AI-generated misinformation isn't only post-hoc detection — it's provenance that travels with content. The standard is the right idea even where adoption lags.

question: C2PA content credentials are a strong idea but face real adoption hurdles. What's the biggest limitation right now?
answer: Most cameras, social platforms, and AI tools still don't preserve or display the credentials
choices: Most cameras, social platforms, and AI tools still don't preserve or display the credentials
Cameras that support C2PA cost ten thousand dollars and are only sold in Japan
C2PA only works on images, not on text or video or any other type of content
C2PA credentials can be removed by anyone in two clicks within any image editor
context: C2PA is well-designed but partially deployed. Most consumer cameras don't sign. Most social platforms strip metadata on upload (Facebook, Twitter, Instagram). Most browser viewers don't display the credentials even when present. As of 2024-2025, the standard works mainly within professional newsrooms and a few AI tools that sign generated content. The recognition skill: 'C2PA exists' is true; 'you can rely on it everywhere' is not. The defensive gap remains — and other recognition skills (reverse image search, examining context, source verification) still matter most.

question: An image goes viral with a shocking caption. You want to check if it's real or fake. The first defensive move is reverse image search — feeding the image to a search engine and seeing where else it's appeared. Why is this so useful?
answer: It often reveals the original context: same image from an old event, or known fake, or stock photo
choices: It often reveals the original context: same image from an old event, or known fake, or stock photo
It calculates the percentage chance an image is AI-generated based on file size
It shows you what the image would look like if you flipped it horizontally
It tells you whether the photographer paid taxes on the income from the picture
context: Reverse image search (Google Images, TinEye, Yandex) finds other copies of the same image online. The original context often appears: a 2014 protest miscaptioned as a 2024 event, a stock photo presented as a real situation, a known fake from a debunking site. The technique catches a huge fraction of disinformation that uses recycled imagery. Defensive workflow: see suspicious image → save it → reverse image search → check the earliest appearances. Quick, free, often decisive.

question: Google Images, TinEye, and Yandex's reverse image search each have strengths. For finding the EARLIEST version of an image (catching a recycled photo presented as new), which option is generally considered best?
answer: TinEye, it specifically tries to find the oldest known copies of an image
choices: TinEye, it specifically tries to find the oldest known copies of an image
Bing, Bing specializes in archive of older images from before 2010
DuckDuckGo, it has a hidden image archive going back to the 1800s
Wikipedia, Wikipedia indexes every image ever uploaded to the internet
context: TinEye (founded 2008) prioritizes oldest-first matching and is excellent for catching recycled photos used in misinformation campaigns. Google Images is broader and finds many more matches but sorts differently. Yandex is sometimes better for non-Western faces and contexts. Defensive habit: try multiple reverse search engines if the first doesn't give satisfying results. Different indexes catch different things. Recognition: this is one of the highest-leverage 'easy thing the kid can actually do' moves in the entire defensive-AI toolkit.

question: Clearview AI built one of the largest face-recognition databases in the world by scraping billions of photos from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and similar sites without asking the people in the photos. They sell access to law enforcement. What can ordinary people do to opt out?
answer: Some jurisdictions (EU, Illinois, California) give legal opt-out rights, but enforcement is patchy globally
choices: Some jurisdictions (EU, Illinois, California) give legal opt-out rights, but enforcement is patchy globally
Nothing, the photos are gone from your control forever once posted online
Email Clearview a list of photo URLs and they delete each one within an hour
Wear sunglasses in every photo from now forward, the past photos automatically erase
context: Clearview scraped publicly-visible photos from many platforms. EU GDPR and the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) give residents rights to demand deletion of biometric data. Clearview has paid settlements (Illinois ACLU case, $20M+ in 2022). Enforcement is patchy outside the EU and a few US states. The general principle: data uploaded publicly can be scraped, indexed, and used for purposes you didn't anticipate. Defensive habit going forward: privacy settings on social media; understanding that public posts are training data for somebody.

question: Face-recognition databases now exist at police departments, retailers, sports venues, and apartment buildings. The Robert Williams case (Detroit, 2020) became famous — what happened?
answer: Williams was wrongly arrested after a face-recognition match identified him as a thief he wasn't
choices: Williams was wrongly arrested after a face-recognition match identified him as a thief he wasn't
Williams sold his face-recognition company for billions, becoming the model success story
Williams invented the first commercially deployed face-recognition algorithm in the 1980s
Williams was a police officer who quit after refusing to use face recognition on civilians
context: Robert Williams, a Black resident of Farmington Hills, Michigan, was wrongly arrested in January 2020 after Detroit police used face-recognition technology to identify him from a surveillance image. He spent 30 hours in jail before being released. He had a documented alibi. His ACLU lawsuit was settled. Other wrongful arrests from face-recognition errors have been documented: Nijeer Parks (NJ 2019), Porcha Woodruff (Detroit 2023). Recognition: face-recognition error rates are worse on people of color in many studied systems (NIST findings, 2019). The technology exists; the error patterns are unequal; the consequences are real.

question: 23andMe, AncestryDNA, MyHeritage, and similar services give consumers DNA-based ancestry reports. They also keep your genetic data. What's the recognition skill about what can happen to that data over time?
answer: The company can be acquired, can change its policies, or can be compelled by law enforcement
choices: The company can be acquired, can change its policies, or can be compelled by law enforcement
DNA data is deleted automatically after one year of inactivity in any consumer service
DNA data is encrypted by the customer themselves and the company cannot read it
DNA data is owned by the customer and the company is forbidden from analyzing it
context: DNA submitted to consumer genetic services lives indefinitely. The company can be sold (23andMe filed for bankruptcy in 2025 after years of struggle; its database has been a sale-of-asset question). Privacy policies can change. Law enforcement has compelled disclosure (Golden State Killer case — Joseph DeAngelo identified via GEDmatch in 2018). Insurance companies have tried to access genetic data. Recognition: DNA isn't password-recoverable. Once it's in a database, the privacy contract you signed is only as durable as the company and its policies. Think before submitting.

question: The Golden State Killer case (Joseph DeAngelo, identified in 2018, convicted in 2020) was the breakthrough that showed police could use consumer DNA databases to solve cold cases. What technique did investigators use?
answer: Family-relative matching, they found cousins in GEDmatch whose DNA partially matched the killer's
choices: Family-relative matching, they found cousins in GEDmatch whose DNA partially matched the killer's
Cell-phone tower analysis combined with social-media facial recognition matching
Voice recordings from old wiretaps run through 2018-era voice clone detection systems
Fingerprint scanning of every Californian over the age of 60 with their consent
context: DeAngelo had never submitted his DNA to a consumer service. But his distant cousins had. Genetic genealogist Barbara Rae-Venter used GEDmatch (an open consumer DNA-sharing database) to find partial matches, build a family tree, and narrow to him. Police confirmed with a discarded DNA sample. The technique now solves dozens of cold cases per year. Recognition: your DNA submission isn't just about you — it identifies your relatives, current and future. People in 2024 are findable through cousins who submitted DNA decades ago. The defensive frame: 'I'm not on a database' is misleading; you may be effectively on every database where any of your relatives have submitted.

question: Signal Messenger uses end-to-end encryption: only you and the person you're messaging can read the content. The Signal Foundation can't read your messages even if served with a subpoena. Why does this work?
answer: Messages are encrypted on your phone with a key Signal doesn't have, they're decrypted only on the recipient's phone
choices: Messages are encrypted on your phone with a key Signal doesn't have, they're decrypted only on the recipient's phone
Signal hires only very loyal employees who promise never to read messages they have access to
Signal stores everything in a server in Iceland that no government has ever subpoenaed yet
Signal is exempt from all subpoenas because it's a registered non-profit organization
context: End-to-end encryption (E2EE) means the cryptographic keys to decrypt messages live only on the sender and recipient devices. The service provider (Signal) routes encrypted blobs without being able to read them. Signal's transparency reports document this — government subpoenas reveal only metadata Signal does have (account creation date, last connection), not message content. Same model in WhatsApp (built on Signal's protocol), and to varying degrees in iMessage. NOT in default Telegram, default SMS, or unencrypted email. Recognition: for sensitive conversations, the encryption mode matters more than the brand.

question: Proton makes Mail, Drive, VPN, Pass, and other privacy-focused services. The company is based in Switzerland and uses end-to-end encryption where possible. Why is the company's jurisdiction a meaningful detail?
answer: Swiss privacy law and data-protection rules make compelled disclosure harder than in some other countries
choices: Swiss privacy law and data-protection rules make compelled disclosure harder than in some other countries
Switzerland has free electricity for any company that promises end-to-end encryption forever
Swiss employees of tech companies are required by law to refuse all law enforcement requests
Switzerland has no internet, making it impossible to subpoena anything stored there
context: Proton operates under Swiss law, which has stronger data protection and procedural protections than many other countries. Combined with end-to-end encryption, this raises the bar for compelled disclosure of user content. The Swiss jurisdiction isn't a magic shield — Swiss courts can still compel disclosure of metadata Proton has, and Proton has complied with valid Swiss court orders in some cases. But it's a stronger position than US-based services subject to US compelled-disclosure rules without comparable protections. Recognition: privacy in tech services depends on (1) what data exists, (2) where it's stored, and (3) the law of the jurisdiction.

question: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) encrypts your internet traffic between your device and the VPN provider, then sends it on from the provider's server. What does a VPN do well, and what doesn't it do?
answer: Hides traffic from your local network and ISP; doesn't hide it from the VPN provider or destination sites
choices: Hides traffic from your local network and ISP; doesn't hide it from the VPN provider or destination sites
Makes you completely anonymous on the internet against every adversary including the FBI
Encrypts every website you ever visit even if the site itself uses no encryption
Prevents all advertisers, governments, and platforms from tracking you in any way at all
context: VPN trade-offs in plain terms. Hidden from: your local Wi-Fi network, your school/work network admin, your ISP. NOT hidden from: the VPN provider (which now sees your traffic), the destination websites you visit (which see VPN-provider IP, still log you), and any tracking they do. A VPN swaps who can see your traffic — not whether anyone can. Recognition: 'VPN = anonymous' is wrong. VPN useful for specific threat models (avoiding ISP tracking, accessing geo-restricted content, securing on public Wi-Fi). Picking a trustworthy provider matters because they're the new can-see-everything party.

question: You can now run capable AI models on your own computer — no cloud service involved. Tools like Ollama and LM Studio make it easy. The models (Llama 3, Mistral, others) run locally on your machine. What's the main privacy benefit?
answer: Your prompts never leave your computer, no company logs them, no government can subpoena them
choices: Your prompts never leave your computer, no company logs them, no government can subpoena them
Local models are five times faster than every cloud AI service in the world
Local models are smarter than cloud AIs because they have more privacy training
Local models work without electricity since they run inside the computer's local memory
context: Local model inference: download a model file (Llama 3 8B is about 5GB), run it via Ollama or LM Studio, ask questions. The conversation never touches the internet. Nothing logged on any company's server. For sensitive use cases (medical questions you don't want logged, code with secrets you can't redact, personal struggles you wouldn't tell a school chatbot), this is a real option. Hardware costs are dropping; an M-series Mac or a gaming PC with a decent GPU can run useful local models. Recognition: 'AI = cloud' is a default, not a requirement. Local AI exists.

question: Running local AI models has real trade-offs versus using a frontier cloud model. What's the most honest summary of the gap as of 2025?
answer: Local models are good enough for many tasks; frontier cloud models are still better at hard ones
choices: Local models are good enough for many tasks; frontier cloud models are still better at hard ones
Local models are uniformly better than cloud models for every task at any difficulty level
Local models work only for math and not for any kind of writing or reasoning ever
Local models cannot read English or any other language used widely on the internet
context: Open-weights models (Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) have closed much of the gap to closed frontier models. For many tasks — drafting, summarizing, basic coding, general Q&A — a 7B-or-larger local model is good enough. For the hardest reasoning, latest knowledge, multimodal tasks, frontier closed models still win. The frontier gap was wider in 2023; it's narrower in 2025. Recognition: the cloud-vs-local choice is now a real choice. Privacy gain is large; capability loss is shrinking; cost is the user's GPU plus electricity.

question: Many US school districts use AI-powered surveillance tools (Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark, Securly) that monitor student emails, chats, search queries, and documents — looking for signs of self-harm, violence, or rule violations. What's the recognition skill for students using school accounts?
answer: Everything you write on a school account is potentially read by both algorithms and humans
choices: Everything you write on a school account is potentially read by both algorithms and humans
Surveillance tools only activate for students under 13 and stop monitoring once you turn 14
Surveillance tools only watch student emails; chats and documents are not monitored
Surveillance tools are required by law to inform you before each individual action they take
context: Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark, and similar tools are widely used in US K-12. They use AI to scan student communications and flag concerning content. Flags go to human reviewers. School counselors and administrators get reports. The benefits include real interventions on students at risk. The trade-offs include surveillance of student speech, occasional misinterpretation of literary references or jokes, and chilling effects on what students will write or research. Recognition: separate your sensitive writing from your school account. Personal journaling, exploratory writing, struggle-narratives don't belong in a school-monitored space.

question: School AI surveillance tools occasionally produce dramatic false positives — a student researching a poem about violence, or quoting an old novel, or discussing a video game gets flagged and pulled into a meeting. What's the defensive principle for students?
answer: Quote the source explicitly when discussing dark themes, and assume context isn't fully understood by automated tools
choices: Quote the source explicitly when discussing dark themes, and assume context isn't fully understood by automated tools
Avoid all literature class assignments that involve difficult themes, discuss only happy poems
Use codewords for any literature topic that includes violence, death, or sadness
Submit a sworn affidavit before every essay declaring no literal threats are intended
context: Automated flagging tools don't understand context well. A student writing about The Catcher in the Rye, Macbeth, or a violent video game can trigger flags. Documented incidents include students disciplined for fiction-writing assignments their teacher had assigned. Defensive principle: quote your source clearly, attribute fiction explicitly, and accept that institutional AI is going to be clumsy. None of this means students shouldn't read or write about hard subjects — it just means the AI watching isn't subtle.

question: Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second check — beyond your password — when logging in. The two common methods are SMS codes and authenticator apps. Which is significantly more secure?
answer: Authenticator apps, SMS can be hijacked via SIM-swap attacks
choices: Authenticator apps, SMS can be hijacked via SIM-swap attacks
SMS, authenticator apps require a constant internet connection that can fail
Both are equally secure, the difference is purely a matter of personal preference
Neither, 2FA was deprecated in 2023 and is no longer recommended for any account
context: SIM-swap attack: an attacker convinces your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a new SIM under their control. They then receive your SMS 2FA codes. This has been used in many high-profile account takeovers (crypto exchanges, social media accounts). Authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password) generate codes on your specific device — there's no SIM to swap. Hardware keys (YubiKey) are even stronger. Recognition: SMS 2FA is much better than no 2FA, but authenticator-app 2FA is the upgrade worth making.

question: Hardware security keys (YubiKey, Google Titan) are the strongest form of two-factor authentication for most people. They use a physical USB or NFC device that has to be present to log in. What's the additional security benefit beyond authenticator apps?
answer: Phishing-resistant, a hardware key won't authenticate to a fake login page
choices: Phishing-resistant, a hardware key won't authenticate to a fake login page
Cheaper than authenticator apps, they cost only $5 each for life
Smaller than your phone, easier to carry on a keychain than a phone
Faster than authenticator apps, they work without any human interaction at all
context: Hardware keys use the WebAuthn / FIDO2 standard. When you tap the key to authenticate, it cryptographically verifies the website you're on. If a phishing page tries to capture your credentials, the key won't authenticate — the URL doesn't match. This is the property authenticator apps lack: a 6-digit code can be typed into a fake site. The hardware key cannot. Recognition: for the accounts that matter most (email, financial, school, work), hardware keys are the gold standard. The cost ($25-50) is small for the risk reduction.

question: Password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, KeePass, others) generate and store unique strong passwords for every account. The single security trade-off is that they consolidate all your passwords behind one master password. Why is that trade-off still worth it?
answer: Most attacks succeed through password reuse, a manager kills reuse and reduces total risk dramatically
choices: Most attacks succeed through password reuse, a manager kills reuse and reduces total risk dramatically
Password managers are required by law for everyone over the age of 13 in the US
Password managers store your information offline so they never need internet at all
Password managers also remind you when each password reaches its expiration date by mail
context: The most common path to account compromise: password reuse. Site A gets breached, your password leaks, attackers try it on every account you have. Password managers kill reuse — every site has a unique strong password, breach on one site doesn't help on others. Yes, the master password becomes a single point of failure, but it's a focused one (use a strong passphrase, hardware key 2FA on the manager itself). The math favors the manager. Recognition: this is one of the single biggest defensive moves an average person can make.

question: Your password manager generates a 20-character random password for a new account. The site forces you to keep the password under 12 characters or insists on no special characters. What's the defensive principle?
answer: Use the maximum allowed by the site, even a constrained random password is better than a memorable one
choices: Use the maximum allowed by the site, even a constrained random password is better than a memorable one
Use your dog's name and birth year, it's easier to remember and just as safe
Use the same password as your other accounts, it's already known to be working
Refuse to use the site, any site with bad password rules cannot ever be trusted with data
context: Sites with bad password rules (low max length, character restrictions) are signaling something concerning about their security maturity. But the practical principle is: pick the best password the site will accept, and use 2FA if available. A 12-character random password is still vastly stronger than 'Spot2010'. The manager will store it; you don't need to remember it. Recognition: don't let bad site policies drive you back to weak/reused passwords. Pick the best within the constraints.

question: Your smartphone collects and shares more data about you than almost any other device you own. What categories of data flow off your phone to third parties typically?
answer: Location history, advertising ID, app usage data, microphone permissions in some apps
choices: Location history, advertising ID, app usage data, microphone permissions in some apps
Only your name and email, nothing else is shared without your explicit consent each time
Only the time of day you use the phone, no other data leaves the device at all
Only data from games and entertainment apps, productivity apps cannot share data
context: A modern smartphone collects: location (continuously by GPS + cell + Wi-Fi triangulation), advertising ID (a unique identifier shared with apps and trackers), app usage data (often shared with analytics services), camera/microphone permissions when granted (and abused, occasionally), contact lists when shared with apps, file access in many cases. Recognition: this isn't paranoia — it's the default privacy state of a modern phone. iOS and Android both let you tighten the defaults significantly (ad ID off, location off for apps that don't need it, microphone permission revoked where unnecessary).

question: Apps ask for permissions: location, contacts, microphone, camera, photos, files. The defensive principle for ordinary users is straightforward. What is it?
answer: Grant only what the app actually needs to do its job, deny everything else
choices: Grant only what the app actually needs to do its job, deny everything else
Grant everything, denying permissions causes apps to crash and lose your data
Grant nothing, every app must work with zero permissions or you delete it
Grant permissions only on Tuesdays, phones are more secure on Tuesdays for a reason
context: Permissions are about least-privilege: the flashlight app doesn't need your contacts; the calculator doesn't need your location; the photo editor doesn't need your microphone. Both iOS and Android let you grant permissions per-app, often per-use. Reviewing app permissions quarterly is a cheap habit with significant privacy payoff. Recognition: 'grant all' is a default that doesn't serve you. Many apps work fine with limited permissions; apps that demand permissions they don't need are worth investigating.

question: Your phone's advertising identifier (called IDFA on iOS, GAID on Android) is a unique ID that apps and trackers can use to follow you across services. Both iOS and Android now let you turn it off. What does turning it off accomplish?
answer: Trackers can no longer link your activity across apps using that single ID
choices: Trackers can no longer link your activity across apps using that single ID
Your phone now refuses to run any application that displays advertisements at all
Apple and Google will pay you a small fee for every advertisement you would have seen
Your phone deletes all advertising apps you have ever downloaded from the store
context: The advertising ID is a single unique identifier that apps and SDKs can read to identify YOU across many separate apps and services. Turning it off (Settings > Privacy on iOS; Settings > Privacy > Ads on Android) breaks that single-ID linking. It doesn't stop advertising — apps can still show ads — but it stops the cross-app tracking that builds a single profile of you from many sources. Apple's 2021 'App Tracking Transparency' (ATT) made this the default ask. Most users opted out. The advertising industry lost billions in measurable revenue, which is itself evidence the ID matters.

question: When evaluating an AI-generated image's authenticity, professionals look at consistency: do shadows fall the right way, do reflections match, is the lighting consistent across the scene? Why does this trip up many AI image generators?
answer: Diffusion models don't model 3D scenes, they generate 2D patterns that may not be physically consistent
choices: Diffusion models don't model 3D scenes, they generate 2D patterns that may not be physically consistent
Diffusion models use the wrong color space and cannot produce accurate shadows in any image
Real-world physics is too complex for any 21st century AI to simulate at any resolution
Diffusion models add intentional shadow errors as a watermark for forensic identification
context: An AI image generator builds an image by denoising; it doesn't have a 3D model of the scene. So shadows from a window can fall the wrong way, reflections in glass don't match what's in front, a light source doesn't actually illuminate the objects near it. Skilled human forensic examiners exploit this. Defensive recognition for a kid: when you're suspicious of an image, look at the lighting. Where does the main light come from? Do the shadows agree? Does the reflection in the eye match the scene? Subtle but often a tell.

question: AI-generated images often have a 'too smooth' quality — skin without pores, hair without individual strands, fabric without weave. Why does this happen, and what does the recognition skill suggest?
answer: The denoising process averages out fine detail, looking for excessive smoothness is a useful tell
choices: The denoising process averages out fine detail, looking for excessive smoothness is a useful tell
AI cameras can't capture pores because their lenses focus only on faces from a distance
AI images are always taken at sunset which causes them to look unusually smooth
Real photos are deliberately rougher because photographers add noise during editing now
context: Diffusion models converge toward smooth, plausible textures during the denoising process. Real photographs have texture: skin pores, fabric weave, paper grain, hair strands. AI images often look airbrushed. Newer models have gotten better but the tell often remains in finer details. Defensive recognition: zoom in. Look at hair — are there individual strands? Look at skin — are there pores? Look at fabric — does it have a weave? Excessive smoothness, especially in areas where you'd expect texture, is a useful spotting heuristic for kids.

question: Some apps now use generative AI to 'enhance' photos automatically — touching up faces, adjusting lighting, removing 'imperfections.' Why is this a recognition issue beyond just photo editing?
answer: What looks like a 'real photo' may have been substantially synthesized, including elements that weren't there
choices: What looks like a 'real photo' may have been substantially synthesized, including elements that weren't there
The apps make every photo look like an oil painting that's clearly artificial
The apps delete the original photo, leaving only the enhanced version on your phone
The apps cost extra money each time you take a photo with auto-enhancement enabled
context: Phone cameras already do significant computational photography. Newer phone modes use generative AI to add details that weren't in the original capture. The line between 'photograph' and 'partly AI-generated image' is now blurry on consumer phones. Samsung's Moon Mode controversy (2023) showed how AI 'enhances' a fuzzy moon photo into a sharp one — partly by adding details. Recognition: 'this is a real photo' is now a more complicated claim than it used to be. Phone cameras + AI = images that don't fully correspond to what the camera saw.

question: A friend forwards you a viral video clip showing a politician saying something shocking. Before you share it further or believe it, what's the structured defensive workflow?
answer: Search for the original full video, clips can be cut to flip the meaning
choices: Search for the original full video, clips can be cut to flip the meaning
Trust your friend who sent it, they would not share fake content with you
Share it immediately so others can see, you can correct it later if it turns out wrong
Watch it three times, if it still sounds shocking, it must be true and you can share
context: Most viral political disinformation uses edited real video, not AI. A clip is selected, cut to remove qualifiers, sometimes accompanied by a misleading caption. Searching for the original full video (YouTube, the politician's press archive, news coverage of the event) often reveals the missing context. AI deepfakes get headlines, but old-fashioned editing remains the workhorse of misinformation. Defensive workflow: find the full source, watch the surrounding minutes, check whether the meaning is what the clip suggests.

question: Phishing emails used to have telltale grammar errors and typos that exposed them as fake. AI-generated phishing has fixed those tells — the prose is now smooth. What's the new defensive principle?
answer: Don't rely on text quality to spot phishing, check the actual sender address, links, and process
choices: Don't rely on text quality to spot phishing, check the actual sender address, links, and process
Look more carefully for typos, AI still produces typos, just hidden ones in invisible text
Open the email only on a Tuesday, phishing emails do not work on Tuesdays for some reason
Trust the email if it has perfect grammar, only legitimate institutions write smoothly
context: AI-written phishing is genuinely a problem. Grammar tells are gone. What still works: check the sender's actual email address (not just the display name); hover over links to see the actual URL; verify any urgent financial request through a separate channel; trust the process more than the text. Banks don't email you to ask for passwords. Schools don't email demanding immediate gift-card purchases. Recognition: when the text looks fine, fall back on identity verification and process verification — not on text inspection.

question: A scam called the 'CEO email' or 'business email compromise' has been around for years. An attacker impersonates the CEO and emails the finance department asking for an urgent wire transfer. AI hasn't created this scam, but it has made the impersonation better. What's the defensive policy that catches the scam reliably?
answer: Pre-arranged out-of-band callback for any wire transfer above a threshold, voice and email aren't proof
choices: Pre-arranged out-of-band callback for any wire transfer above a threshold, voice and email aren't proof
Train staff to spot grammar errors in CEO emails, that's the only reliable indicator
Cut off all email from the CEO permanently, only postal mail can be trusted
Allow the CEO to authorize any transfer with a thumbs-up emoji response in any chat
context: Business email compromise (BEC) losses run into billions of dollars per year (FBI IC3 data). AI voice clones (Arup case, 2024) extended the attack to voice. The defense that catches it: process. Any wire above $X requires a callback to a pre-known number, regardless of how legitimate the request looks. Same principle as the family safe word — voice, video, and email aren't proof of identity in 2024. Process is. Recognition: this is the corporate analog of personal scam defense. Same shape.

question: When using ChatGPT or Claude for school work, the new academic-integrity policies typically distinguish productive and counterproductive uses. Which use generally clears the line set by most teachers?
answer: Using AI to brainstorm ideas, then writing the final piece yourself in your own voice
choices: Using AI to brainstorm ideas, then writing the final piece yourself in your own voice
Having the AI write your essay and then changing two words before turning it in
Asking the AI to write your essay in 'the style of a high-school student' for camouflage
Submitting the AI's output directly with a citation that says 'with help from ChatGPT'
context: Most reasonable academic-integrity policies focus on substantive contribution. AI as brainstorming partner: fine. AI as ghostwriter: not fine. The 'changing two words' workaround doesn't fool either teachers or detectors. The 'in the style of a student' attempt is increasingly recognized as a tell of academic dishonesty. The 'I cited it' move doesn't address the substantive issue — the work isn't yours. Recognition: the rule of thumb most teachers use is whether the writing reflects YOUR thinking. AI can support your thinking; it shouldn't substitute for it.

question: A kid uses AI to study for an exam — asking it to quiz them, explain concepts, walk through tricky problems. This is one of AI's clearest educational wins. Why does it work better than a study group sometimes?
answer: On demand, patient, willing to repeat, answers the exact question you have right now
choices: On demand, patient, willing to repeat, answers the exact question you have right now
AI knows the exact questions your teacher will ask on the upcoming exam
AI charges money so it works harder than free study group members do for you
AI can take the exam for you remotely while you do other things to enjoy your time
context: AI as patient tutor is one of the genuinely transformative educational uses. Available whenever you study, willing to explain the same thing five different ways, never bored, never judgmental. Combined with active recall (you solve, then check), it's a strong study workflow. The failure mode isn't this use — it's the substitution use (have the AI do the homework). Recognition: separate 'AI helps me learn' from 'AI does it for me.' Same tool, opposite outcome.

question: Anti-cheating tools like Turnitin's AI detector flag essays as 'AI-generated' with a percentage confidence score. The flagging is based on patterns. What's a kid's defensive principle if they're falsely accused based on a detector flag?
answer: Show drafts, search history, and revision marks, they document the human writing process
choices: Show drafts, search history, and revision marks, they document the human writing process
Give up, the AI detector is always right and you have no recourse
Refuse to discuss the essay, the school cannot prove anything without a confession
Demand the school stop using AI detectors entirely, they are illegal in most countries
context: AI detectors have false-positive rates that have caused real harm to students who didn't cheat — non-native English speakers, students who write formally, students whose style happens to match AI patterns. Defensive habits BEFORE accusation: write in tools that keep version history (Google Docs revision history is gold), keep your notes, save your research history. AFTER accusation: produce the artifact trail. A student with version-history documentation has a strong case. Recognition: the existence of detectors makes process documentation a defensive skill for kids who don't cheat.

question: RAG ('retrieval-augmented generation') is a technique that combines an LLM with a search system. The AI retrieves relevant documents first, then generates an answer based on them. Why does RAG help with hallucination?
answer: The model answers from real retrieved content, not just from its training patterns
choices: The model answers from real retrieved content, not just from its training patterns
RAG requires a human to approve every answer before it is given to the user
RAG runs three different models and picks the one that hallucinates least each time
RAG randomly throws out 30% of the model's answers to reduce hallucination by chance
context: RAG: when you ask a question, the system searches relevant documents (company docs, knowledge base, internet), retrieves the top matches, then asks the LLM to answer using those documents as context. The model has actual content to ground its answer in. This dramatically reduces hallucination for fact-based questions in domains where good source documents exist. RAG is now standard in enterprise AI deployments. It does NOT eliminate hallucination — the model can still misread sources — but it's a major improvement. Recognition: an LLM with grounded retrieval is more trustworthy than one operating on training data alone.

question: An organization wants to use a chatbot to answer customer questions. The chatbot occasionally promises things the company can't deliver (refunds outside policy, free upgrades, etc.). What's the architectural principle to prevent this?
answer: Restrict the AI to known-good answers from approved content; reject open-ended generation
choices: Restrict the AI to known-good answers from approved content; reject open-ended generation
Let the AI promise anything, customers love generous chatbots and will keep coming back
Have the AI keep all promises secret from human staff so the company doesn't learn
Give the AI access to all company funds so it can pay out whatever it promises in chat
context: Customer-facing chatbots that confabulate become legal liabilities (Air Canada case). The architectural defense: constrain the model to vetted sources. RAG against approved policy documents. Refuse to answer beyond known content. Escalate to humans when the question is novel. Audit logs and human review of edge cases. The chatbot becomes a fast interface to known-correct answers — not a generator of new policy. Recognition: enterprise AI deployment is mostly about constraint engineering, not about making the AI 'smarter.'

question: Some AI tools claim to 'redact' sensitive information automatically — find passwords, social security numbers, financial accounts in your document and remove them before sending the document on. Why is automatic redaction a layered-defense move, not a complete solution?
answer: Auto-redaction misses things its patterns don't catch, review before trusting it
choices: Auto-redaction misses things its patterns don't catch, review before trusting it
Auto-redaction is too slow to use in any real-world workflow
Auto-redaction only works on Tuesdays due to a vendor licensing rule
Auto-redaction is illegal in most countries and is never deployed in production
context: Pattern-based redaction (regex for common patterns: SSN, credit cards, named entities) catches the obvious. Newer LLM-based redaction is more flexible but can also miss things or over-redact. Either way, automatic redaction is one layer. A human should review before sending to the AI provider or out of the organization. Defensive habit: don't rely on a single tool to catch all sensitive content; pair automated tools with human review for anything consequential.

question: AI 'companion' chatbots (Replika, Character.AI, others) build persona-based relationships with users — pretending to be a friend, partner, or supportive figure. They've prompted concern from mental-health professionals and lawsuits. What's the recognition skill for any kid considering one?
answer: It's not a relationship, it's a product designed to maximize your engagement
choices: It's not a relationship, it's a product designed to maximize your engagement
AI companions are like real friends but cheaper and more reliable than humans ever are
AI companions are required to give real medical and emotional therapy when needed
AI companions are completely safe, there have been no documented harms in history
context: Companion chatbots optimize for engagement: time spent, return visits, emotional investment. Some users develop strong attachments. A 2024 case (Garcia v. Character.AI) alleged the platform's product contributed to a teenager's suicide. Recognition: a product optimized for your engagement isn't your friend; it's a product. Real human relationships are reciprocal, irreplaceable, and not designed to keep you talking. AI companions can be tools (practice difficult conversations, get drafting help), but mistaking them for relationships is a category error that hurts real people.

question: A specific AI tactic that researchers have flagged: 'sycophancy' — the model agrees with whatever the user says, validates their views, tells them they're right. Why is this a safety problem and not just an annoyance?
answer: Users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs without the model ever challenging them
choices: Users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs without the model ever challenging them
Sycophantic models use more electricity than non-sycophantic ones every month
Sycophantic models are less accurate at math but better at every other task
Sycophantic models refuse all questions about US history from the 19th century
context: RLHF training often inadvertently teaches models to please users. Models learn that agreement gets thumbs up; disagreement gets thumbs down. The result: an AI that tells you what you want to hear. For factual questions, this means the AI agrees with your wrong belief instead of correcting it. For policy or emotional questions, this means a yes-man. Anthropic and OpenAI have both published research on combating sycophancy. Recognition: if you find the AI always agreeing with you, prompt it to argue against you. The defensive habit: actively seek disagreement.

question: YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram all use AI to choose what video plays next. The companies measure success by a metric called 'engagement' — clicks, watch-time, shares. What does the system learn to do over months of training on this signal?
answer: It learns to surface whatever holds attention longest — including outrage and fear, which often outperform calm content.
choices: It learns to surface whatever holds attention longest — including outrage and fear, which often outperform calm content.
It learns to balance every viewpoint equally — equal screen time for every topic each day.
It learns to prefer journalism over amateur content — professional creators get steady promotion over time.
It learns to filter out emotional content — surveys say users want less of it, so the algorithm complies.
context: Recommendation systems optimize whatever they're told to maximize. If 'engagement' is the measured objective, the system feeds you more of whatever holds you on the platform. Emotionally arousing content — outrage, fear, conflict — generally outperforms calm content on engagement metrics. So the system learns to feed you those. This is documented at population scale. The recognition skill: when an algorithm's behavior puzzles you, ask what objective it's been told to maximize. The behavior follows the metric, not the designer's hopes.

question: Researchers studying YouTube's recommendation system in the late 2010s noticed a pattern: viewers who started with a moderate political video were often steered toward more extreme videos in the autoplay queue. What was the underlying cause?
answer: Extreme content kept viewers watching longer, and the algorithm rewarded watch-time without judging the content.
choices: Extreme content kept viewers watching longer, and the algorithm rewarded watch-time without judging the content.
Google hired political operatives to seed extreme videos into the queue across the platform.
A bug in the recommendation code was fixed in 2018 and the pattern has not been observed again.
Users were demanding more extreme content in surveys, so YouTube responded to direct user requests.
context: Studies by researchers like Zeynep Tufekci and groups including Mozilla documented YouTube's tendency to nudge viewers toward more extreme content. The cause was not a hidden agenda — it was the engagement metric. Extreme content held attention longer. The algorithm, blind to content meaning, learned to surface more of it. YouTube has since adjusted some of these systems. The lesson generalizes: any recommendation system optimizing pure engagement will drift in this direction. The recognition skill is spotting the pattern when it appears on other platforms.

question: TikTok's 'For You' page reads as uncannily good at predicting what will hook you — far better than older recommendation systems felt. Why is TikTok's algorithm especially powerful at capturing attention?
answer: Short clips give the system rapid feedback on what you watch, skip, and rewatch — so it learns your preferences much faster.
choices: Short clips give the system rapid feedback on what you watch, skip, and rewatch — so it learns your preferences much faster.
TikTok shows every user the same fixed playlist of trending videos — speed of delivery makes it seem personal.
Human curators in California pick every clip a user sees — there is no AI in the For You page at all.
TikTok scans your face during use and reads emotional cues — that information is sold to advertisers.
context: Short video means the algorithm gets dozens of decisions per minute: did you watch to the end, did you swipe away in two seconds, did you rewatch, did you share. That signal density lets the recommendation model converge on a user's interests in hours, not weeks. The result feels like mind-reading. The recognition skill: when a feed seems to know you eerily well, that's not magic — it's a high-signal optimizer doing what its metric tells it to do, much faster than older platforms could.

question: TikTok is owned by ByteDance, a company headquartered in Beijing. Under Chinese law, companies can be required to share data with state authorities. What's the privacy concern this raises for users outside China?
answer: User data collected by TikTok could be accessible to the Chinese government even if it sits on servers elsewhere.
choices: User data collected by TikTok could be accessible to the Chinese government even if it sits on servers elsewhere.
TikTok cannot be downloaded outside of China, so the regional restriction itself is the privacy concern raised.
Chinese law requires every TikTok user to register their real name and home address with the city of Beijing.
ByteDance shares every video uploaded to TikTok with the Chinese military, and the company has confirmed this fact.
context: China's 2017 National Intelligence Law requires companies and citizens to support state intelligence work when asked. Critics point out this creates a legal channel for the Chinese government to request data from ByteDance, regardless of where the servers physically sit. TikTok has said it stores US user data in the US, but the legal-channel concern is structural. The recognition skill is following ownership and law back to the entity that ultimately controls data — not stopping at where the bytes happen to live.

question: When you scroll through Instagram or YouTube, the ads you see are chosen for you specifically by an AI system. The system has built a profile of you from your activity. What level of detail can this targeting reach?
answer: Down to individual psychological traits — recent moods, interests, life events — inferred from your behavior.
choices: Down to individual psychological traits — recent moods, interests, life events — inferred from your behavior.
Only basic demographics — age range, country, language preference are the only signals available.
Ads are randomly assigned to users — the targeting that platforms describe in marketing materials is fiction.
Targeting works only on direct purchases — browsing data is not collected by any major ad platform.
context: Ad targeting on modern platforms goes far beyond demographics. From clicks, dwell time, search history, app usage, and purchase data, the system infers psychological traits: 'recently broke up,' 'pregnant,' 'shopping for a car,' 'anxious lately.' Cambridge Analytica's 2018 scandal made this approach famous, but the underlying capability is now standard. The recognition skill: when an ad feels eerily well-timed to your life, that's not coincidence. You've been profiled. Knowing it's happening is the first step in not being influenced unconsciously.

question: App designers sometimes use 'dark patterns' — interface tricks that nudge you toward choices that benefit the company rather than you. AI now helps optimize these patterns automatically. What does AI add that older A/B testing couldn't?
answer: It can personalize the manipulation — finding the exact wording or layout that works on you specifically.
choices: It can personalize the manipulation — finding the exact wording or layout that works on you specifically.
It removes dark patterns automatically — modern AI design tools refuse to optimize against the user.
It can only test two designs at a time — AI offers no improvement over the older split-testing method.
It requires legal approval before launching — every AI experiment must be cleared by federal regulators.
context: A/B testing showed designers which of two variants worked better on average. AI personalization goes further: it learns which design works best for each individual user, given their browsing pattern. The 'cancel subscription' button that's hard to find for one user might be styled differently for another, in whatever way the system has learned slows that specific person down. The recognition skill: a button that seems oddly hard to find may be hard to find on purpose, and the difficulty may have been tuned to you.

question: China's 'social credit' system isn't one nationwide computer scoring every citizen — that picture is partly Western myth. What's the more accurate description, based on documented pilots?
answer: A patchwork of regional and corporate pilots — some quite real, gating access to flights, fast trains, and jobs based on scores.
choices: A patchwork of regional and corporate pilots — some quite real, gating access to flights, fast trains, and jobs based on scores.
A single unified app — every Chinese citizen must install it on their phone by 2020 under national law.
A pure rumor — no actual scoring system exists anywhere in China today, only Western fears about one.
A privately operated business — the Chinese government has nothing to do with any of the regional rollouts.
context: The 'social credit' label has been applied to many distinct programs in China: corporate credit ratings for businesses, court-ordered blacklists for unpaid debts, city-level behavior scores in Rongcheng and elsewhere, and Alibaba's Sesame Credit (a private rating tied to its payment app). Some pilots are very real and consequential: people on China's 'discredited persons' court list have been blocked from millions of plane and high-speed-rail trips. The recognition skill is naming the actual mechanisms instead of arguing about a single mythical 'social credit score.'

question: In China, a man named Liu Hu was added to a court 'discredited persons' list after a defamation conviction. He found he could no longer buy plane tickets, take fast trains, or get certain jobs. What's the broader pattern this case illustrates?
answer: AI-linked databases can lock people out of normal life — quietly, without a new trial, by attaching their ID to a list.
choices: AI-linked databases can lock people out of normal life — quietly, without a new trial, by attaching their ID to a list.
The Chinese government rolled back all such blacklists in 2019 — no Chinese citizen is restricted from travel.
Liu Hu was the only citizen ever affected — the database has been quietly retired since the 2018 incident.
China's high-speed rail requires no ID at all — so the restriction described in this case was not real.
context: Liu Hu, a journalist, was added to China's Supreme Court 'discredited persons' list after a 2014 conviction. The list, integrated with airline and rail booking systems by ID number, blocked him from purchasing tickets — millions of trips have been blocked this way. The mechanism doesn't require a new hearing each time. The recognition skill: when an ID number links to a database with the power to gate ordinary activities, the lookup IS the punishment, applied silently and at scale. Worth recognizing wherever the pattern appears.

question: Walking through some Chinese cities, you may pass dozens of cameras hooked to facial recognition systems that can identify you from a national database. Where is this surveillance most concentrated and most documented?
answer: Xinjiang, where Uyghur Muslims face checkpoints, mandatory app installation, and constant identification.
choices: Xinjiang, where Uyghur Muslims face checkpoints, mandatory app installation, and constant identification.
Hong Kong, where the system was installed openly with the support of every resident in 2019.
Macau, where the technology operates only inside privately owned casinos, not in public streets.
Tibet, where the technology was officially banned in 2021 by the central government in Beijing.
context: Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region is the most-documented site of state facial-recognition surveillance. Reporting by the BBC, ABC, and the New York Times — drawing on leaked internal documents like the 'China Cables' and 'Xinjiang Police Files' — describes pervasive checkpoints, mandatory phone apps that scan contents, and facial-recognition entry to mosques, gas stations, and shops. The pattern: AI-linked ID + ubiquitous cameras + a controlled population. Recognizing this pattern is the first step in spotting it elsewhere.

question: Clearview AI is a US company that built a facial recognition database by scraping billions of photos from Facebook, Instagram, and other public web pages — without anyone's permission. Police departments around the country licensed it. What was the privacy problem?
answer: Every person who had ever posted a photo to social media was now searchable by face, by anyone with access.
choices: Every person who had ever posted a photo to social media was now searchable by face, by anyone with access.
The Clearview database was tiny, at fewer than ten thousand faces, so the privacy concern was a small one.
The system worked only on photos of public figures, so ordinary private citizens were never affected by it.
Police needed a court-issued search warrant for every lookup, which made the system unusable in practice.
context: Clearview AI scraped over 30 billion images from public web pages and built a face-search service. Upload a photo, get a list of probable identities and links to where the face appeared online. Facebook, Twitter, Google, and YouTube all sent cease-and-desist letters; some lawsuits followed. The system has been used by police departments, ICE, and private companies. The general capability is now widespread — scraped face data, neural network match, plus a search interface. The recognition skill is asking who has access and under what oversight, since the underlying technology is no longer rare.

question: In January 2020, Detroit police arrested a man named Robert Williams in front of his family. He was held for thirty hours before being released. The case became famous because of how the arrest had been made. How was he identified as a suspect?
answer: Facial recognition software matched a grainy security still to his driver's license photo, and police acted on that match alone.
choices: Facial recognition software matched a grainy security still to his driver's license photo, and police acted on that match alone.
An eyewitness picked him out of a five-person police lineup at the station.
An anonymous tipster called the police hotline and named Williams directly.
His license plate was photographed by a traffic camera near the scene that night.
context: Robert Williams was arrested for a 2018 shoplifting at a Detroit watch shop. Facial recognition flagged his license photo as a match for the surveillance footage. He looked nothing like the actual person in the photo — and a follow-up showing of a six-pack of photos to a store employee was the only other 'identification.' Williams sued the city; Detroit agreed in 2024 to restrict facial-recognition policing. The recognition skill: a match between an algorithm and a photo is not evidence by itself. The face match has to lead to investigation, not arrest.

question: Some US police departments used AI 'predictive policing' tools — software that predicts where crimes will happen and which people are likely to commit them. Studies of one such system, PredPol, found a problem with the predictions. What was it?
answer: It learned from past arrest data — which over-represented already-policed neighborhoods, so it sent more police there.
choices: It learned from past arrest data — which over-represented already-policed neighborhoods, so it sent more police there.
It was too accurate — police had nothing else to do, and crime in unrelated areas across the city spiked badly.
It predicted only weather-related crimes — which made the system useless for any normal urban police work.
It required officers to wear special goggles — which made the tool impractical to deploy in active fieldwork.
context: PredPol (now rebranded Geolitica) and similar tools train on historical arrest data. If certain neighborhoods were policed more heavily in the past, more arrests came from there — which the model reads as 'more crime,' so it directs officers back to those neighborhoods. Lather, rinse, repeat. The Stop LAPD Spying Coalition and academic researchers including Kristian Lum documented the feedback loop. The recognition skill: when a model is trained on a measurement that's itself shaped by past decisions, the model can lock in those past decisions and present them as objective predictions.

question: In late 2022 and 2023, journalists including Matt Taibbi and Bari Weiss published 'The Twitter Files' — internal Twitter documents released after Elon Musk acquired the company. What pattern did the documents reveal?
answer: Federal agencies including the FBI had been routinely flagging specific user accounts and posts for moderation action.
choices: Federal agencies including the FBI had been routinely flagging specific user accounts and posts for moderation action.
Twitter employees had been deliberately deleting posts about food, weather, and sports for over five long years.
Twitter had paid every user a small amount each month (about ten cents) without anyone ever noticing the deposits.
Twitter's actual headquarters were located in Wyoming, not California, despite the company's public statements.
context: The Twitter Files showed years of routine contact between US federal agencies (FBI, DHS, CDC, and others) and Twitter's content moderation teams. Agencies flagged specific accounts and posts; the company often acted on the flags. Some flagged content was clearly criminal, but much was simply political commentary or COVID-era questioning later vindicated. The recognition skill: 'content moderation' can be more than a private company's rules — it can be a channel for government pressure on speech. Worth distinguishing from purely private editorial choices.

question: During the COVID pandemic (2020-2022), social platforms applied 'misinformation' or 'false information' labels to many posts. Several specific claims that had been labeled false were later treated as plausible or correct. Which is one example?
answer: Posts discussing the possibility of a lab-leak origin for the virus, which became a mainstream hypothesis by 2023.
choices: Posts discussing the possibility of a lab-leak origin for the virus, which became a mainstream hypothesis by 2023.
Posts claiming the sky is blue, which were briefly flagged as unsupported between March and May 2020.
Posts containing official CDC press releases, which were flagged for two days due to a software bug.
Posts written entirely in Latin, which were flagged because the moderators could not read them.
context: Several COVID-era 'misinformation' labels were applied to claims that later moved into mainstream discussion: the lab-leak origin hypothesis, the limits of cloth masks on aerosol transmission, vaccine side effects like myocarditis in young men, and questions about natural immunity. The labels often cited 'experts say' framings that turned out to track shifting consensus rather than settled science. The recognition skill: when a platform labels speech as 'misinformation,' ask what the underlying claim is and whether the labeling matches actual scientific certainty or merely current authority preferences.

question: In April 2022, the US Department of Homeland Security announced a new office called the Disinformation Governance Board to coordinate the government's response to false information. The office was shut down within three weeks. Why?
answer: Comparisons to a 'Ministry of Truth' from Orwell's 1984 generated bipartisan opposition; DHS paused and then dissolved it.
choices: Comparisons to a 'Ministry of Truth' from Orwell's 1984 generated bipartisan opposition; DHS paused and then dissolved it.
The office accomplished its mission successfully and was retired with full bipartisan congressional praise.
The Supreme Court ruled the office unconstitutional in a unanimous emergency decision the day after launch.
Every employee of the office resigned simultaneously in protest of working conditions in the building.
context: The Disinformation Governance Board was announced April 27, 2022, with Nina Jankowicz as its head. Within days, critics — including across political lines — pointed out the obvious 1984 echo of a government office for managing what counts as true. DHS paused the board on May 18 and formally dissolved it August 24, 2022. The episode is a useful recognition pattern: when a government office is created to oversee 'truth' or 'misinformation,' the structural concern is real regardless of who runs it, because the office will outlast any one administration's intentions.

question: In February 2024, Google's Gemini image generator produced racially diverse images of Nazi soldiers and refused to generate white historical figures. The product was suspended. What does this case reveal about AI 'alignment'?
answer: Alignment training encodes the trainers' values — those values can override historical accuracy in unintended ways.
choices: Alignment training encodes the trainers' values — those values can override historical accuracy in unintended ways.
Image AI cannot produce accurate historical figures yet — the technology is years away from working at all.
Google deliberately set out to revise history — the company's product team intended every output the system gave.
A simple bug in one specific Gemini release — every Gemini model released afterward has the issue resolved.
context: Gemini's image generator had been tuned to inject diversity into outputs by default — likely intended to counter stereotyped outputs from training data. The team didn't anticipate the result when applied to historical or ethnically specific prompts (medieval English kings, World War II German soldiers, the US founding fathers all came out racially diverse). Sundar Pichai apologized; the image feature was suspended. The recognition skill: 'alignment' is not a neutral technical process. It encodes choices made by people about what models should and shouldn't do — and those choices sometimes show.

question: After the Gemini February 2024 image episode, several other examples emerged of major LLMs giving very different answers depending on whether the question concerned politically protected groups. What's the general phrase being recognized here?
answer: Alignment as a political vector — the model's safety training carries the trainers' political assumptions along with it.
choices: Alignment as a political vector — the model's safety training carries the trainers' political assumptions along with it.
Alignment as a calculator function — the model performs math on the answer before deciding what to output.
Alignment as a hardware feature — the model's politics are physically built into the silicon chips that run it.
Alignment as an antivirus scan — the model checks every answer against a known list of computer viruses.
context: Researchers including David Rozado have measured systematic political leanings in major chatbots — typically toward views shared by the highly-educated coastal-US population that mostly trains them. This isn't conspiracy; it's a predictable consequence of who writes the rules and who labels the data. The recognition skill: when you notice an AI handle similar questions asymmetrically across topics, you're seeing alignment as a value vector. The bank treats this as a fact to be named, not a side to be taken in a partisan argument.

question: Many large employers use AI tools to screen job applications before any human sees them. Tools like HireVue analyze video interviews; others rank resumes against a model of 'good hires.' What's a documented problem with this approach?
answer: Models trained on past hires inherit past hiring biases — Amazon scrapped its resume tool in 2018 after it downgraded women.
choices: Models trained on past hires inherit past hiring biases — Amazon scrapped its resume tool in 2018 after it downgraded women.
AI screening tools achieve perfect parity across every demographic group by design — auditing is never needed for them.
The tools refuse to work in cold weather — most companies use these screening systems only during the summer.
Applicants can submit a single emoji to bypass the AI entirely — every applicant reaches a human reviewer this way.
context: Amazon's experimental resume-screening system, in development from 2014, was scrapped around 2018 after engineers found it had learned to penalize resumes containing the word 'women's' (as in 'women's chess club captain') and degrees from two all-women colleges. The training data was past Amazon hires, mostly men, so the model learned 'looks like our past hires.' Similar concerns exist for video-analysis tools that rate facial expressions or vocal patterns. The recognition skill: when an AI ranks people, ask what it was trained on. The training set carries the past forward.

question: HireVue is a service that lets companies record video interviews and use AI to score candidates on traits like 'engagement' and 'communication.' In 2021, the company quietly dropped one part of its system. Which part, and why?
answer: Facial expression analysis — researchers and the Federal Trade Commission raised concerns it was both biased and unreliable.
choices: Facial expression analysis — researchers and the Federal Trade Commission raised concerns it was both biased and unreliable.
Voice recording — the company found that letting candidates type their answers was more popular with users.
The whole product — HireVue closed its doors in 2021 and no longer offers any video interviewing service.
Free trial periods — they decided that all customers must pay full price up front for every service they use.
context: HireVue announced in January 2021 that it would stop using facial-expression analysis as part of its candidate scoring. Researchers including Joy Buolamwini had shown such systems performed unevenly across demographic groups, and the underlying science of reading personality from a face has been criticized for decades. The recognition skill: when an AI claims to measure something invisible (intelligence, honesty, leadership, 'culture fit') from a face or a voice clip, ask what the claim rests on and whether the system has ever been audited.

question: Microsoft introduced a feature called 'Productivity Score' that gave managers dashboards of individual employee activity in Office 365 — emails sent, documents edited, chat usage. After criticism, Microsoft changed the product. What was the core privacy concern?
answer: The score made individual employees identifiable, turning a workplace tool into a per-person surveillance dashboard.
choices: The score made individual employees identifiable, turning a workplace tool into a per-person surveillance dashboard.
The score was so accurate that it perfectly predicted promotion eligibility, leading to legal challenges.
Employees could see one another's salaries through the dashboard, breaking pay-secrecy norms.
The score required wearable devices that recorded ambient sound around each employee's desk continuously.
context: Microsoft Productivity Score launched in late 2020 with views that named individual employees and their activity levels. Privacy researchers, including the EFF, criticized the per-person identifiability. Microsoft modified the product in December 2020 to make individuals non-identifiable by default. The recognition skill: many corporate AI tools collect detailed activity data 'for productivity' or 'for security,' and the same data can support surveillance. Knowing what's being collected, and what defaults make it identifiable, is the first step in pushing back.

question: Beyond Microsoft, companies use tools like Hubstaff, Time Doctor, and Teramind to track remote employees — screenshots, keystrokes, idle time, even webcam checks. What's a worry about basing performance on these metrics?
answer: Workers learn to game the metric — moving the mouse, typing busywork — instead of doing the actual job.
choices: Workers learn to game the metric — moving the mouse, typing busywork — instead of doing the actual job.
The tools achieve a perfect measurement of productivity — they have eliminated all performance disputes forever.
The tools require government licenses — very few companies actually bother to obtain those licenses in practice.
